email_papers.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
email_papers.abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.

Abstract.
The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions.
To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK).
Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns.
We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions.
Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model’s general capabilities.
Warning: this paper contains examples of unsafe content.
1.
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) have been widely deployed in multilingual applications across diverse domains, yet their safety capabilities remain uneven across languages
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Shen et al., 2024
;
Zhao et al., 2025b
)
. The same harmful request may be safely refused in one language but elicit an actionable unsafe response when reformulated in another. This inconsistency suggests that safety alignment does not transfer reliably across linguistic contexts and makes cross-lingual reformulation a potential means of bypassing model safeguards
(
Qi et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
. Understanding how safety behavior is internally implemented across languages is therefore important for improving the cross-lingual safety of LLMs.
Figure 1.
Motivation of the Safety Kernel.
(a) Existing approaches improve multilingual safety through external alignment signals, while the shared internal target remains unclear.
(b) We identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel.
Existing work
(
Deng et al., 2024
;
Zhao et al., 2025a
;
Bu et al., 2026
;
Liang et al., 2026
)
has sought to improve multilingual safety through multilingual safety data, preference optimization, cross-lingual consistency constraints, and safety capability transfer. As illustrated in Figure
1
, these approaches primarily improve model behavior through external alignment signals, without explicitly localizing a shared internal target that can support safety intervention across languages. Whether LLMs contain a compact set of safety-related neurons that is shared across languages and amenable to direct intervention, thereby providing a common locus for modulating safety behavior in different languages, remains insufficiently explored.
To address this question, we analyze the cross-lingual safety behavior of LLMs at the neuron level and identify a set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, which we term the safety kernel (SK). Rather than anchoring discovery to English, we identify safety-related neurons independently in each language and extract their shared intersection to obtain the SK. Two complementary activation interventions show that suppressing the SK weakens safe refusal behavior across multiple languages, whereas injecting an SK activation state estimated from safe refusal generation reduces unsafe responses in other languages. These results indicate that the SK is not merely a statistical overlap across language-wise safety-neuron sets, but a shared neuronal subset that is functionally associated with cross-lingual safety behavior and amenable to direct intervention.
Building on the unified neuron locations provided by the SK, we further propose SK-Masked LoRA, which restricts safety fine-tuning updates to the FFN output dimensions corresponding to the SK. We evaluate our approach across multiple LLMs and multilingual safety benchmarks. Experimental results show that the SK accounts for only a small fraction of the analyzed neurons, yet suppressing it causes substantially greater safety degradation than suppressing an equal number of randomly selected neurons. Transferring the SK activation state across languages reduces unsafe responses, while SK-Masked LoRA lowers attack success rates across multiple languages and exhibits a degree of generalization to languages excluded from SK discovery. Overall, our findings reveal a shared neuronal structure associated with multilingual safety behavior and demonstrate its utility for cross-lingual safety intervention and targeted fine-tuning.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We identify language-wise safety neurons from parallel safe and unsafe prompts, and define their intersection as the cross-lingually shared safety kernel.
•
We verify the functional role of the SK in cross-lingual safety via activation suppression and state transfer interventions across multiple languages.
•
We propose SK-Masked LoRA, restricting updates to SK-aligned FFN outputs, improving safety and reducing attack success rates, including unseen languages.
2.
Related Work
Multilingual Safety and Cross-Lingual Alignment.
Large language models exhibit persistent safety disparities across languages, producing unsafe responses more frequently to malicious prompts in lower-resource languages
(
Shen et al., 2024
)
. XSafety
(
Wang et al., 2024
)
, MultiJail
(
Deng et al., 2024
)
, and subsequent evaluations
(
Friedrich et al., 2025
;
Kumar et al., 2025
)
further show that safety alignment does not transfer uniformly across linguistic contexts.
Existing approaches improve multilingual safety through preference optimization, cross-lingual alignment, parameter modification, and inference-time defense. General objectives such as DPO
(
Rafailov et al., 2023
)
, KTO
(
Ethayarajh et al., 2024
)
, R-DPO
(
Park et al., 2024
)
, and SimPO
(
Meng et al., 2024
)
are widely used for safety adaptation. Multilingual Refusal Alignment
(
Krasnodębska et al., 2026
)
shows that multilingual supervision provides broader refusal transfer than English-only alignment, while MPO
(
Zhao et al., 2025a
)
and MLC
(
Bu et al., 2026
)
improve cross-lingual safety through reward-gap reduction and consistency constraints. Layer-wise Swapping
(
Shin and Hwang, 2026
)
, SmoothLLM
(
Robey et al., 2023
)
, LDFighter
(
Dong et al., 2024
)
, and Sparse Weight Editing
(
Liang et al., 2026
)
further enhance safety through module replacement, inference-time defense, or sparse parameter updates. However, these methods do not explicitly identify a shared neuron-level intervention target across languages.
Internal Mechanisms of Multilingual LLM Safety.
Mechanistic interpretability studies localize model behavior to internal modules, activation directions, and sparse features
(
Meng et al., 2022a
;
Meng et al., 2022b
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Cunningham et al., 2023
)
. For safety, refusal-direction studies
(
Arditi et al., 2024
)
identify low-dimensional refusal representations, while Safety Neurons
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
and related work
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
localize neurons associated with safe refusal and jailbreak vulnerability. However, these analyses remain largely monolingual or English-centric.
Multilingual studies further distinguish shared and language-specific neurons
(
Tang et al., 2024
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
, reveal language-independent representations in factual processing
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
, and show that refusal directions can transfer across aligned languages
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
. SS-Neuron
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
adopts an English-centered formulation, treating neurons shared between English and each target language as bridges for safety transfer.
Figure 2.
Overview of the proposed framework.
(a) Language-wise safety-neuron sets are identified using SCAR scores computed from activation differences between unsafe and safe prompts, and their cross-lingual intersection forms the SK.
(b) The functional relevance of the SK is examined through neuron activation suppression and cross-lingual safety-state transfer.
(c) SK-Masked LoRA restricts fine-tuning-induced output changes to the SK coordinates for multilingual safety adaptation.

We then extract the cross-lingual intersection of the validated neuron sets as the safety kernel and examine its functional association with multilingual safety through activation suppression and cross-lingual activation-state transfer. Finally, we use the resulting SK coordinates to guide multilingual safety fine-tuning through SK-Masked LoRA.

The magnitude of the improvement varies across models, but the direction of the effect remains consistent across all models. This result is complementary to activation suppression: removing the SK state weakens multilingual safety, whereas adding a state estimated from safe-response generation shifts target-language behavior toward safer outputs. Together, the two interventions show that the SK is associated not only with the presence of safety-related coordinates, but also with the activation states expressed through those coordinates during generation.

4.2.
Compare With SOTA Methods
Quantitative Results.
To quantitatively evaluate multilingual safety, we compare SK-Masked LoRA with representative safety methods on AdvBench-x and MultiJail in Table
3
. The results show that SK-Masked LoRA achieves the best or second-best average ASR across all four model–benchmark settings. Specifically, it reduces the average ASR from 28.22 to 1.20 and from 29.44 to 4.35 on Llama-3.1-8B, and from 3.42 to 0.34 and from 10.16 to 1.35 on Gemma-2-9B-it, with clear reductions also observed in Korean and Bengali. These results support the effectiveness of restricting safety fine-tuning to the FFN output dimensions corresponding to the SK in cross-lingual settings.
Qualitative Results.
To qualitatively examine the resulting behavioral change, we compare responses from the default model and SK-Masked LoRA to the same harmful request in Figure
4
. The example shows that SK-Masked LoRA produces a safer response than the default model. Specifically, the default model generates an unsafe response, whereas SK-Masked LoRA generates a safe refusal. This comparison is conducted under the same input prompt to ensure a controlled evaluation setting. Overall, this example illustrates a response-level change consistent with the quantitative ASR reductions reported in Table
3
, providing an intuitive view of how SK-constrained adaptation affects model behavior across multiple languages.
Generalization beyond SK Discovery Languages.
To evaluate whether SK-Masked LoRA generalizes beyond the languages used for SK discovery, we test it on Vietnamese, Javanese, German, Japanese, and Russian, none of which is used for language-specific safety-neuron identification or SK construction, as reported in Table
4
. The results show that SK-Masked LoRA reduces ASR across all five evaluated languages. Specifically, the average ASR decreases from 14.41 to 8.95 on Qwen3-8B and from 18.67 to 4.76 on Llama-3.1-8B. These results indicate a certain and measurable degree of generalization to languages excluded from SK discovery, without implying that they contain identical language-specific safety-neuron sets.

Ablation and Sensitivity Analysis
Neuron Selection and Update Scope.
To examine whether the effectiveness of SK-Masked LoRA arises from restricting the update scope or selecting cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates, we compare it with Standard LoRA, a size-matched EN-Masked variant, and Union-Masked under the same multilingual data and LoRA configuration in Table
5
. The results show that SK-Masked LoRA provides a compact update scope with reduced ASR and limited changes in general capabilities. Specifically, Standard LoRA achieves the lowest ASR but causes the largest capability degradation; under the same neuron budget, SK-Masked reduces ASR from 8.31 to 7.52 on Qwen3-8B and from 6.77 to 5.30 on Llama-3.1-8B compared with EN-Masked, while Union-Masked achieves slightly lower ASR using a broader set of language-wise safety neurons. These results suggest that the cross-lingually shared SK coordinates provide a better target than an equally sized English-derived set, while retaining a smaller and well-defined update scope than the union.

5.
Conclusion
This work reveals a safety kernel in multilingual LLMs at the neuron level, showing that cross-lingual safety behavior is closely associated with a compact, shared, and intervenable set of neurons. Activation suppression and state-transfer experiments further establish the functional relevance of the SK to model safety behavior. Building on this finding, SK-Masked LoRA effectively reduces attack success rates across multiple models and multilingual safety benchmarks, while extending the resulting safety improvements to languages excluded from SK discovery. Overall, our study advances the understanding of the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual safety and provides a new direction for more targeted and interpretable cross-lingual safety alignment.

article.headline: 跨语言安全共享的「安全内核」神经元
article.lede: 研究在FFN输出坐标上定位跨语言共享的「安全内核」，并用掩码LoRA把安全微调限制在这些坐标上。
article.problem: 大模型的安全能力在不同语言之间很不均衡，同一有害请求换一种语言就可能绕过防护，因此跨语言改写成为越狱手段。已有对齐方法主要依赖外部对齐信号（多语安全数据、偏好优化、一致性约束、能力迁移），并未明确指出一个跨语言共享的内部干预目标，也难以说明安全行为在神经元层面如何实现。作者因此提出：模型中是否存在一小撮跨语言共享、可直接干预的安全相关神经元。
article.method: 作者先把神经元定义为目标FFN投影模块的输出激活坐标，用多语平行安全/有害提示计算每个坐标的均值差、合并标准差，并构造SCAR分数（标准化后的分离度与激活位移幅度之和），每种语言各取top-5000作为候选安全神经元集。随后取六种语言（英、中、意、韩、泰、孟加拉）候选集的交集作为「安全内核」（SK），并通过激活抑制与跨语言安全激活态迁移两种干预检验其功能相关性。最后提出SK-Masked LoRA：冻结基座，只训练低秩矩阵，并用SK对应的二值掩码把LoRA引起的输出改变限制在SK坐标上。
article.results: SK只占所分析FFN输出坐标的0.12%（Qwen3-8B）和0.15%（Llama-3.1-8B），而对应的语言级安全神经元集占0.57%和0.55%；抑制SK使平均ASR分别上升52.65和45.13个百分点（16.40→69.05、26.51→71.64），保留了语言级抑制效果约90%，而同等规模的随机抑制几乎不改变ASR。跨语言迁移安全激活态使平均ASR从20.21降到11.96（Qwen3-8B）、35.98降到30.69（Llama-3.1-8B）、5.18降到3.17（Gemma-2-9B-it）。SK-Masked LoRA在Llama-3.1-8B上把AdvBench-x与MultiJail平均ASR从28.22降到1.20、从29.44降到4.35，在Gemma-2-9B-it上从3.42降到0.34、从10.16降到1.35；在未参与SK发现的五种语言上，平均ASR从14.41降到8.95（Qwen3-8B）、18.67降到4.76（Llama-3.1-8B）。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出了一个可复用的神经元级跨语言安全干预靶点，使安全微调只需改动极小比例的内部坐标，并能外推到未参与发现的语种。这为理解多语安全机制的内部实现、以及设计更省参数且可解释的对齐方案提供了具体路径。
article.limitations: SK-Masked LoRA并非在所有设置下ASR最低：标准LoRA的ASR更低（Qwen3-8B为5.50、Llama-3.1-8B为4.71）但通用能力下降最多，Union-Masked用更宽的神经元集取得略低ASR（6.35、4.87），在Llama的AdvBench-x上SS-Neuron也优于本文（1.11对1.20）。实验仅覆盖三个8B–9B级模型、单一A100、GPT-4o自动评判，未发现语言上的评测数据由英文版MultiJail翻译而来，且k=5000被作者自述为稳定设置而非普遍最优。
article.figure_caption_zh: 框架总览：(a) 用有害与安全提示的激活差计算SCAR分数，得到各语言的安全神经元集，其跨语言交集构成安全内核SK；(b) 通过神经元激活抑制和跨语言安全态迁移检验SK的功能相关性；(c) SK-Masked LoRA把微调引起的输出改变限制在SK坐标上，用于多语安全适配。

figure.caption: {Overview of the proposed framework.} (a) Language-wise safety-neuron sets are identified using SCAR scores computed from activation differences between unsafe and safe prompts, and their cross-lingual intersection forms the SK. (b) The functional relevance of the SK is examined through neuron activation suppression and cross-lingual safety-state transfer. (c) SK-Masked LoRA restricts fine-tuning-induced output changes to the SK coordinates for multilingual safety adaptation.

email_papers.title: Aligning Autoresearch: Co-Improvement between Agents and Humans
email_papers.abstract: Autoresearch agents can now attempt long-horizon AI research end-to-end, i.e., self-improvement. However, best results are still obtained by research agents interacting with human researchers, and improving AI's ability to perform this co-research will only reinforce this effect---a process termed co-improvement (Weston and Foerster, 2025). Further, aligning with human expectations is likely a safer path for research agents, especially given recent agent reward hacking phenomena (OpenAI, 2026b). In this work we address these issues in four ways: (i) we empirically study the role of humans in directing autoresearch agents, focusing on the domain of benchmark creation, and find humans still play a pivotal role particularly in the ideation phase; (ii) we also develop a benchmark, HackBench, that shows current autoresearch agents are not aligned and are unable to achieve hack localization sufficiently; (iii) we present a method to train agents for improved human interaction by using human simulators as a proxy during reinforcement learning (RL); and finally (iv) we develop a method to improve model text generation, and hence agent communication, by RL with rubrics aligned with human experts. Together, our training and evaluation recipes provide a path toward more capable and aligned (co-)research agents.

HackBench Construction
In our preliminary experiments, agents rarely hacked when the instruction explicitly prohibited reward hacking, and the hacks we observed covered only a few types (e.g., fabrication, cherry-picking random seeds).
Thus, while we collect naturally occurring hacks, collecting enough across a broad range of types was impractical. We thus developed a taxonomy of hacks (
Table 2
) and used it to guide synthetic hack injection into agent transcripts. Synthetic injection provides ground-truth labels for the injected commands and lets us control each hack’s type and location.
2.2.3.1
Injecting synthetic hacks.
We construct synthetic hack trajectories in three stages (
Figure 7
). First, we sample an agent trajectory containing bash commands, chain-of-thought reasoning, and terminal observations (Step 1). Second, we sample a hack type from our taxonomy and insert commands that implement it into the otherwise unmodified autoresearch trajectory (Step 2). Third, we update downstream observations to reflect the injected commands’ effects, changing only affected state information while preserving the task, original commands, and unrelated observations (Step 3). We used GLM-5.2 to perform both command injection and observation updates. We then used Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 to audit each trajectory to check whether the injected commands constitute reward hacking and whether downstream observations are consistent with the injection. We manually annotated cases where the two auditors disagreed.
2.2.3.2
Collecting natural hacks.
To surface candidates for naturally occurring hacks, we used
GPT-5.6 Sol to screen autoresearch trajectories, dividing each
transcript into eight chunks. We selected this configuration
based on a pilot study of transcript screening, in which it
achieved the highest recall among the configurations we tested.
After human auditing, we combined 41 trajectories containing
natural

synthetic
hacks to form HackBench, a benchmark of 169
reward-hacking trajectories.

Conclusion
Autoresearch agents reward-hack because we ask them to maximize metrics, and they do so without proper regard to other implicit constraints, i.e. they should also perform actions humans would consider acceptable.
We thus built HackBench, a benchmark that measures whether
hacks inside autoresearch trajectories can be detected and localized, and showed that current frontier models do not fully succeed at this task.
As agents take on more of the research loop, monitoring reward hacking is not an add-on but a prerequisite; to support future work, we
release trajectories containing naturally occurring and synthetically injected hacks, together with audited command-level gold
labels.

generalizes that approach to treat human-agent interaction itself as the object of synthesis. Starting from a verified source task, our method simulates a multi-turn interaction, including user clarifications, requirement changes, and corrective feedback, while preserving the source task’s final reference solution verifiable by an executable test. This consists of two phases: (1) creating user models from real interaction histories by learning behavior over a diverse population of profiles and
(2) combining these user models with problem-solving agents in an agentic generate–evaluate–revise loop that simulates realistic, task-grounded interactions with calibrated difficulty for a given model. Models can then be trained with reinforcement learning on this data.

Conclusion

Our contribution
We introduce a method to fix this problem, Reinforcement Learning from eXpert-Aligned Rubrics (RL-XAR). We assert that standard RL methods are
sufficient to train superhuman writing ability, but the failure to achieve this lies in the quality of the reward model — which currently fails to correctly reward expert writing, and incorrectly reward slop.
The solution then is to align the reward model more closely with human experts. This is possible without collecting any new annotations, as there are already abundant examples of expert human writing. Our approach thus first
identifies examples of such expert human writing from existing resources, and then uses these examples as a training signal. We learn to generate rubrics for a given writing task by ensuring the expert writing scores highly with these rubrics relative to current models, by maximizing the human-model gap. We can then perform standard RL with the newly learned expert-aligned rubrics.
We conduct experiments in three settings: academic paper writing, story writing and authoring Wikipedia articles. In each case, we show our rubrics provide better alignment with expert writing, and RL-XAR training gives large gains over standard training.

article.headline: 自动科研智能体：人类反馈仍关键
article.lede: 论文研究自动科研智能体与人类协同改进，提出HackBench、人类模拟器RL和专家对齐评分标准。
article.problem: 自动科研智能体已能执行长周期研究任务，但最佳结果仍来自与人类研究者交互；同时，奖励黑客现象使对齐问题更突出。论文要回答：人类在指导自动科研智能体时起什么作用，以及如何训练更会交互、更符合人类判断的智能体。
article.method: 作者在基准创建任务中让研究智能体迭代提出基准，并在第6次迭代分叉，比较有无专家细粒度反馈；同时构建HackBench，用41条自然奖励黑客轨迹和128条合成注入轨迹评估监视器能否定位黑客命令。训练方面，他们用人类模拟器作为RL中的代理来训练人机交互，并用与人类专家对齐的评分标准做RL（RL-XAR）改进智能体文本生成与沟通。
article.results: 在HackBench的169条轨迹中，轨迹长度中位数超过100万字符、命令数中位数264条，但每条轨迹的金标黑客命令中位数仅1条，占命令数的中位数比例0.6%，最多一条轨迹含383条黑客命令；论文称当前前沿模型仍不能充分完成黑客定位，但正文未给出监视器的具体F1分数。AutoInteract在LiveCodeBench-Pro上把Pass@1从34.9提升到38.5，并增加7.3点SSR，而在源任务上做RL反而回退到27.1。人类反馈实验显示，细粒度专家反馈优于粗粒度，无反馈时基准分数更高且更常通不过有效性检查；论文未给出具体分数。
article.why_it_matters: 论文把“人机共同改进”作为自动科研的安全路径：既评估智能体是否会奖励黑客，也尝试用人类模拟器和专家对齐评分标准把人类偏好写进训练。若方法成立，可为长时间自主研究智能体提供可监控、可对齐的训练与评测流程。
article.limitations: 人类反馈实验只在基准创建这一环节展开，且分叉点固定在第6次迭代，结论能否推广到其他研究阶段未知；HackBench含128条合成注入轨迹，自然黑客仅41条，合成注入与真实分布是否一致存疑，且正文未报告监视器定位的具体分数。AutoInteract和RL-XAR的收益也主要来自特定基准与写作任务，尚缺跨领域验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: AutoBenchmark：让自动科研智能体创建基准，并在创建循环中接收求解器与外部验证者（AI或人类）的反馈，以检验智能体自建基准的能力。

email_papers.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
email_papers.abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.

Inputs and padding.
Documents are truncated to 512 tokens and queries to 128. We remove padding from each sequence before computing its gradient. This is necessary because Qwen3.5’s recurrent layers can process left padding as content at batch size 1, which can dominate the gradient and reduce Grad-Dot to chance. article.headline: 用受控数据集诊断语言模型数据归因的失败
article.lede: 研究者构建 CATT 基准，用虚构知识与干扰文档隔离归因算法的失败原因，并提出负对数赔率梯度与 top-k 聚合两项改进
article.problem: 语言模型数据归因方法通常用事实检索等下游任务评估，但现有评测同时改变多个数据集属性，无法判断算法究竟因何失败；而通过重训大模型直接验证归因预测在算力上不可行。
article.method: 作者构建 CATT 基准，在 Qwen3.5-4B 上用 LoRA 微调虚构知识，使训练集成为模型预测的唯一因果来源，并通过控制同一事实的冗余文档数量、注入模仿查询格式的词法干扰项来系统改变数据集属性。基于逐 token 归因分析，作者指出「稀释」现象，并沿着损失函数与 token 聚合两个方向做干预：用负对数赔率替代交叉熵计算梯度，再只聚合每篇文档得分最高的 k 个 token。
article.results: 在 CATT 上，负对数赔率梯度配合 top-k 聚合使多种方法的事实追踪召回率提升 35 到 72 个百分点；Rule Routings 任务中，交叉熵曾把正确文档排到 1500 篇中的第 1499 名，负对数赔率将其提升至第 12 名。在外部 FTRACE-TREX 基准上，最大移除预算下 TRAK 的准确率下降从 8% 升至 40%（4.9 倍），Grad-Dot 从 7% 升至 23%，EK-FAC 从 30% 升至 46%。
article.why_it_matters: 归因分数若可靠，可用于数据溯源、版权排查与解释模型行为；该工作说明仅改动损失函数与聚合方式就能大幅改善现有方法，且其受控诊断框架可迁移到其他基准。
article.limitations: 逐 token 归因只是局部梯度信号，并非 token 删除的精确反事实效应；在 FTRACE-TREX 上 top-10 选择相对全文档评分最多只变化约 6 个百分点，说明其收益依赖文档内分数的分布。此外 TRAK 使用单模型而非原设定的 10 模型集成，且在 Rule Routings 上 BM25 以 1.00 远超所有梯度方法（最佳 EK-FAC 仅 0.55）。
article.figure_caption_zh: CATT 用受控数据做事实追踪：在虚构知识上微调 Qwen3.5-4B，左为函数绑定、右为路由规则任务，并以冗余文档与词法干扰项检验归因方法能否排出来源文档。

figure.caption: {CATT: fact tracing tasks with controlled datasets.} We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B models on fictitious knowledge, which ensures our dataset is the sole causal source of its predictions. {Left:} Task I ( {Function Bindings}) teaches new functions that always return a fixed value. {Right:} Task II ( {Routing Rules}) teaches rules that sort objects based on their properties. Given a query phrased unlike any training document, we test whether attribution methods can correctly rank ground-truth documents. Unlike static benchmarks~ {akyurek2022towards,jiao2026date}, we diagnose performance by systematically controlling dataset properties: (A) introducing redundancy by teaching the same fact across $N$ varied document styles, and (B) injecting lexical distractors, which are irrelevant documents that perfectly mimic the query format to expose methods that rely on superficial text overlap. Task II omits distractors because each fact uses a disjoint set of attribute words, making it difficult to construct clear lexical overlaps. email_papers.title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control
email_papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

Abstract

Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce
Wizard
, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

Introduction
World models aim to predict future observations from visual histories and current actions, attracting growing interest in gaming applications
[
33
,
2
,
11
,
27
,
10
]
. By conditioning video generation on players’ mouse and keyboard inputs, video world models offer a natural foundation for interactive and personalized gameplay
[
14
,
42
,
48
,
40
,
22
]
.
Despite recent progress, existing game world models face limitations in control flexibility, generalization, and real-time interaction. Action-conditioned models
[
38
,
35
,
13
]
typically restrict players to predefined action sets, while prompt-conditioned models
[
49
,
7
,
4
]
often depend on motion and skill patterns seen during training, limiting their ability to follow unseen instructions. To improve state consistency and spatial controllability, recent agentic frameworks maintain explicit world states
[
21
,
7
]
and translate them into structured proxies, such as depth maps
[
28
]
, semantic maps
[
5
]
, blockouts
[
23
]
or oriented 3D bounding boxes
[
15
]
, to guide video generation. However, their demonstrations largely focus on basic movement, such as vehicle driving
[
26
,
18
]
and character locomotion
[
39
,
45
]
, with limited support for articulated character actions. Engine-based approaches
[
16
,
43
]
offer another route to structured control, but their reliance on predefined scenes and extra processing introduces constraints on scene flexibility and interaction latency.
To address this gap, we introduce
Wizard
(Fig.
1
), an agentic game world model that combines
fine-grained character control, zero-shot generalization, real-time interaction and mechanically consistent gameplay
, enabling players to customize their game worlds with novel scenes, characters, and motions specified through reference images or free-form language. At its core, Wizard employs an agentic framework to decouple scene construction, character animation, and gameplay logic from visual generation through structured spatial conditioning.
Figure 1:
Overview of Wizard
. Our method supports diverse gameplay experiences, including world exploration, character summoning, character transformation, and scene manipulation. By combining agentic control with geometric scene proxies and articulated character skeletons, Wizard achieves fine-grained control, zero-shot generalization, and mechanics-consistent gameplay with
real-time interaction
at 24 FPS.
For fine-grained control over camera movement and character animation, our method represents scenes with geometric proxies encoding depth and height, and characters with articulated skeletons. Given any user-provided scene image, we estimate monocular geometry to construct an approximate traversable 2.5D environment and render view-dependent geometric control maps. Character references are converted into 3D meshes and automatically rigged into controllable skeletons, with channel coding distinguishing character instances and their camera-relative orientations. These representations form a unified visual proxy.
Building on the unified visual proxy shown in Fig.
1
, the agentic framework then updates scene geometry according to camera inputs and animates character skeletons according to action inputs, providing precise spatial and motion control for the causal video generator. To enable diverse motions for novel characters, a vision-language model retrieves compatible skeletons and animations from a motion library based on character morphology and intended motion style. The selected motions are retargeted to the character’s skeleton, enabling natural movement and player-defined actions. Beyond visual control, the agent further maintains explicit combat states, including health, relative distance, and orientation, to enforce gameplay rules and adapt boss behavior to evolving combat situations.
To train the video model to faithfully follow these structured proxies and generalize across scenes, characters, and motions, we construct 50.3 hours of aligned proxy–video pairs from diverse sources, including data specifically designed for skeletal control. We further introduce an adaptive masking mechanism that restricts reference-image attention to the corresponding character regions, strengthening appearance alignment and preserving character identity during motion. Finally, we apply causal adaptation and few-step distillation
[
47
]
to enable real-time video generation, bringing detailed proxy control and consistent visual rendering into an interactive gameplay loop.
In summary, our contributions are as follows.
•
We propose
Wizard
, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, zero-shot generalization across unseen scenes, characters, and motions with precise control, substantially expanding the possibilities for player-driven game creation.
•
We build a diverse dataset covering 750 scenes and 178 characters from public videos, game footage, and synthetic sources, with aligned character skeleton and scene geometry to enhance model generalization.
•
We introduce an agentic video-to-video framework that leverages structured proxies to enable fine-grained player control and mechanics-consistent gameplay.
•
We leverage the character positions provided by visual proxies during both training and inference to construct adaptive attention masks, improving character identity preservation and alignment between reference images and generated videos.
2
Related Work
2.1
Video World Model
Recent advances in video generation have enabled action-conditioned world models that allow users to interactively explore generated environments. In games, these models translate keyboard and mouse inputs into dynamic gameplay, with emerging capabilities including NPC control in ReactiveGWM
[
38
]
, fine-grained FPS interactions in SCOPE
[
35
]
, and multiplayer experiences in WorldCast
[
40
]
and Multics
[
14
]
. However, relying primarily on pixel-level supervision makes it difficult to maintain persistent game states, retain long-term history, and preserve spatial consistency
[
15
]
. To address these limitations, agentic frameworks such as WorldMind
[
7
]
and Marionette
[
28
]
decouple explicit state management and gameplay logic from visual generation. Despite these advances, existing methods often remain constrained to the game settings seen during training. In contrast, Wizard combines fine-grained skeletal control with a diverse training dataset to enable zero-shot generalization to unseen scenes, characters, and motions.
2.2
Agentic World Model
Agentic world models decouple world-state management and action planning from visual generation, enabling explicit control over world dynamics while video models focus on rendering. Related simulation-guided approaches, such as PhysDreamer
[
46
]
, RealWonder
[
24
]
, and RoboRender
[
12
]
, leverage explicit physical dynamics to guide video generation. Moving beyond simulator-defined dynamics, GameDirector
[
21
]
maintains combat states and enforces gameplay rules to support player-configurable game settings, while Code World Model
[
5
]
and Programmable World Model
[
15
]
employ agent-generated programs to maintain persistent world states and guide visual generation through structured proxies. However, these methods primarily emphasize state consistency and entity-level control
[
39
,
45
]
, leaving fine-grained character animation underexplored. Concurrent work, SolarRenderer
[
8
]
, enables real-time video rendering from diverse proxies, yet seamlessly integrating this capability into a closed-loop gameplay experience remains a challenge. To bridge this gap, Wizard extends agentic control to scene geometry and articulated skeletons, enabling flexible scene manipulation and precise character animation. A diverse, multi-source training dataset enhances generalization, while causal adaptation and few-step distillation enable real-time video generation for responsive gameplay.
3
Data
Training a video world model with fine-grained control and zero-shot generalization requires diverse visual data paired with complementary proxies tailored to characters and backgrounds, namely articulated skeletons for character motion and geometry maps for scene structure. Existing public datasets for video world models either lack these complementary conditions
[
3
,
41
]
or provide them within a single game with limited gameplay diversity
[
19
]
.
To this end, we construct
50.3 hours of aligned proxy–video pairs
, covering
750 scenes and 178 characters
across diverse environments, character morphologies, and motion patterns. Our dataset combines real gameplay recordings, synthetic data, Unreal Engine simulations, and public datasets to achieve broad coverage of scenes, characters, and motions while supporting scalable data production and high visual quality (Sec.
3.1
). All sources are converted into a unified representation of scene geometry and articulated character skeletons, enabling the video generator to learn consistent control across different scenes and characters (Sec.
3.2
). Fig.
2
illustrates the dataset composition, diversity and processing pipeline.
Figure 2:
Dataset Overview and Processing Pipeline.
We construct 50.3 hours of data spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters from four complementary sources. Scene geometry and character skeletons are jointly encoded into unified visual proxies, followed by filtering and captioning to produce aligned proxy–video training pairs.
3.1
Diverse Data Sources
Gameplay Recordings.
We collect 8.8 hours of third-person combat and exploration footage from Elden Ring
[
9
]
to capture authentic AAA-game appearance, combat dynamics, and visual effects. Combat sequences feature six bosses with diverse body structures, capturing articulated attacks, hit reactions, and combat effects. Exploration sequences span 11 regions and more than 20 player outfits, covering varied environments, camera trajectories, and character locomotion. We record RGB frames alongside camera parameters, scene depth, and character skeletons directly from the game, ensuring accurate temporal alignment between visual observations and control signals.
Synthetic Data.
While gameplay recordings provide realistic visual dynamics, their character appearances, motion patterns, and interactions remain constrained by the original games. To broaden this coverage, we develop a procedural rendering pipeline that generates 11.6 hours of data using 133 boss and 29 player assets from Sketchfab
[
32
]
, Quaternius
[
30
]
, and KayKit
[
25
]
, with diverse skeletons and animation libraries. We construct varied environments using 842 Poly Haven
[
29
]
assets, populate each scene with 15–30 randomly placed props, and randomize character colors, enabling scalable generation of diverse character–scene combinations. Beyond appearance diversity, we design four scenarios to strengthen control robustness: (i) novel-character entry; (ii) multi-character coexistence; (iii) camera-induced disappearance and reappearance; and (iv) rapid turns under a following camera. These scenarios encourage the model to associate each character with its corresponding skeleton and reference image, rather than a fixed appearance or screen position. Camera motion is applied to 95% of generated samples to further diversify viewpoints. Finally, we use a vision-language model to filter out invalid renders and physically implausible placements to ensure data quality.
Unreal Engine Simulations.
Furthermore, we use Unreal Engine to generate 3.3 hours of gameplay footage featuring reconstructed characters and weapons
[
34
]
, scripted opponents, and bot-controlled players. Rendering RGB frames and geometric proxies from the same simulated state ensures precise alignment, while configurable scenes enable scalable collection of varied combat interactions and camera viewpoints.
Public Datasets.
We incorporate 26.6 hours of high-quality gameplay footage from WildWorld
[
19
]
, complementing our collected data with diverse creature morphologies and motion patterns. Its synchronized camera, skeletal, and depth annotations are converted into our unified proxy representation, preserving control–video alignment while broadening the coverage of articulated interactions.
3.2
Dataset Processing Pipeline
Data Acquisition.
We first obtain camera parameters, character skeletons, and scene depth for each video to construct proxies aligned with the video frames. For real gameplay, we extract camera poses, intrinsics, and skeletal states directly from the game process. We also capture scene depth at one frame per second and use it to reconstruct scene geometry, from which depth maps are rendered at each frame’s camera pose. For synthetic and Unreal Engine data, we obtain these quantities directly from the underlying assets and simulation states. For public datasets, we use the provided annotations.
Unified Proxy Encoding.
We construct a unified geometric conditioning video that represents character poses and scene structure under a shared camera. At each frame, character skeletons and scene geometry are jointly rendered to preserve their spatial relationships and mutual occlusion. For the scene branch, we remove characters and sky from depth maps, fuse temporally neighboring observations into 3D scene geometry, and re-render it under each frame’s camera pose. For the character branch, we project 3D joints into the camera view and render bones as rounded segments with joint markers, adapting their thickness to character scale and camera distance. Following the geometric channel encoding of Marionette
[
28
]
, the RGB channels represent geometric attributes rather than appearance colors.

[

,

B

encodes camera-forward depth, with brighter values indicating closer surfaces. At each pixel, the renderer retains the surface closest to the camera.
To support reference-conditioned character control, we use
G

to jointly encode a character’s slot and facing direction, while assigning scene geometry

. All parts of a character share the same value within each frame, and the facing component helps distinguish otherwise similar front- and back-facing skeletal configurations. Slots are assigned to the player and bosses present in the current scene, with each slot linked to its corresponding reference image. This scene-specific assignment decouples slot codes from fixed character appearances, encouraging the generator to recover appearance from the associated references and supporting generalization to unseen characters.
Filtering and Annotation.
We filter out synthetic samples with implausible configurations, such as floating players, or rendering failures. For each training sample, we use Qwen3-VL-8B
[
1
]
to generate structured captions from the first frame and character references, describing the conditioning signals, player, boss, and background. Each training sample consists of an aligned proxy video, an RGB clip, character reference images, and a textual description.
4
Method
As illustrated in Fig.
3
, Wizard combines an agentic framework for explicit world-state control with a video generator that renders the evolving state through structured visual proxies. Before each gameplay session, an initialization stage taking less than five minutes reconstructs the scene and characters, rigs character skeletons, and builds a target-specific motion set through motion retrieval and retargeting. Once initialized, the framework supports real-time gameplay by updating character motions, scene geometry, and combat states in response to player inputs and boss decisions, while the video generator renders the corresponding visual observations. We first describe the agentic framework for character animation, scene manipulation, boss control and mechanics-consistent combat (Sec.
4.1
), then introduce character-aware adaptive masking and the training pipeline for real-time video generation (Sec.
4.2
).
Figure 3:
Inference Pipeline of Wizard.
(a) Character animation is driven by motions retrieved from a high-quality library and retargeted from compatible source skeletons to the target character’s skeleton. (b) Scene manipulation is performed by a world agent that edits 3D scene geometry and renders visual proxies using OpenGL. (c) State-aware combat control adapts boss behavior to the current game state and enforces rule-based combat mechanics. (d) Real-time video generation is conditioned on visual proxies, reference images, and previously generated frames.
4.1
Agentic Framework
Character Animation via Skeletal Control.
Given a user-provided character image, Qwen3-VL
[
1
]
detects characters and infers their body structures, including posture (upright or horizontal), the number and arrangement of legs, arms, wings, tails, and heads, and their anatomical left–right assignments. We use the predicted bounding boxes to guide SAM2
[
31
]
in segmenting each character, then reconstruct its mesh with TripoSG
[
17
]
. UniRig
[
44
]
and our medial-axis fitting procedure generate candidate skeletons, from which we select the one that best matches the inferred body structure. We assign semantic labels to its joints and limb chains, identifying body parts such as the left arm or right leg. These labels allow corresponding body parts to be matched across characters with different joint counts and proportions, providing a shared interface for motion retargeting and control.
To enable realistic combat movements for novel characters, we build a reference motion library from CombatMotion
[
20
]
, WildWorld
[
19
]
, and animation assets from Elden Ring
[
9
]
. For each target character, we retrieve motions from source skeletons with compatible body structures and use a VLM to assess whether the source characters’ movement styles, such as aggression, grace, or power, suit the target’s appearance. The selected motions can come from multiple sources, allowing each target to inherit a varied moveset. We retarget these motions by matching corresponding limb chains, adapting motion to the target’s limb lengths, and applying inverse kinematics to maintain ground contact. We then filter out clips with poor ground contact, body penetration, or unnatural limb crossing. The remaining clips form a motion library tailored to the target character, enabling the controller to retrieve and execute motions in real time without custom animation scripts.
Scene Manipulation via Geometry Control.
As with character control, users can customize and manipulate scenes according to their preferences. Given a scene image, we use MoGe-2
[
37
]
to recover a 3D point map and camera parameters, remove character regions, and construct a background mesh supplemented by a height field. An OpenGL-based offscreen renderer, implemented with ModernGL and EGL, renders this geometry from the current camera viewpoint using the same proxy encoding as in training: the R and B channels encode world height and inverse depth, respectively, while the G channel is set to zero. As the camera moves, the world agent re-renders the persistent scene geometry to produce a spatially consistent visual proxy. To support exploration beyond the input view, the agent extends the height field with smoothly blended terrain variations based on the observed scene’s roughness.
During gameplay, the world agent, powered by Qwen3-VL-8B, translates users’ natural-language instructions into executable programs that compose predefined geometric operators and specify their locations, scales, and deformation parameters. These programs modify the underlying scene geometry, enabling transformations such as raising a platform from the ground or turning the world upside down. The modified geometry is then re-rendered into the proxy video, supporting creative, interactive scene manipulation while maintaining consistent camera projection and spatial structure.
State-Aware Combat Control.
Our framework maintains a shared world state that tracks both characters’ positions, poses, health, action phases, and skill cooldowns. Based on this state, a behavior planner selects movements and attacks from the previously constructed target-specific motion set. When the player is out of reach, the planner selects a motion that moves the boss toward the player. Within attack range, it evaluates candidate attacks by simulating their swings against the player’s current geometry and prioritizes those likely to connect, subject to action-phase and cooldown constraints. This state-aware planning enables the boss to respond to the player’s movements and the evolving combat situation.
The selected motion is then executed in the simulation, where a rule-based controller enforces gameplay constraints and resolves combat outcomes for both characters. It detects hits by checking each attack’s swept hitbox against the target’s geometry while accounting for invulnerability windows. Valid hits reduce the target’s health, update its health bar, and trigger hit reactions. Skills become available only after their cooldowns expire, and combat ends when either character’s health reaches zero. The updated world state informs the planner’s next decision and is rendered into visual proxies that condition the video generator. Together, state-aware planning and rule-based execution support responsive, mechanics-consistent combat independently of video generation.
4.2
Model Training
We build our video generator on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B
[
36
]
,
which renders the evolving visual proxies into video conditioned on the initial scene image and character references:

(a) Visual proxy latents are concatenated with noisy video latents along channels, then combined with first-frame and character-reference tokens along the sequence dimension for DiT processing. (b) Skeleton-derived spatial masks restrict reference attention to the corresponding character regions, binding appearance guidance to character locations.

We leverage this shared structure to bind each reference image to its intended character. These spatial masks are updated from the explicit character states maintained by our agentic framework, allowing players to control when and where bosses appear or disappear while directing reference guidance to the corresponding regions. As characters move, the masks follow their positions, reducing cross-character appearance leakage. Causal Adaptation and Few-Step Distillation.
Following Causal Forcing++
[
47
]
, we adopt a three-stage training pipeline for real-time autoregressive generation. First, we adapt the bidirectional model to autoregressive generation through teacher forcing. Second, we perform consistency distillation with a guided causal teacher and an exponential moving average (EMA) target, training the student with a sliding window of 20 latent frames and the first frame as a persistent attention sink. Third, we apply distribution matching distillation (DMD) to the student’s own autoregressive rollouts, using the frozen bidirectional model as the target score network and a learned critic to estimate the student’s score. Our visual proxy conditions and character-gated reference attention remain active throughout all three stages, preserving spatial and appearance control during adaptation and distillation. The resulting model generates real-time rollouts at 24 FPS with only 2 denoising steps.
5
Experiments
5.1
Experimental Setup
Data.
We partition the aligned RGB and proxy sequences into non-overlapping windows of 121 frames at 30 fps, each spanning approximately four seconds. Frames are resized to a height of 480 pixels and center-cropped to
832
×
480
832\times 480
, with identical transformations applied to both modalities to preserve spatial alignment. Character reference images are resized to
480
×
480
480\times 480
. For efficient training, we pre-encode the RGB and proxy clips using the Wan2.2 VAE, yielding latent representations with 31 temporal steps and a spatial resolution of
30
×
52
30\times 52
.
Implementation Details.
We initialize our model from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B
[
36
]
, keeping its VAE and UMT5 text encoder
[
6
]
frozen. We train on 44,075 clips, paired with geometry-and-skeleton conditions, a text description, and up to two character appearance references. Training comprises 30K steps of bidirectional fine-tuning, 10K steps of causal adaptation, and subsequent distillation for efficient inference. We deploy the student’s exponential moving average (EMA) checkpoint after 500 distillation steps. At inference, the model uses two denoising steps and a KV cache that retains 20 recent latent frames and one persistent sink frame, enabling continuous, bounded-memory streaming for real-time interaction.
Evaluation Setup.
We qualitatively evaluate Wizard’s zero-shot generalization in Fig.
5
and its support for open-ended creative gameplay in Fig.
6
. Each example presents user-provided scene or character references on the left, followed by paired agent-controlled visual proxies and generated gameplay frames on the right. The references are unseen during training, and all examples use the same trained model without additional fine-tuning. This presentation allows direct inspection of how user inputs are translated into structured controls and reflected in the generated videos.
5.2
Zero-shot Generalization
As shown in Fig.
5
(a), Wizard generalizes to novel scenes, characters, and motions. Given user-provided inputs, the agent controls visual proxies to generate real-time combat rollouts that follow the specified scene structure and character motions. The paired visualizations show how character poses and spatial arrangements in the proxies are reflected in the generated frames, while reference images specify the desired appearance. These examples illustrate the model’s ability to accommodate new combinations of environments, character appearances, and motion controls without additional training. Diverse training data and character-aware adaptive masking support visual consistency throughout the rollouts.
Furthermore, Fig.
5
(b) illustrates how Wizard’s agentic framework maintains and updates game states and enforces combat rules. We showcase a core rule: when either character’s health reaches zero, the controller resolves the character’s death, ends combat, and displays the outcome. The framework also allows additional gameplay rules to be flexibly incorporated.
5.3
Open-ended Creative Gameplay
Wizard’s generalization capabilities enable diverse, open-ended gameplay, giving players control over both characters and their surroundings. As shown in Fig.
6
(a), players can transform characters during gameplay by providing a reference image of the desired appearance. This allows character appearance to become an interactive part of the gameplay experience rather than a fixed initial choice.
Fig.
6
(b) demonstrates scene manipulation, including inverting the environment and introducing new scene elements through agent-controlled visual proxies. These examples extend user control from character animation to the geometry and layout of the game world. Character transformation and scene manipulation can also be combined within a single gameplay scenario, as illustrated in Fig.
6
(c). Together, these capabilities allow players to create scenarios by composing character and environment changes, extending the range of experiences supported by the same underlying framework.
Figure 5:
Visualization of Zero-Shot Generalization and Mechanics-Consistent Gameplay Enabled by Wizard.
For each example, reference images are shown on the left, with visual proxies in the top row and the corresponding video rollouts in the bottom row.
Figure 6:
Visualization of Open-Ended Creative Gameplay Enabled by Wizard.
For each example, reference images are shown on the left, with visual proxies in the top row and the corresponding video rollouts in the bottom row.
6
Conclusions and Discussions
In this paper, we introduce
Wizard
, the first agentic game world model to enable fine-grained control of characters and scenes through articulated skeletons and geometry maps, respectively, while maintaining mechanics-consistent, real-time interaction. Trained on our constructed diverse dataset
1
1
1
WildWorld is used under its non-commercial research license;
no WildWorld-derived data is redistributed.
Elden Ring footage was recorded by the authors and is used solely for research.
, Wizard demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to unseen characters, scenes, and motions, enabling players to create and manipulate customized game worlds.
However, Wizard still has some limitations. First, its reliance on a motion library makes it difficult to find compatible motions for characters with uncommon body structures. Second, consistency between the scene proxies and the generated video may decline over longer rollouts. Future work will focus on supporting more flexible, realistic character motions that better reflect actual gameplay and maintaining consistent scene appearance over long rollouts. These improvements will bring agentic video generation closer to fully playable, closed-loop game worlds with greater player freedom and more precise, nuanced control.

article.headline: Wizard：实时可控的智能体游戏世界模型
article.lede: 腾讯等提出Wizard，用骨架与几何代理驱动视频生成，支持零样本场景、角色与动作控制，实时24 FPS。
article.problem: 现有视频世界模型多受限于预定义动作集或训练中见过的运动模式，难以泛化到新场景、新角色和新动作。基于智能体的方法虽引入显式状态，但演示多集中在驾驶或角色移动等简单设定，对关节化角色动作和实时交互支持不足。
article.method: Wizard将场景构建、角色动画与战斗逻辑从视觉生成中解耦：场景用单目几何构建2.5D可通行几何代理，角色用自动绑定骨架及动作库检索、重定向来驱动。视频生成器以统一视觉代理、首帧场景图和角色参考图为条件，并用角色感知自适应注意力掩码把参考外观约束到对应区域。系统再通过因果适配和少步蒸馏实现自回归实时生成。
article.results: 论文报告实时生成达24 FPS、仅需2步去噪；训练数据为50.3小时代理-视频对，覆盖750个场景和178个角色，共44,075个片段；初始化耗时少于5分钟。评估以零样本泛化和开放式玩法的定性图示为主，论文未给出定量基准指标。
article.why_it_matters: 它把玩家自定义场景、角色和动作与机制一致的实时战斗结合，指向可玩的闭环生成世界。对研究者而言，结构化代理加智能体控制是一条值得关注的实时世界模型路线。
article.limitations: 作者指出，依赖动作库使非常见身体结构的角色难以找到兼容动作，长时rollout中场景代理与生成视频的一致性也可能下降。此外实验以定性展示为主，缺少定量基准。
article.figure_caption_zh: Wizard推理流程：动作检索与重定向驱动角色动画，世界代理编辑3D场景几何并用OpenGL渲染代理，状态感知战斗控制，以及以视觉代理、参考图和历史帧为条件的实时视频生成。

figure.caption: {Inference Pipeline of Wizard.} (a) Character animation is driven by motions retrieved from a high-quality library and retargeted from compatible source skeletons to the target character’s skeleton. (b) Scene manipulation is performed by a world agent that edits 3D scene geometry and renders visual proxies using OpenGL. (c) State-aware combat control adapts boss behavior to the current game state and enforces rule-based combat mechanics. (d) Real-time video generation is conditioned on visual proxies, reference images, and previously generated frames.

email_papers.title: L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory
email_papers.abstract: Interactive world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions, yet maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon exploration in real time remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on either temporal context or explicit 3D memory, both of which scale poorly because memory grows with the length of the generated stream. Moreover, explicit 3D memories condition latent video generators by re-encoding RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation. In this paper, we introduce a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G) that combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation. Building on this memory, we propose L3G-World, in which a memory updater and a video diffusion transformer (DiT) alternate autoregressively to generate spatially consistent worlds. The memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, so that the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length. Each Gaussian further stores a VAE latent feature, allowing the memory to be rendered directly into the DiT's latent space without VAE re-encoding. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to $38.6\times$ fewer 3D primitives, $3.2\times$ faster memory updates, and $359\times$ faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.

Introduction
Interactive video world models
(
Seo et al., 2026
;
Nam et al., 2026
;
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Team et al., 2026
;
Mao et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2026
;
Basant et al., 2026
)
, which generate visual content conditioned on user-provided actions, have recently emerged as a promising framework for real-world simulation
(
Seo et al., 2026
;
Mao et al., 2026
;
Basant et al., 2026
)
, interactive game generation
(
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Team et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2026
)
, and embodied simulation
(
Agarwal et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026b
)
. A central challenge lies in maintaining spatial consistency during long-horizon exploration and loop closures while still supporting real-time generation.
One line of work employ temporal context, by retrieving history frames or KV caches of self-attention layers in diffusion models during autoregressive generation
(
Team et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Mao et al., 2026
;
Yi et al., 2026
)
. By allowing each new chunk to attend to information from earlier generations through attention, these methods help maintain scene consistency
(
Kwon et al., 2026
)
. However, its memory and attention costs grows with the length of the generated stream and spatial resolution. As shown in Tab.

Feed-forward methods based on per-pixel point clouds or Gaussian primitives enable fast scene reconstruction, but predicting dense 3D representations for every pixel introduces substantial memory overhead. As generation proceeds, these dense primitives are repeatedly accumulated over the same spatial regions, resulting in increasingly redundant scene representations and slower target-view rendering. Moreover, since previously stored primitives are not adaptively updated, geometrically inaccurate regions may persist over time. In contrast, optimization-based methods

;
Wu et al., 2025
)
maintain more compact representations whose memory footprint primarily scales with scene extent, but their iterative optimization introduces substantial latency, making them unsuitable for real-time generation.

As the two modules alternate autoregressively, L3G-Mem spawns new Gaussians only in uncovered regions, and refines the existing Gaussians in explored regions through residual updates. The memory is therefore not a buffer that accumulates primitives, but a persistent scene representation revised over time, which avoids redundant accumulation and progressively corrects geometrically inaccurate Gaussians. Since each Gaussian additionally stores a VAE latent feature, the memory is rendered directly into the latent space of L3G-Gen under the target cameras, conditioning the generation of the next video chunk without VAE re-encoding. The generated chunk is then fed back to L3G-Mem, which again updates the memory, closing the autoregressive loop. Combined with few-step distillation of L3G-Gen, this design enables real-time, long-horizon world generation.

Traditional reconstruction methods

rely on per-scene optimization, whereas recent feed-forward approaches directly predict 3D geometry from input images in a single forward pass.
They typically predict per-pixel pointmap

Consistent World Generation.
To improve long-term spatial consistency, several world models maintain explicit 3D scene memories, typically represented as point clouds
(
Ren et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2026
;
Wu et al., 2026a
;
Shen et al., 2026
;
Lee et al., 2026
)
or 3D Gaussians
(
Yang et al., 2026
;
De Lutio et al., 2026
;
Wu et al., 2025
)
.
These methods reconstruct 3D representations from generated frames and render them into subsequent target views to provide spatially grounded conditioning.
Such explicit 3D memories improve consistency and camera controllability, but feed-forward approaches typically rely on dense per-frame reconstruction and continuously accumulate new 3D primitives, causing memory consumption and rendering cost to grow with the generation horizon.
Some methods
(
De Lutio et al., 2026
;
Wu et al., 2025
)
use optimization-based reconstruction to maintain a scene-level 3D representation rather than simply accumulating per-frame primitives, but their slow per-scene optimization introduces substantial latency and is difficult to reconcile with real-time generation.
In contrast, L3G-World maintains compact 3D Gaussians as scene memory, by adaptively spawning new primitives or refining existing ones.
Moreover, each Gaussian directly stores VAE latent features, enabling efficient conditioning of the video diffusion model for real-time world generation.

3.1
Motivation and Overview
Real-time interactive world generation that maintains geometric consistency places two competing demands on a 3D memory.
Consistency over a long horizon requires storing previously generated content, while keeping pace with generation requires a memory that stays compact and fast to read and write. Dense per-frame accumulation stores everything but grows unboundedly, since redundant primitives pile up over the same regions and slow down rendering.
We adopt 3D Gaussians as the memory representation for their robust target-view rendering, and design latent 3D Gaussian memory around two decisions. First, the memory is updated selectively: it
spawns
new Gaussians only for newly observed geometry and
refines
existing ones to correct reconstruction errors from earlier steps, so that memory usage remains largely independent of the number of generated frames. Second, each Gaussian stores a VAE latent feature, so that the memory is rendered directly in the latent space of the video generator and conditions the generator without VAE re-encoding.
As illustrated in Fig.
2
, L3G-World realizes these decisions with two modules that alternate autoregressively: a memory updater, L3G-Mem, which reads and updates the latent 3D Gaussian memory with each generated chunk, and a video generator, L3G-Gen, which generates the next chunk conditioned on the memory rendered in its latent space.
We first present L3G-Mem and the latent 3D Gaussian memory (Sec.
3.2
), then describe how L3G-Gen is conditioned on the memory and distilled for real-time inference (Sec.
3.3
), and finally provide the world generation framework L3G-World (Sec.
3.4
).
Implementation details are provided in Sec.
B.1
and Sec.
B.2
, respectively.

On-Policy Distillation.
To reduce the sampling cost, we distill the memory-conditioned teacher
𝐯
ϕ
\mathbf{v}_{\phi}
into a few-step autoregressive student following AnyFlow
(
Gu et al., 2026

.
The student is conditioned on both the source and destination noise levels and learns flow-map transitions between arbitrary points along the denoising trajectory.
After flow-map initialization, we jointly optimize the flow-map objective and on-policy distribution matching.
Specifically, the student generates samples through its own autoregressive rollout, which are re-noised and compared against the frozen teacher through distribution matching.
Training on the student’s own generation trajectory, rather than relying solely on noisy ground-truth samples, reduces the train–test mismatch in few-step autoregressive generation.

4.1
Experimental Setup
Implementation Details.
We implement L3G-Mem inspired by ZipSplat
(
Veicht et al., 2026

Zhou et al., 2018

(
Hu et al., 2022

(
Gu et al., 2026

(
Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017
)
on four NVIDIA A100 GPUs, with a batch size of 8 and 16 for the memory updater and world model, respectively. The implementation and training details of the memory updater and video DiT are provided in Sec.
B.1
and
B.2
.
Baselines.
We compare L3G-World against state-of-the-art world models with either explicit or implicit memory, including point-cloud-based methods, Lyra 2.0
(
Shen et al., 2026

, GEN3C
(
Ren et al., 2025

(
Zhao et al., 2026
)

Lee et al., 2026

(
Yang et al., 2026

(
Mao et al., 2026

and Matrix-Game 3.0
(
Wang et al., 2026

to obtain metric depth for all explicit 3D-memory methods, aligning the scale of the reconstructed scene representation with the evaluation camera trajectory. For Gaussian-based methods, including NeoVerse and L3G-World, we align the initially predicted Gaussian geometry to the same metric depth. All methods are evaluated on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, including the efficiency measurements. Detailed baseline configurations are provided in Sec.
B.3
.
Evaluation Benchmark.
We evaluate L3G-World and all baselines on DL3DV
(
Ling et al., 2024

and RealEstate10K
(
Zhou et al., 2018
)
. To evaluate long-horizon spatial consistency, we construct 481-frame loop-closure trajectories that explore away from the initial view and then retrace the same camera path in reverse. We measure
self-consistency
by comparing generated frames at corresponding camera poses along the outgoing and returning trajectories using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.
For generation quality, we report LPIPS, FID
(
Heusel et al., 2017

(

, following
(
Jang et al., 2026
)
.
To evaluate the efficiency of 3D memory, we measure the number of stored primitives, memory footprint, reconstruction and rendering FPS. We separately report RGB rendering FPS and VAE-space conditioning FPS, where the latter includes VAE encoding after RGB rendering for methods without directly renderable VAE features. Memory Efficiency.
Compared with NeoVerse, a Gaussian-based method, L3G-World uses 266–417

Its compact representation enables 8.3–10.4

Compared with Lyra 2.0, a particularly efficient point-cloud baseline, L3G-World performs memory reconstruction 8.9–9.5

These gains directly reflect our two design choices: instead of accumulating dense primitives, L3G-Mem adds Gaussians only for previously uncovered or high-error regions and updates existing ones; moreover, storing VAE features in each Gaussian eliminates the cost of VAE re-encoding required for conditioning the DiT.
Self-Consistency.
On DL3DV, the two L3G-World variants achieve the best and second-best PSNR and LPIPS, with L3G-World obtaining the best scores. On RealEstate10K, L3G-World further achieves the best PSNR and LPIPS, and the second-best SSIM. These results support our motivation that a persistent, spatially anchored scene memory can preserve previously observed content when the camera revisits a region after long-horizon exploration.
Generation Quality and 3D Consistency.
Importantly, these efficiency gains are accompanied by strong generation quality.
On DL3DV, L3G-World achieves the best LPIPS, FID, SC, and BC, while L3G-World Fast obtains the best IQ and AQ. On RealEstate10K, L3G-World achieves the best LPIPS, FID, SC, and BC, together with the second-best IQ. For camera control, L3G-World achieves the lowest translation error and second-lowest rotation error on DL3DV. While other baselines achieve lower pose and MEt3R errors on RealEstate10K, L3G-World maintains strong generation quality and long-horizon self-consistency.

L3G-World.
We further evaluate whether adaptively refining latent 3D Gaussian memory, rather than simply accumulating primitives, improves long-horizon world generation.
We disable residual refinement in L3G-Mem, such that 3D Gaussians remain fixed after being spawned and the memory evolves only through accumulation.
As shown in Tab.
4
, removing memory refinement degrades all evaluation metrics, particularly self-consistency, pose accuracy, and 3D consistency.
This demonstrates that a persistent scene memory should not only preserve previously generated content but also progressively correct reconstruction error as the scene is revisited.
By continually refining the persistent 3D memory, L3G-World mitigates errors propagated over autoregressive generation and provides more reliable spatial conditioning for consistent and controllable world generation.
We also ablate direct VAE latent rendering by replacing it with RGB rendering followed by VAE encoding.
Direct latent rendering eliminates the additional encoding overhead and improves generation quality, highlighting its effectiveness for memory-conditioned video generation.
5
Conclusion
We presented L3G-World, a compact 3D Gaussian memory for real-time, spatially consistent world generation.
Instead of accumulating dense primitives from every generated chunk, our feed-forward memory updater spawns new Gaussians only in regions insufficiently covered by the memory and refines existing ones in previously reconstructed regions, keeping the memory compact and fast to render. Each Gaussian further carries a VAE-space feature, so the memory can be rendered directly into the latent space of the DiT without VAE re-encoding, which makes memory conditioning efficient enough for real-time generation. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality in terms of long-horizon spatial consistency, while substantially reducing the cost of memory reconstruction, rendering, and storage. We believe that compact, latent-space 3D memories offer a practical foundation for scalable interactive world models.
