B.2
Video Diffusion Model Details
B.2.1
Teacher Model
Architecture.
We build the teacher model on Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B
(
Ali et al., 2025
)
.
The pretrained DiT backbone is kept frozen, while LoRA adapters, the UCPE
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
camera-conditioning branches, and the widened input projection are trained.
For memory conditioning, the noisy video latent is channel-concatenated with the VAE feature rendered from the current latent 3D Gaussian memory, together with its validity mask and conditioning indicator.
We additionally retrieve up to three previously observed latents according to camera-pose proximity and provide them as clean reference tokens.
Training.
We train the teacher using rectified flow matching on DL3DV
(
Ling et al., 2024
)
and RealEstate10K
(
Zhou et al., 2018
)
.
The anchor frame is provided as a clean image latent and excluded from the denoising loss, while the remaining target latents are jointly denoised with full bidirectional attention.
During training, we randomly drop text and reconstruction conditioning and vary the number of retrieved reference latents to improve robustness to different conditioning configurations.
The teacher is fine-tuned with rank-16 LoRA adapters
(
Hu et al., 2022
)
together with the UCPE modules and input projection.
Inference.
At inference, the teacher generates one 81-frame clip at a time using 35 denoising steps with classifier-free guidance
Ho and Salimans (2022)
.
After each generated clip, the reconstructed scene memory is updated from the generated observations and rendered under the cameras of the next clip.
Reference latents are retrieved only from the generated history, and the final generated frame is used to initialize the following clip.
B.2.2
Student Model
Architecture.
The student retains the same backbone, reconstruction conditioning, reference conditioning, and UCPE camera modules
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
as the teacher, but converts the bidirectional DiT into a chunk-causal autoregressive model.
Each training clip is divided into short latent chunks, and the current chunk attends to compressed long-term history, retrieved reference latents, and the most recent full-resolution chunks.
Older history is spatially compressed, while the two most recent chunks remain at the original latent resolution.
At inference, the corresponding keys and values are cached independently for the standard self-attention and UCPE attention branches.
Flow-Map Distillation.
We first initialize the student through flow-map distillation following AnyFlow
(
Gu et al., 2026
)
.
Unlike the teacher, which predicts the instantaneous denoising velocity at a single noise level, the student is conditioned on both the source and destination noise levels and learns transitions between arbitrary points along the denoising trajectory.
Training combines standard diffusion, direct consistency, and intermediate flow-map transitions.
We initialize the student from the teacher and increase the LoRA rank to 128, while preserving the teacher initialization for the shared camera and reconstruction-conditioning modules.
On-Policy Distillation and Inference.
We further train the student with on-policy distribution matching using samples generated from its own autoregressive rollouts.
A frozen teacher provides the real-data score, while a trainable copy of the teacher estimates the student distribution, and the flow-map objective
(
Boffi et al., 2024
)
is retained during this stage for stable optimization.
At inference, the student generates three latent frames per autoregressive step using 4 denoising steps without classifier-free guidance.
The generated latents are continuously added to the reference pool and periodically used to update the latent 3D Gaussian memory, which is then rendered to provide reconstruction guidance for subsequent chunks.
B.3
Baselines
Depth and Scale Alignment.
Our evaluation considers a single-image-to-video setting, where the explicit 3D-memory baselines
(
Ren et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2026
;
Wu et al., 2026a
;
Shen et al., 2026
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
must initialize their scene representation from a single input image. This introduces a scale ambiguity between the monocularly reconstructed 3D scene and the metric camera trajectory used for evaluation, which can lead to incorrectly rendered target views even when the reconstructed geometry is otherwise accurate. To ensure a consistent metric scale across methods, we use Depth Anything 3 GIANT-1.1-NESTED
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
as the depth estimator for all explicit 3D-memory baselines. The predicted metric depth is used to place the reconstructed 3D representation at the same scale as the evaluation camera trajectory. For Gaussian-based methods, NeoVerse
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
and L3G-World, we additionally align the depth rendered from the initially predicted Gaussians with the metric depth estimated from the input image.
Baseline Implementations.
The official implementations of SPMem
(
Wu et al., 2026a
)
and 3DScenePrompt
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
initialize their first generation chunk using multiple input views or video frames, from which they reconstruct a 3D point-cloud representation and render it under subsequent target cameras. Since our benchmark provides only a single input image, we modify their initialization stage to reconstruct the 3D representation from the first frame alone and render it to the target cameras of the first chunk. For subsequent autoregressive generation chunks, we retain the behavior of the official implementations.
NeoVerse
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
is designed for single-image world generation, but its released implementation does not provide the complete autoregressive generation pipeline required by our long-horizon evaluation. We therefore build an autoregressive inference pipeline on top of the official implementation, repeatedly reconstructing and updating its Gaussian representation from generated observations and rendering the resulting memory under the target cameras for subsequent generation.
Yume 1.5
(
Mao et al., 2026
)
and Matrix-Game 3.0
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
are action-conditioned world models that use discrete keyboard-style controls rather than continuous camera parameters. To evaluate them along the same camera trajectories as the other methods, we convert the provided camera motion into the corresponding sequence of discrete action inputs and use these actions for autoregressive generation.
B.4
Evaluation
Datasets.
We evaluate L3G-World and all baselines on the test splits of DL3DV
(
Ling et al., 2024
)
and RealEstate10K
(
Zhou et al., 2018
)
. To explicitly evaluate long-horizon consistency under revisitation, we construct 481-frame loop-closure trajectories. Starting from the input view, the camera first follows an exploration trajectory and subsequently retraces the same trajectory in reverse, eventually returning to the initial camera pose.
Self-Consistency.
The loop-closure trajectory provides pairs of generated frames corresponding to the same camera pose but generated at different points in the autoregressive sequence. We pair each frame on the outgoing trajectory with its corresponding frame on the returning trajectory and compute PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS between them. We report the average over all corresponding frame pairs as our self-consistency metrics. This evaluation directly measures whether scene appearance and structure are preserved after long-horizon generation and subsequent loop closure.
Camera Controllability.
Following
(
Seo et al., 2026
)
, we estimate the camera trajectory from each generated video using the feed-forward geometry estimator
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
, and compare the estimated trajectory against the ground-truth camera trajectory used for generation. We report translation error (TransErr) after resolving the global scale ambiguity of the estimated trajectory, together with rotation error (RotErr) in degrees.
Efficiency.
For explicit 3D-memory methods, we measure the number of stored 3D primitives and their memory footprint after long-horizon generation, together with memory reconstruction throughput in processed views per second. We further measure target-view rendering throughput in two settings: RGB rendering FPS and VAE-space conditioning FPS. For methods whose 3D memory stores only RGB appearance, VAE-space conditioning includes both target-view RGB rendering and subsequent VAE encoding. In contrast, L3G-World directly renders the stored VAE features into the target-view latent space without RGB rendering or re-encoding. Reconstruction FPS includes Gaussian retrieval, mask computation, the updater forward pass, and the residual update. All efficiency measurements in Tab.
2
are performed on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.
Appendix C
Qualitative Results
Figure 8:
Additional qualitative results of video generation on DL3DV and RealEstate10K.
For each scene, all methods start from the same input view (top), explore unseen regions (middle), and return to the initial camera location (bottom). L3G-World preserves scene structure and appearance upon loop closure, whereas the baselines exhibit drift, blur, or rendering artifacts.
Fig.
8

6
to additional scenes from DL3DV and RealEstate10K under the same long-horizon loop-closure trajectories. Starting from the same input view, each method explores previously unseen regions and eventually returns to the initial camera location, so that the final frame directly reveals whether the generated world remains consistent after long-horizon exploration.
The baselines exhibit distinct failure modes.
Temporal-context-based methods, Yume 1.5 and Matrix-Game 3.0, generally follow the camera motion during exploration, but fail to preserve spatial consistency upon return: the final frame often shows a layout or appearance different from the input view, and in some cases even a different viewpoint, indicating that camera control also degrades over the long trajectory.
Among explicit 3D memories, SPMem tends to hallucinate inconsistent content once the camera leaves the initially observed region, and NeoVerse progressively collapses into blurry textures over the long trajectory.
Among the baselines that return to the starting scene more reliably, GEN3C recovers the input view quite well, but struggles to extrapolate plausible content in regions unseen in the input view, producing distorted or incomplete frames during exploration.
Lyra 2.0 returns reasonably close to the input view, but its final frame is still not fully spatially aligned with it, indicating drift from the original scene.
In contrast, L3G-World both generates plausible content in unseen regions and returns to a scene spatially aligned with the input view in both structure and appearance, as its latent 3D Gaussian memory anchors previously generated content while continually refining it throughout exploration.
Appendix D
Comparison with Online 3DGS Methods
Existing online 3D Gaussian Splatting methods
Cheng et al. (2026)
;
Chen et al. (2026a)
provide strong feed-forward reconstruction and could, in principle, serve as an external 3D memory for world generation. However, these methods are primarily designed for high-fidelity reconstruction and novel-view synthesis (NVS), whereas a memory for real-time world generation must satisfy a different operating regime: it must be continuously updated throughout autoregressive generation, remain compact as exploration proceeds, and render the conditioning signal for every subsequent video chunk with very low latency. In particular, a dense representation that is effective for reconstruction can introduce substantial memory and rendering overhead when repeatedly queried by a video diffusion model. Our goal is therefore not to outperform dedicated online 3DGS methods as a standalone reconstruction system, but to construct a sufficiently faithful 3D memory that can be efficiently updated and directly consumed by L3G-Gen.
To characterize this trade-off quantitatively, we evaluate latent 3D Gaussian memory with online 3D Gaussian reconstruction models
Cheng et al. (2026)
;
Chen et al. (2026a)
on DL3DV
(

(

After each chunk processing, we render the current 3D Gaussians to four target viewpoints and evaluate both RGB- and VAE-space NVS. We visualize the ground-truth and generated video, with target-view rendered VAE condition from the latent 3D Gaussian memory, illustrating that spatially aligned latent memory provides consistent conditioning for video generation.
More importantly, the utility of this reconstruction is determined by how the memory conditions subsequent video generation. Fig.

The rendered latent remains spatially aligned with the target camera and preserves the structure of previously observed regions. By directly conditioning L3G-Gen on these spatially anchored VAE features, the model can generate novel content while remaining consistent with the persistent scene memory. Thus, latent 3D Gaussian memory is not merely an efficient reconstruction module: it provides a compact, continuously updated, and directly renderable latent interface between the accumulated 3D scene and autoregressive video generation.
Appendix E
Limitations and Future Work
Despite its efficiency, L3G-World has several limitations that suggest directions for future work. First, latent 3D Gaussian memory is primarily designed for static scenes and does not explicitly model independently moving objects. Extending the persistent memory to disentangle dynamic content from static geometry would enable more general interactive environments. Second, although the memory grows with explored spatial extent rather than generation length, its size can still increase under extremely large-scale exploration; adaptive pruning or hierarchical memory representations could further improve scalability. Finally, while the refinement mechanism can progressively correct inaccurate Gaussians, errors introduced during long-horizon autoregressive generation may still propagate to subsequent memory updates.

article.headline: 用隐空间3D高斯记忆做实时无限世界生成
article.lede: 把3D高斯记忆存进VAE隐空间、只在新区域生成并在线精修，L3G-World以9.02 FPS实时生成空间一致的长时世界
article.problem: 交互式世界模型要在长时探索和闭环回到旧视角时保持空间一致，同时还得实时出帧。依赖时序上下文（历史帧、KV cache）的方法开销随生成流长度线性增长，表1中WorldKV在400帧、464×832下直接OOM；依赖显式3D记忆的方法则两头为难：前馈式逐帧累积稠密图元，同一区域反复堆积导致冗余和渲染变慢，优化式虽紧凑但逐场景迭代延迟过高。此外显式记忆必须先渲染RGB再用VAE重编码才能条件化隐扩散生成器，这本身就不允许实时。
article.method: L3G-Mem把3D高斯当作持久场景记忆：先用当前记忆渲染出的不透明度与RGB误差构造spawn mask，只在未覆盖或高误差区域用K-means初始化查询来生成新高斯，同时对当前可见高斯做残差精修，使记忆随场景范围而非生成帧数增长。每个高斯额外携带一个VAE隐特征，记忆因此可以直接渲染到DiT的隐空间，省去VAE重编码。L3G-Gen基于Cosmos-Predict2.5的DiT，把渲染出的隐特征与alpha掩码按通道拼接到噪声隐变量上作为几何条件，并用AnyFlow做少步蒸馏得到L3G-World Fast。
article.results: 在481帧闭环轨迹上，L3G-World在DL3DV存储33K个高斯、11.88 MiB，重建40.09 FPS、RGB渲染460.73 FPS、VAE空间渲染1086.58 FPS，自一致性PSNR 16.00、LPIPS 0.366，生成质量LPIPS 0.547、FID 40.57；RealEstate10K上为25K高斯、8.91 MiB、自一致性PSNR 18.36。论文称相对各指标最高效的先前3D记忆基线，最多用38.6×更少图元、3.2×更快重建、359×更快VAE渲染，单卡达9.02 FPS（表2的效率测量在A100上完成）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「一致性记忆」做成可直接渲染进DiT隐空间、随探索范围而非视频时长增长的紧凑表示，让长时一致性与实时吞吐不再是二选一，为可扩展的交互式世界模型提供了实用接口。
article.limitations: 论文自述记忆面向静态场景、不显式建模独立运动物体，超大范围探索下记忆仍会增长，长时自回归中的误差仍可能通过记忆更新向后传播；另外在RealEstate10K上其平移/旋转误差（0.216、1.23°）与MEt3R（0.029）均不如GEN3C（0.112、0.46°、0.027），说明相机控制与几何一致性并非全面领先。
article.figure_caption_zh: 流水线：视频生成与记忆更新按块循环交替，每生成一块就更新持久3D记忆，记忆又反过来条件化下一块的生成。

email_papers.title: TouchBridge: Tactile-Conditioned Human-to-Robot Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation
email_papers.abstract: Human demonstrations offer an efficient and scalable source of data for dexterous robot manipulation, but differences in sensing and hand morphology complicate the transfer of contact-rich interactions. We present TouchBridge, a hardware--software co-designed framework for human-to-robot data transformation. A wearable human demonstration interface and a corresponding robot interface establish cross-embodiment correspondence in visual and fingertip tactile sensing. We introduce Tac-Retarget, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to align fingertip contact patches and preserve their spatial relations within and across hands. Unlike object-aware or simulation-based transfer pipelines, Tac-Retarget requires no object mesh, object-pose estimate, or physics simulation for retargeting, enabling direct and scalable conversion of human demonstrations into robot-domain training data. Combined with visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, TouchBridge produces robot-domain demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, policies fine-tuned solely on TouchBridge-converted human demonstrations achieve a 72.5% average success rate, compared with 77.5% using an equal number of teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstration collection is 7.0x faster. Under the same policy and training setup, Tac-Retarget outperforms DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively.

TouchBridge

Tac-Retarget
, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to align fingertip contact patches and preserve their spatial relations within and across hands. Combined with visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, TouchBridge produces robot-domain demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model. I
INTRODUCTION
Building foundation models for contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires large-scale demonstrations that capture not only hand motion, but also physical interaction with the environment. Collecting such data directly on dexterous robots, however, is slow and demands substantial operator effort. Human demonstrations provide a natural and potentially scalable source of manipulation experience, and have increasingly been used for large-scale pretraining
[
1
,
2

and direct human-to-robot transfer
[
3
,
4
]
. Realizing this potential, however, requires transforming human experience into robot-executable training data both faithfully and efficiently.
This transformation faces two key challenges. First,
kinematic correspondence alone does not preserve physical interaction
. Conventional retargeting methods typically match hand poses, fingertip positions, or hand-centric vectors
[
5
,
6
,
1
]
. While effective for free-space motion, these objectives do not explicitly capture contact. As a result, fixed human-derived fingertip targets can displace a contacting finger from its support region, distort relations among simultaneous contacts, or break contact altogether. For contact-rich manipulation, kinematically plausible motion may therefore still be physically ineffective.
Second,
preserving physical interaction should not come at the cost of data scalability
. Object-aware approaches incorporate hand–object geometry or physics-based constraints
[
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
]
, while other human-to-robot pipelines refine transferred trajectories or policies through simulation and reinforcement learning
[
11
,
12
]
. Such methods can improve physical consistency, but require object meshes, object-pose estimation, environment reconstruction, or simulation-based rollout and refinement. These object- and task-specific requirements introduce substantial modeling and engineering overhead, making them difficult to scale with increasingly large and diverse human datasets.
Our key observation is that
physical contact itself provides a natural correspondence across embodiments
. Tactile sensing directly reveals which fingertips are in contact, where contact occurs, and how strongly different regions are loaded. Because these signals are measured directly during human demonstrations, they provide interaction constraints without requiring explicit object reconstruction or simulation-based refinement. Tactile sensing therefore addresses both challenges simultaneously: it augments kinematic retargeting with physical interaction information while preserving a direct human-to-robot data conversion pathway.
Building on this idea, we present
TouchBridge
, a hardware–software co-designed framework for scalable conversion of human demonstrations of contact-rich dexterous manipulation into robot-domain data. At the hardware level, we develop
TouchBridge-Cap
, a wearable capture interface that records RGB observations, hand motion, and fingertip tactile measurements. The corresponding robot interface approximately matches the wrist-camera-to-hand geometry, fingertip sensor placement, and tactile sensing layout of TouchBridge-Cap, establishing cross-embodiment correspondence in visual and tactile observations. At the software level, TouchBridge transforms these human demonstrations into robot-domain observations and actions for policy learning without task-specific robot demonstrations or object-specific environment modeling.
At the core of TouchBridge is
Tac-Retarget
, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to guide motion transfer across embodiments. Tac-Retarget combines
contact-patch alignment
, which aligns tactile contact regions between human and robot fingertips, with a
contact-activated graph
, which preserves spatial relations among simultaneous contacts within and across hands. Together, these objectives transfer not only fingertip motion but also the geometry and spatial structure of demonstrated contacts. The optimization operates directly on measured human kinematics and tactile responses, requiring no object mesh, object-pose estimate, or physics simulation. Combined with robot-domain visual synthesis and camera-anchored action construction, the resulting pipeline converts raw human demonstrations into robot-domain training sequences.
We evaluate TouchBridge on four contact-rich real-world manipulation tasks: bulb screwing, sauce application, fragile-object grasping, and page flipping. Under the same policy and training setup, demonstrations converted using Tac-Retarget yield an average real-robot policy success rate of

Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We present
TouchBridge
, a hardware–software co-designed framework that transforms contact-rich human demonstrations into robot-domain training sequences. Through aligned visual and fingertip tactile sensing across human and robot interfaces, TouchBridge enables policy learning for contact-rich dexterous manipulation without task-specific teleoperated robot demonstrations.
•
We introduce
Tac-Retarget
, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact-patch alignment and a contact-activated graph to preserve physical interaction across embodiments. Compared with kinematic retargeting, Tac-Retarget substantially improves both contact preservation and downstream real-robot policy success.
•
TouchBridge converts human demonstrations without object meshes, object-pose estimates, or simulation-based rollout refinement. Together, the

We align the wrist-camera and fingertip tactile-sensor configurations across the human demonstration and robot deployment interfaces. As shown in Fig.

III-A
1
Human Demonstration Interface
We develop
TouchBridge-Cap
, a wearable human demonstration
interface that records egocentric RGB observations using an Intel
RealSense D455, together with bilateral wrist-view RGB observations
from two Hikrobot cameras. A pair of Manus gloves captures articulated
hand kinematics, while a PaXini Hall-effect tactile array mounted on each
fingertip records spatially distributed contact responses.
Multi-face AprilTag fiducials mounted near the wrists are localized
offline in the egocentric video. Using the detected fiducial poses and calibrated fiducial-to-glove transformations, we transform the glove-estimated fingertip poses into the D455 camera frame.
III-A
2
Robot Deployment Interface
The robot is equipped with an egocentric camera, bilateral wrist cameras,
and five PaXini tactile sensors on each dexterous hand. Custom mounts position the wrist cameras similarly to those on
TouchBridge-Cap
and place tactile sensors at
corresponding fingertip locations. Together with the matched tactile sensing layouts,
this design provides aligned wrist-view observations and fingertip-local
tactile representations across the human and robot embodiments.

IV
Experiments
Overview
: We evaluate TouchBridge through data analyses and real-robot experiments to address four questions:
1.
How closely do our human-derived robot demonstrations resemble real-robot demonstrations in visual observations and actions?
2.
Can policies fine-tuned solely on our human-derived
demonstrations achieve task performance comparable to that of policies fine-tuned on an equal number of teleoperated
robot demonstrations?
3.
How effective is Tac-Retarget compared with existing simulation-free retargeting methods, and how do its tactile components contribute to its performance?
4.
How does policy pretraining affect learning from our human-derived robot demonstrations?

III-A2
. All policies use the same observation acquisition procedures,
low-level controllers, and action-execution rate.

IV-A
2
Task Descriptions
We evaluate all methods on four contact-rich tasks: Flip Book, Screw Bulb, Apply Sauce, and Grasp Egg Roll. These tasks involve diverse contact interactions, from precise fingertip manipulation to force-sensitive object handling. Representative rollouts are shown in Fig.
5
.
Flip Book.
The robot turns a single page of a book using the right index finger.
The motion requires sustained fingertip contact throughout
the page turn while avoiding displacement of the book.
Screw Bulb.
The robot screws a light bulb into a socket until the bulb lights up.
The task requires stable multi-finger contact and accurate rotational motion.
Apply Sauce.
The robot holds a baguette with its left hand and squeezes ketchup onto
it from left to right with its right hand. The task requires precise
fingertip force control to produce the desired amount of ketchup.
Grasp Egg Roll.
The robot picks up a fragile egg roll with the right hand and places it
onto a plate. The robot must apply sufficient grasp force to prevent slippage without causing visible deformation or breakage.
IV-A
3
Data Collection
We construct separate human-derived and teleoperated robot datasets for
the four evaluation tasks. The human demonstrations are converted into robot
training sequences using the pipeline in
Sec.
III-C
. Tactile measurements are used only for retargeting,
not as policy inputs.
For each task, we collect
60
60
human demonstrations and
60
60
teleoperated robot demonstrations. The teleoperated demonstrations serve as a reference for data-quality analysis and are used to train separate policies for the data-source comparison. They are not mixed into the training data of our method or the human-data baselines. Within each human demonstration, the operator is instructed to minimize head motion to reduce
frame-to-frame viewpoint changes. Across demonstrations, we vary the
camera position and viewing angle to increase the diversity of
camera-object configurations.
IV-A
4
Evaluation Protocol
Policy Success Rate.
We evaluate each policy over 20 real-world trials per task.
Success rate is the percentage of trials satisfying the
task-specific success criterion.
Replay Success Rate.
We replay 20 human-derived converted demonstrations per task and report
the percentage of replays satisfying the same task-specific
success criteria used for policy evaluation.
Data Collection Time.
For each task and collection method, we report the average
collection time per successful demonstration by dividing the total elapsed collection time by the 60 successful demonstrations.

V
Conclusion
We presented TouchBridge, a hardware–software co-designed
framework for learning contact-rich dexterous manipulation
without task-specific robot demonstrations. It combines
TouchBridge-Cap for efficient human demonstration collection
with Tac-Retarget for contact-preserving motion transfer,
producing robot-domain data without object meshes,
object-pose estimates, or simulation-based refinement.
With faster demonstration collection and policy success
rates close to those obtained from robot-collected data,
we believe TouchBridge can serve as a practical framework
for the community to scale robot learning from human
demonstrations. Our current study uses a modest demonstration
set; extending the framework to larger and more diverse
human datasets remains an important direction for future work.

article.headline: 触觉引导的人到机器人灵巧操作数据转换
article.lede: 清华等团队提出 TouchBridge，用指尖触觉把人手演示转换成机器人训练数据，平均成功率 72.5%，采集快 7 倍
article.problem: 人类演示是灵巧操作数据的廉价来源，但人手与机器人手在形态和传感上不一致，纯运动学重定向只对齐指尖位姿、不约束接触，容易出现接触点偏移、多点接触关系被破坏甚至脱手。若引入物体网格、物体位姿估计或物理仿真来保接触，又会带来大量建模与工程开销，难以随数据规模扩展。
article.method: 作者软硬件协同设计：TouchBridge-Cap 用腕部相机、Manus 手套和指尖霍尔触觉阵列采集人类演示，机器人端按相近的腕部相机与指尖触觉布局对齐，建立跨本体的视觉与触觉对应。核心方法 Tac-Retarget 在重定向优化中同时对齐指尖位姿、按触觉响应加权的接触斑块中心与激活触元分布，并用触觉激活的接触图保持双手内外同时接触点之间的空间关系，全程不需要物体网格、物体位姿估计或物理仿真。再用 SAM 2 与 ProPainter 抹除人手并渲染机器人模型合成机器人域观测，配合相机锚定的动作构造生成训练序列。
article.results: 在四个真实接触密集任务（翻书页、拧灯泡、挤酱、抓蛋卷）上，仅用 TouchBridge 转换的人演示微调 GR00T N1.7，平均成功率 72.5%，而用等量遥操作机器人演示为 77.5%；人类演示采集平均每次 11.7 秒，遥操作为 81.7 秒，快 7.0 倍。同等设置下 Tac-Retarget 比 DexPilot 和 UniDex 分别高 25.0 和 42.5 个百分点，仿真中平均接触误差 4.667 mm（DexPilot 6.354 mm、UniDex 7.715 mm）。转换数据的动作回放平均成功率 87.5%。消融显示去掉接触图或接触对齐都会降低成功率，两者都去掉时降幅最大；预训练影响显著，GR00T N1.7 与 π0.5 预训练版成功率为 72.5% 与 38.8%，从头训练仅 6.2% 与 3.8%，Diffusion Policy 为 13.8%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把触觉当作跨本体的天然对应信号，绕开了物体建模与仿真精修，让灵巧手策略可以主要靠采集更快的人手演示来训练。若这一路线成立，接触密集操作的数据瓶颈有望从遥操作工时转向可穿戴采集。
article.limitations: 作者自述演示规模有限（每任务 60 条、四个任务、每策略 20 次真机试验），扩展到大而多样的人类数据集仍是未来工作，且 72.5% 与 77.5% 之间仍有差距。此外触觉只用于重定向、并未作为策略输入，接触误差也仅在抓蛋卷这一项任务上借助重建网格在 Isaac Sim 中评估。

article.headline: 好视图比下一词预测更易对齐图文
article.lede: 在 Flickr 上，好视图图像 JEPA 与文本编码器的对齐明显优于坏视图 JEPA 与下一词预测，后两者几乎重合。
article.problem: 论文要回答的问题：图像与文本两种模态能否仅靠各自的几何结构对齐，以及什么样的自监督目标决定这种可对齐性。作者此前的理论预测，好视图（caption 视图）可以对齐，坏视图（掩码片段）和下一词预测则不行，但缺少系统的实验检验。
article.method: 作者用 JEPA 训练图像编码器，文本侧用一个随机初始化的 BERT 编码器：好视图保留 caption 的连续片段，坏视图保留掩码片段，另外训练一个下一词预测模型作为对照。随后在 Flickr、COCO、MSR-VTT 等数据上测量互 10-NN、R@1、零样本检索与无配对 captioner 等指标，并对谱解给出理论证明。
article.results: 在 PRH 基准上，好视图 JEPA 配 DINOv2 ViT-B 达到 .184，高于 Qwen2.5 的 0.5B 到 72B、Llama-3-8B 与 70B 以及 Mistral-7B，并在所有 DINOv2 尺寸上保持领先；换成线性 CKA 或五倍大的 COCO 基准，结论不变。文本侧 caption→caption 的 R@1 为：好视图 .606、坏视图 .381、下一词预测 .331、TF-IDF .442。只用无配对池、不碰测试数据的零配对 captioner 在 Flickr 上 CIDEr 为 .158±.042（目标函数选出的映射为 .208），而 30k 配对旋转为 .430，随机映射仅 .028；109M 的好视图 JEPA 在零样本指标上超过 Schnaus 等人的无配对方法。消融还显示，因果模型用均值池化时对齐 R@1 为 .119，用末 token 只有 .061。
article.why_it_matters: 结果提示，跨模态能否对齐更多取决于视图与训练目标的设计，而非语言模型的规模。这为无配对数据条件下的多模态对齐与检索提供了可操作的思路。
article.limitations: 理论结论只对谱解证明，作者也承认没有实验满足其假设；多个配置只跑一个种子，统计稳健性有限。坏视图与下一词预测的劣势是在特定编码器与数据集上测得的，普适性仍待验证。

Abstract
Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm,
unified training
. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy–compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

Introduction
Foundation models are conventionally trained through a sequence of stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL)
(
deepseek2025v3
;
olmo2025olmo3
)
. These stages have become embedded in specialized training recipes and infrastructure, and are often treated as separate learning problems. In this paper, we argue that this separation is not fundamental to the training process. Instead, the full training pipeline admits a strikingly simple view:
Foundation-model training can be viewed as a single learning objective
driven by an evolving distribution of training data.
This shift changes the central design problem. Conventional pipelines organize design decisions around separate stages, each with its own training recipe.
Under a unified view, the learning algorithm stays fixed from start to end, and the central design choices concern the evolving distribution of training data: which data the model learns from, in what proportions, and when.
Pretraining text, demonstrations, and model generations selected with verifiable rewards become different data sources for the same underlying learning process.
Conventional staged training is then one particular choice, in which the proportion of each data source abruptly shifts from one stage to the next.
The unified view also changes the scientific question. Our understanding of foundation-model training has historically developed one stage at a time: pretraining scaling laws characterize the relationship between data, compute, and model performance
(
kaplan2020scaling
;
hoffmann2022computeoptimal
)
, while a growing literature studies scaling during RL
(
nimmaturi2025predictive
;
khatri2026art
;
tan2026rlscaling
)
.
Research on transfer and interactions across stages shows that earlier training decisions also affect subsequent learning
(
hernandez2021transfer
;
isik2025downstream
;
runwal2026prism
;
shen2026understanding
)
.
As a result, we know much less about how decisions made throughout training jointly determine the capabilities of the final model. A unified formulation lets us study these decisions together and judge them by their effect on the final model rather than by stage-specific metrics. This opens the door to a science of training trajectories: principles for how data and compute should evolve over the lifetime of a foundation model.
Making this view concrete requires bringing RL under the maximum-likelihood formulation already used for pretraining, midtraining, and SFT. Building on Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (

5.1
Full Unified Training under Controlled Reasoning Tasks

Experimental setup
We study how data composition and schedule affect the full training pipeline in a controlled setting.
We train a 124M-parameter model from scratch using a fixed 20B-token pretraining corpus and a fixed 510M-token midtraining corpus across runs.
Staged training uses these sources sequentially before RL; unified training mixes midtraining data into the final part of pretraining and throughout RL (

The midtraining corpus contains oracle-generated solutions that demonstrate the underlying reasoning operations.

5.2.2

Discussion
This work presents a common mathematical formulation and training infrastructure for foundation models, bringing static data and suitable RL updates together through maximum likelihood learning. The resulting flexibility allows data sources to overlap and their proportions to change throughout training. Our experiments demonstrate practical benefits from these choices and show that the value of a data source depends on both when it is introduced and how it interacts with subsequent learning.
A central open question is how to select these mixtures systematically. Our experiments reveal tradeoffs among accuracy, coverage, and retention, but do not identify a universally preferred mixture or schedule. The compute study likewise characterizes the evaluated configurations without establishing scaling laws with predictive power. Extending these analyses across model sizes and data budgets could support more predictive choices about when to reuse static data, generate new responses, and change their relative contributions. In addition, our current results are not established with in depth study on how optimization should change with different data schedule and mixture design
(
wen2026data
)
, and we leave this as an important direction for future work.
The scope of the experiments also remains small-scale. Most runs optimize a single RL task at a time, whereas joint training across tasks may require accounting for competing learning dynamics and unequal rates of progress. Furthermore, our work does not fully eliminate the notion of stages as downstream adaptation of a foundation model to a new task will inevitably require a separate training stage. Our continual learning results provide initial evidence that the preceding training process can improve this adaptation; studying longer task sequences would clarify how that advantage interacts with retention. Together, these questions motivate studying data allocation throughout training as a coupled learning problem.

article.headline: 统一训练：预训练到RL共用似然目标
article.lede: 论文将预训练、SFT与RL统一为最大似然拟合，并在124M模型上混合静态数据和RL生成做验证。
article.problem: 常规基础模型按预训练、中期训练、SFT、RL分阶段训练，各阶段使用不同数据和算法，常被当作独立学习问题。这种分法使研究者难以联合考察数据组成、比例和时机如何共同决定最终能力。论文主张算法上的阶段划分并非根本必要。
article.method: 作者把合适的RL目标推导为对模型生成目标分布的最大似然拟合，使预训练、中期训练、SFT和RL都落在同一个基于似然的训练算法下。他们实现了一个统一训练器，在同一训练过程中混合静态数据和RL生成，并允许数据来源重叠、比例随训练变化。传统分阶段训练成为该框架的一个特例。
article.results: 在受控推理任务中，124M参数模型使用20B token预训练语料和510M token中期语料；统一训练在相同总计算预算下取得更高准确率和覆盖率，最佳统一模型在RL后超过分阶段参考，尽管其RL前Base准确率更低。真实数据实验的四组混合调度中，Math pass@1为24.01–24.80%、pass@32为68.32–68.94%，MMLU为39.96–40.17%，Coding pass@32为46.16–46.93%，且各调度在保留、准确率和覆盖率上的排序并不一致。WebInstruct RL实验中，统一模型初始验证/测试准确率低于分阶段训练，但3000次更新后更高；2%中期比例模型的test pass@64更高，5%模型在该指标上略低于分阶段训练。
article.why_it_matters: 这把基础模型训练生命周期变成选择数据来源、比例和时机的单一问题，为跨阶段缩放规律和持续学习提供可实验框架。
article.limitations: 作者承认实验规模较小、多数只优化单一RL任务，未找到普遍最优的混合或调度，计算研究也未建立有预测力的缩放律。下游新任务仍不可避免需要单独适应阶段，更长任务序列的影响尚待研究。

Abstract
An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track
of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore
involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a
persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to
guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that
support such a state?
We study this question through four levels of spatial capability—spatial
structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and
actionability—using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under
streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments.
The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and
prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure
accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval.
Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual
history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial
structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer
to predicted features unchanged.
Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable
continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet
supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress.
Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on
camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene
readout.
Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not
only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is
maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for
goal-directed action.
Figure 1
:
Spatial state representations from streaming egocentric observations.
A moving observer builds an internal spatial representation from partial
views of an environment.
L1
(
spatial structure
) captures scene geometry and object
identity across views.
L2
(
object persistence
) retains the observer-relative
locations of previously seen objects after they leave the field of view.
L3
(
predictive spatial update
) anticipates what the
observer would see after an action or a sequence of actions.
L4
(
actionability
) uses the represented state and a
specified goal to select an action that makes progress toward that goal.
1
Introduction
Spatial representation is one of the most fundamental capacities of
biological perception. Humans and other animals do not experience the world
as a sequence of independent retinal images. Through continuous exploration,
they maintain information about the surrounding space, keep track of objects
that are no longer visible, update their own location as they move, and use
this information to guide subsequent behavior. These abilities are not
inherently linguistic: they arise from perception and from sensorimotor
interaction with the environment.
Several classical ideas in perception and spatial cognition point to this
view. Object-file theories describe how object-specific information remains
associated with the same entity across changes in its visual appearance
[
17
]
. Spatial updating and path integration describe how
an internal estimate of location is continuously revised from self-motion
[
26
]
. Sensorimotor contingency theories further emphasize
that perception involves knowledge of how sensory input would change under
possible actions
[
30
]
. Together, these perspectives suggest
that a useful representation of space should describe more than what is
visible in the current image: it should maintain a state of the surrounding
world that persists and evolves as the observer interacts with it.
An observer’s
spatial state
is the configuration of the surrounding
environment relative to the observer, including previously observed objects
that are no longer visible. A
spatial state representation
is an
internal encoding of this configuration inferred from the observer’s visual
history. We do not prescribe an explicit 3D map, an object-centric scene
graph, a coordinate system, or a neural architecture. Instead, we
characterize the functional usefulness of a representation through four
capabilities:
L1
Spatial structure.
Recover the spatial organization of the observed scene through metric
geometry, instance identity, and view consistency.
L2
Object persistence.
Retain the location of a previously observed object after it has left
the field of view.
L3
Predictive spatial update.
Anticipate changes in the observer-relative state under ego-motion,
evaluated through direct prediction and path integration.
L4
Actionability.
Use the represented state and a specified goal to predict an action that
makes progress toward that goal.
These capabilities, summarized in
Figure
2
, are
ordered by what each demands beyond the current observation: L1 reads the
visible scene; L2 additionally requires information retained from earlier
views; L3 requires anticipating views that have not yet been observed; and
L4 requires relating the represented state to a goal and an action. Which
lower-level ingredients the higher levels actually draw on is an empirical
question that we return to in
Section
4.6
.
We study these functions in a streaming setting: the observer receives past
and current visual evidence but no future observations, and representations
are extracted from causal visual prefixes of increasing length. Each prefix
is encoded independently, so the question is what the representation of a
causal prefix affords, not whether the model maintains an online state.
Our experimental scope is observer motion through static indoor
environments; object dynamics, contact physics, and complete physical world
modeling are outside it.
The question spans the full range of
visual foundation models
,
including image and video encoders, 3D models, multimodal models, video
generators, and world models. Strong performance on a model’s training
objective does not establish all four spatial functions, and success at one
level need not carry over to the next.
We therefore conduct a
functional probing study
of ten frozen
representations. Six main diagnostics yield seven measurements of spatial
structure, object persistence, and predictive spatial update, since metric
geometry contributes separate depth and camera-pose metrics; goal-conditioned
action prediction additionally tests actionability in a candidate-selection
and a continuous-output setting. Rather than relying on a single extraction
point, we organize the analyses along two axes, network depth and streaming
context, and add matched controls that alter motion, history, transformation
order, or goals while keeping the relevant predictor and target fixed.
Findings.
No representation leads on all tasks: Fast3R has the strongest camera-pose
and object-persistence readouts, DINOv2 leads direct future-feature
prediction, and V-JEPA2 leads path integration (
Section
4.1
).
VideoMAE localizes previously seen objects more accurately than DINOv2 and
Qwen2.5-VL despite weaker depth, instance, and view-consistency readouts;
across the ten representations, object persistence aligns with camera-pose
readout rather than with these visible-scene metrics. The profiles shift
with layer, and longer prefixes worsen persistence for all eight models in
the endpoint comparison while their effects on prediction vary
(
Section
4.2
). Separate matched controls distinguish
decodability
from
input use
: copying the last feature exceeds
learned prediction for V-JEPA2, and visual history helps V-JEPA2 and Wan
but shows no clear benefit for VideoMAE (
Section
4.3
). Native
prediction keeps recoverable geometry but not the original readout
interface (
Section
4.4
), and input use is not
functional utility
: changing the goal rotates predicted actions by
30–46
∘
, yet the correct goal does not reliably improve progress
(
Section
4.5
). Across levels, the results reveal two
ingredient chains: object persistence and actionability build on
camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene
readout (
Section
4.6
).
Contributions.
We (i) characterize spatial state representations operationally through
four functional capabilities; (ii) develop a frozen-feature probing
framework covering ten representations, with controls for history, motion,
predictive readout, and goal use; and (iii) show that readout accuracy,
input use, and goal-specific utility dissociate across models, layers, and
prefix lengths, motivating multidimensional evaluation of spatial state.

We ask what spatial information is accessible in frozen visual features,
which inputs support that information, and whether it remains useful for
prediction and goal-directed action.

Readout metrics.
Instance identity uses a cross-entropy loss on per-pixel embeddings, with
prototypes computed from ground-truth instance groups within the evaluated
sample; it measures identity separation, not mask quality or segmentation
IoU. Direct prediction and path integration retrieve future features within
each model’s own target space, so their scores do not lie on a common scale
of physical prediction error. Global R@1 is the fraction of predictions
whose most similar candidate is the correct future feature. Camera-pose
AUC@30 is the area under the pose-accuracy curve up to a 30-degree error
threshold. Probes in the main comparison use training seed 42. Intervals
are 95% scene-clustered bootstrap intervals over the 69 validation scenes
(1,000 resamples shared by all cells, so model, prefix, and coordinate
differences are paired); they reflect evaluation sampling, not
training-seed variability (
Section
A.3
).
Evaluation scope.
The main table reports final-checkpoint evaluations on 276 validation
windows per prefix. The MiniMax-H3 prediction probes are evaluated on 171
of these windows and are marked accordingly. Direct prediction for the
other nine models pools three future targets per window into a gallery of
828 candidates, whereas MiniMax-H3 direct prediction uses 171
next-observation candidates. Path integration pools the same three
waypoints, giving 828 candidates for the other models and 513 for
MiniMax-H3. Object persistence scores only windows with an eligible,
previously visible target: 80 windows at prefix 8 and 171 at each of
prefixes 12, 16, and 24.
Section
A.2
reports
results on the 171 shared validation windows together with a matched
next-observation evaluation. The matched input controls, the
native-prediction readout, the motion-composition study, and the action
experiments follow their own protocols, described below.

Two ingredient chains run through the levels

5
Related Work
Probing spatial and 3D structure in frozen representations.
Frozen-feature probing asks what information is already accessible in a
representation without updating the backbone. Self-supervised image
encoders such as DINO and DINOv2 revealed that semantic organization,
object boundaries, and strong local correspondences emerge without dense
labels
[
6
,
29
]
. More recent work extends
this methodology to video foundation models: VidFM3D evaluates whether
shallow readouts recover depth, camera pose, and 3D point structure from
frozen video-model features, and analyzes how these signals vary with
network depth and diffusion timestep
[
15
]
. Related
probes of image foundation models test depth, surface normals, and
multi-view correspondence
[
11
]
, scene-level tasks
such as 3D question answering, visual grounding, and registration
[
25
]
, and novel-view synthesis from features read out
as 3D Gaussians
[
9
]
. Feed-forward 3D reconstruction
models, from DUSt3R to VGGT and Fast3R, provide a geometry-specialized
reference point because their training directly targets multi-view
reconstruction and camera estimation
[
37
,
35
,
38
]
; streaming variants
such as Spann3R and CUT3R carry an explicit spatial memory or a persistent
state that is updated with every new frame
[
34
,
36
]
. Our streaming prefixes ask a
related question of general-purpose representations without assuming such
a state. Our work
starts from the same evidence-first principle but changes the object of
evaluation: metric geometry is one functional diagnostic rather than a
definition of spatial state, and we also ask whether a representation
supports view consistency, object persistence, predictive spatial update,
and actionability. Two models with similar depth readout can therefore
receive very different spatial-state profiles, and strong future-feature
retrieval is not credited as predictive spatial update unless it passes
matched motion controls.
Internal representations of diffusion and video generation models.
Large video generators such as Wan and CogVideoX are optimized for
denoising and visual synthesis rather than for downstream readout
[
33
,
41
]
. Nevertheless, work on image
diffusion models has shown that semantic and geometric consistency can be
extracted from internal activations, and that useful information is
distributed across both network layers and diffusion timesteps
[
31
,
23
]
. Recent probing of
video diffusion transformers similarly reports that physical and
3D-related signals are most accessible at intermediate blocks and
nontrivial noise levels
[
15
,
12
]
.
This motivates our layer
×
\times
generation-coordinate
×
\times
streaming-prefix analysis: we compare selected extraction settings rather
than assuming that one hidden state characterizes an entire model. Such
profiles describe accessibility during computation, not when a capability
emerges during training.
Spatial representations in foundation models.
Spatial ability is often evaluated through language. SpatialVLM and
SpatialRGPT improve quantitative and region-level spatial question
answering by training vision-language models on large synthetic spatial
data
[
7
,
10
]
, and VSI-Bench asks
multimodal LLMs to remember and recall the layout of a space from video,
finding that generating cognitive maps improves distance estimates
[
39
]
. Cambrian-S argues that such training
alone does not yield robust implicit spatial representations and proposes
predictive sensing, in which latent next-frame prediction decides what to
remember
[
40
]
. A growing set of studies probes the
representations themselves. SeeSE3 finds subspaces of self-supervised
vision features that align with 3D Euclidean space, with camera motion
linearly accessible from feature displacements
[
8
]
;
SpaRRTa shows that visual foundation models differ markedly in how well
they encode the relative positions of objects
[
19
]
;
probes of V-JEPA 2 and VideoMAE-v2 decode camera motion best at 60–70%
of network depth while intuitive physics stays near chance
[
28
]
, and in video encoders, motion direction
becomes decodable only within an intermediate-depth zone
[
16
]
. For multimodal LLMs, the spatial benefit of
a visual representation tracks its 3D structure, measured by the
cross-view consistency of latent features or the accuracy of explicit
geometry
[
14
]
. Our study complements these probes by reading
several functional levels of spatial state, including object persistence,
predictive update, and goal use, from the same ten representations under
matched controls.
World models and embodied representations.
Video world models aim to support interaction and planning. Genie learns
an action-controllable interactive environment from unlabeled Internet
videos
[
5
]
; Navigation World Models predict future
observations from past observations and navigation actions and use them to
plan
[
3
]
; DINO-WM and V-JEPA 2 plan with predictors in a
pre-trained or self-supervised feature space
[
43
,
1
]
; and Aether jointly learns 4D
reconstruction, action-conditioned video prediction, and goal-conditioned
visual planning
[
44
]
. Whether video generators capture
physical regularities remains contested: diffusion models trained on
simulated motion generalize within the training distribution but fail
outside it
[
18
]
. For embodied learning, SPA shows that
adding 3D spatial awareness to a vision encoder improves downstream policy
learning across many simulated tasks
[
45
]
. Our L3 and L4
probes ask a narrower question of frozen features: whether ego-motion
updates and goal-conditioned actions can be read out from the represented
state.
Object-centric representations and persistence.
Object-centric learning explicitly decomposes scenes into entity-level
latent variables. Slot Attention learns exchangeable slots that bind to
objects, and sequential extensions such as SAVi propagate and correct
object slots through video
[
21
,
20
]
.
These approaches build an object-centric format into the architecture,
whereas the foundation models we evaluate generally use distributed patch
or video tokens, and we do not assume that their internal state is
slot-based. Our question is operational: can an object’s bearing be
recovered after it is no longer visible? This differs from
violation-of-expectation benchmarks such as IntPhys 2, which assess the
discrimination of possible from impossible events involving permanence,
continuity, solidity, or immutability
[
4
]
; V-JEPA
surprise scores perform well on several such conditions
[
13
]
, but plausibility discrimination does
not measure object persistence directly. In generated video, current world
models usually resume a target that comes back into view in the state it
was left in, rather than letting its event progress while it was unseen
[
22
]
. We therefore predict an explicit
bearing in the current camera frame and use history interventions to test
which visual evidence supports that readout.
6
Discussion and Conclusion
We characterized spatial state representations through four functional
levels: spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update,
and actionability. Across ten frozen representations, no model leads on
every task, and the readouts vary with the extraction layer and the
streaming prefix. The levels are linked by two ingredient chains:
camera-pose readout supports object persistence, which in turn supports
goal-conditioned action, whereas feature prediction builds on
visible-scene readout and is unrelated to persistence. Matched controls
show that decodability, input use, and functional utility dissociate: a
probe can localize accurately without using history, a natively predicted
feature retains recoverable structure but not the original readout
interface, and a goal-sensitive action readout need not benefit from the
correct goal. Together, these results support multidimensional evaluation
of spatial state beyond a single task score. Our conclusions concern
frozen feature interfaces, trained probes, and offline indoor
trajectories: independently encoded causal prefixes characterize what a
representation of the observed history affords rather than an incremental
state update, and retrieval scores in different target feature spaces do
not share a physical error scale.

over the same resampled scenes. Each metric is recomputed from the saved
per-sample predictions as a ratio of per-scene sums, and the recomputed
point estimates equal the reported values for every cell shown. For
retrieval, the gallery stays the full validation set and only the queries
are resampled; the action gains in
Table
9
are
paired per query. The intervals describe evaluation sampling for the
single training seed; they do not estimate training-seed variability.

A.7
Additional protocol details
One-step prediction and history interventions.
The correct/copy and matched-wrong-motion tests use 276 samples from 69
scenes per prefix; the restricted retrieval pool contains eight
pose-displacement-matched candidates drawn with candidate seed 42. The
p12 object-persistence controls use 165 samples from 65 scenes. Both
studies use probe training seed 42. Reported intervals are paired 95%
scene-clustered bootstrap intervals. The two tested prediction prefixes
are not strictly target-paired, so agreement across them does not isolate
a history-length effect.
For localization, the appearance query is pooled using a historical
object mask; neither that mask nor the camera pose is supplied to the
spatial readout. Content-only shuffling and reversal retain the final
frame and the temporal identifiers. Moving tokens together with their
identifiers is a permutation sanity check, not a distinct temporal-order
intervention.

A.9
Action readout protocol and controls
Goal-conditioned action prediction: candidate-selection setting.
The candidate experiment uses 844 training queries (650 fit and 194
development) from 289 scenes and 227 validation queries from 77 disjoint
scenes. A shallow scorer receives the frozen current and goal features
plus each candidate 9D action. Ground-truth poses, utilities, realized
endpoints, and scene identities are not given to the scorer. Accuracy is
summarized across three training seeds. The endpoint reference observes
realized outcomes and is diagnostic rather than a candidate-selection
method with the same information.

scenes (803 fit and 221 development before refitting) and 256 validation

article.headline: 视觉基础模型四种空间能力逐层探测
article.lede: 研究用冻结特征探针在流式第一视角观测中评估十种视觉基础模型的四层空间能力，发现能力排序随任务、层和前缀长度变化。
article.problem: 空间感知不只是识别单帧图像，还需要在自我运动下维持一个可更新的空间状态：记住已离开视野的物体、预测未来观测，并用它指导行动。论文追问：视觉基础模型的冻结表征是否真的支持这种状态？
article.method: 作者把空间状态拆成四级功能——空间结构、物体持久性、预测性空间更新和可行动性，在ScanNet++的流式第一视角室内轨迹上用冻结特征探针评估十种表征。实验扫描网络层和因果前缀长度，并加入运动、历史、变换顺序与目标的匹配控制，以区分“可解码”与“真正使用输入”。
article.results: 没有模型在所有任务领先：Fast3R的相机位姿AUC@30最高（0.3870）、物体持久性误差最低（32.79°），但直接未来特征预测R@1仅0.0133；DINOv2直接预测最高（0.2373），V-JEPA2路径积分最高（0.1588）。物体持久性与相机位姿读出的跨模型秩相关为ρ=0.76；在56个模型—指标端点对中45个偏向更短前缀p8，八个模型的物体持久性配对全部在更长前缀下变差。目标条件动作中，替换目标使预测方向旋转29.8–45.6°，但连续输出设置下FULL相对CURRENT-ONLY的正进度差为−3.6到−2.0个百分点，仅V-JEPA2区间排除零；候选选择准确率为75.9–79.9%，高于67.8%的动作基线，但打乱目标会降低12.2–20.7个百分点。
article.why_it_matters: 结果提示，评估空间表征不能只看当前场景能否被解码，还要看信息能否在离开视野后保持、能否预测性更新、能否用于目标导向行动。这对世界模型和具身智能中的表征选择与探针评测有直接参考价值。
article.limitations: 结论仅针对冻结特征、训练探针和离线静态室内轨迹，独立编码的因果前缀并不等同于在线状态更新，不同模型特征空间的R@1也不共享物理误差尺度；此外Fast3R训练数据含ScanNet++，部分验证场景可能在其训练场景中，其领先可能部分来自场景熟悉。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从流式第一视角观测构建空间状态：L1空间结构、L2物体持久性、L3预测性空间更新、L4可行动性。

figure.caption: {Spatial state representations from streaming egocentric observations.} A moving observer builds an internal spatial representation from partial views of an environment. {L1} ( {spatial structure}) captures scene geometry and object identity across views. {L2} ( {object persistence}) retains the observer-relative locations of previously seen objects after they leave the field of view. {L3} ( {predictive spatial update}) anticipates what the observer would see after an action or a sequence of actions. {L4} ( {actionability}) uses the represented state and a specified goal to select an action that makes progress toward that goal.

email_papers.content:
Cross-Controller Transfer via In-Context Behavior Adaptation
Jonathan Yang
Affiliation:
Department of Computer Science
Stanford University
Stanford, CA, USA
Chelsea Finn
Affiliation:
Department of Computer Science
Stanford University
Stanford, CA, USA
Dorsa Sadigh
Affiliation:
Department of Computer Science
Stanford University
Stanford, CA, USA
Abstract
Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. We study how to transfer robot data across both embodiments and controllers without allowing conflicting action interpretations to interfere with learning. Our setting spans six controller types as well as variations in controller gains and compliance. We propose a framework that encodes behavioral interaction under a controller through examples of commanded actions and the resulting robot motions. A transformer context encoder summarizes these interactions, allowing a single policy to adapt in context. Across real-world experiments, our method improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50% success on unseen controller modes and 52% on unseen controller gains, and transfers to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, behavioral interaction context enables the policy to adapt not only its actions but also its strategy. Our results provide a path toward generalist robot policies that can leverage data collected across diverse action interpretations. For more information, visit
https://controller-transfer.github.io
.
Index Terms:
Robot Learning, Cross-Controller Transfer, In-Context Adaptation, Imitation Learning, Manipulation.
Fig. 1:
Cross-Controller Transfer.
We train a generalist policy that adapts its manipulation strategy across a dense spectrum of unseen controller types and continuous gains by conditioning on interaction history.
I
Introduction
Deploying a policy on a new robot raises a deceptively simple question:
how will its actions actually move the robot?
Scaling robot datasets has produced increasingly general policies that operate across diverse scenes, tasks, and embodiments. Yet most policies assume that large portions of their data share the same controller per robot and that the controller used at deployment is known a priori. This assumption is limiting: in reality, data contains significant variability across control spaces (e.g., joint vs. Cartesian), control targets (e.g., position vs. velocity), and control parameters (e.g., varying stiffness or gains). For example, data collected through VR teleoperation might encode compliant Cartesian commands, while data collected through puppeteering might encode stiff joint targets, causing the exact same action vector
𝐚
\mathbf{a}
to have substantially different physical interpretations. Moreover, even on the same embodiment, different tasks may benefit from different controllers. In this paper, we study the question:
how can we learn from data collected across this wide range of controller configurations?
Two lines of prior work inform controller transfer, but address different parts of the problem. Cross-embodiment research has shown that data can transfer across robots with different morphologies, sensors, and action spaces, but typically assumes a single, fixed controller for each robot setup. For example, in large-scale multi-robot policies like RT-X
[
1
]
, a specific robot and its associated controller are uniquely tied to a distinct physical lab or background. Consequently, the policy can easily infer the controller setup purely from the visual scene, sidestepping the challenge of conflicting action interpretations. Meanwhile, research on compliant control shows that controller choice directly impacts task performance
[
2
]
. For example, data collected with a controller that feels natural to a human teleoperator may not produce the data most beneficial for policy learning
[
3
]
. However, this line of work typically studies how to select or tune a controller for a particular robot and task, rather than how to learn from data collected under many controllers. Our work bridges these two directions: we study how a generalist policy can pool demonstration data with conflicting action interpretations and adapt its behavior when the active controller cannot be inferred from the visual scene.
At first glance, one might treat controller transfer as a dynamics problem: identify the active controller and analytically remap actions to match nominal forces or kinematics. However, dynamics remapping only preserves how an existing motion is realized under new dynamics, not how an expert would choose to act. Consider USB insertion: under a compliant controller, a human demonstrator deliberately presses against the port and searches laterally for alignment. Under a stiff controller, that same contact-seeking trajectory causes the connector to jam, requiring a cautious, alignment-first approach that avoids contact altogether. While system identification or torque matching can predict how a controller will respond to an action, it cannot invent the strategy an expert would adopt. Cross-controller transfer is therefore not a matter of remapping dynamics, but of inferring the appropriate behavioral strategy and determining the actions that will realize that strategy.
Learning controller-dependent strategies from controller parameters and the current observation alone would require dense demonstration coverage across task–controller combinations, which is costly to collect on physical robots. Instead, we condition the policy on interaction trajectories collected under the deployment controller, even when those trajectories come from other tasks. A transformer context encoder inspired by Perceiver
[
4
]
compresses these interactions into a fixed set of tokens that condition a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy. By learning across source tasks, the policy can reuse this behavioral interaction context to select an appropriate strategy for a target task with little or no target-task data under that controller. Finally, since physical demonstrations inevitably have limited controller coverage, we also introduce a synthetic data augmentation scheme that analytically remaps actions across controllers; the behavioral context disambiguates the resulting multimodal action modes, enabling safe scaling across diverse controllers.
We make three contributions. First, we formulate cross-controller transfer as behavioral adaptation under conflicting action interpretations, distinguishing the problem from system identification and action remapping. Second, we develop a context-conditioned VLA policy that combines synthetic controller relabeling with a Perceiver encoder, which compresses commanded–achieved interaction histories into fixed-length tokens for adaptation without test-time training. Third, we evaluate the approach across five real-world manipulation tasks, six controller types, and continuous gain variations. When tasks are demonstrated under only a single controller type, our method improves zero-shot success by
23
23
percentage points over task-neutral dynamics context, improves success by
35
35
percentage points over synthetic relabeling alone on unseen controller modes, and transfers behavioral context across contact-rich tasks while retaining
78
%
78\%
of in-domain performance.
II
Related Work
Cross-Embodiment Learning.
Recent generalist policies have demonstrated positive tranfer scaling data by by aggregating demonstrations across diverse robots, scenes, and tasks
[
5
,
6
,
1
,
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
]
. To accommodate varying kinematic limits and command formats, architectures such as CrossFormer
[
12
]
and Octo
[
13
]
use embodiment-specific action heads and encoders, while UniVLA
[
14
]
learns latent actions decoded into platform-specific controls. While these approaches bridge structural differences across action
spaces
, they treat the underlying controller for each embodiment as fixed, implicitly assuming the control stack can be inferred from the visual scene. At scale, this assumption breaks down: when the same robot uses different controllers across tasks or teleoperation setups, the visual scene no longer identifies how commands are realized, leading to conflicting action interpretations.
Controller Adaptation and Policy Learning.
A complementary line of research studies how low-level controllers and action-space representations govern policy learning and physical interaction
[
15
,
16
,
17
,
18
,
19
,
2
]
. These works demonstrate that controller choice and compliance strongly shape learnability, with compliant impedance control outperforming stiff position control in contact-rich tasks
[
3
]
. Recent methods further expand this capability by making compliance practical on commodity arms without dedicated force-torque sensing
[
20
,
21
,
22
]
. However, this body of work almost universally studies controllers in isolation: selecting, tuning, or learning a specific controller for a single robot and task. A related direction conditions policies on execution factors such as speed
[
23
]
, showing that a single policy can flexibly modulate how it acts. However, these works do not address how a policy can learn from datasets pooled across heterogeneous controllers.
Online Policy Adaptation.
Our work is closely related to a learning-based line that adapts policies to physical variation without re-tuning. System identification and dynamics randomization
[
24
]
help policies accommodate changes such as terrain friction or payload; however, they target plant dynamics rather than manipulation strategy. In parallel, in-context and memory-augmented policies
[
25
,
26
,
27
]
adapt behavior directly from past trajectory context without retraining. Our method bridges both: rather than identify physical parameters, we cast cross-controller transfer as in-context policy conditioning, compressing a short history of commanded-versus-achieved transitions so that a generalist VLA infers how the deployment controller behaves and adapts its manipulation strategy accordingly.

VII
Conclusion
Our investigation demonstrates that the standard recipe for scaling generalist robot policies, pooling demonstrations across laboratories, breaks down at scale without considering controllers. Classical dynamics remapping and system identification fail to bridge this divide: matching instantaneous forces along an existing path can replicate motions, but cannot synthesize the compliant or exploratory strategies that are more robust under different dynamics. Our method compresses interaction histories through a fixed-size bottleneck, yielding a compact representation that can transfer useful behavioral evidence across distinct manipulation tasks. A key limitation of this approach is that analytical relabeling assumes impedance-style causality and may not directly extend to admittance controllers; furthermore, our conclusions reflect a single VLA architecture and laboratory setting.

article.headline: 跨控制器迁移：从交互历史推断操作策略
article.lede: 斯坦福团队提出跨控制器迁移框架，用交互历史让单个VLA策略适应六类控制器和连续增益，并在真实操作任务上验证。
article.problem: 通用机器人策略通常假设每台机器人对应单一控制器，但不同控制空间、控制目标和增益会让同一动作向量具有不同物理含义。直接把多控制器数据合并训练，会让策略在冲突的专家行为之间平均，而系统辨识或动力学重映射只能复现既有运动，无法恢复专家在新控制器下会采用的策略。
article.method: 作者把跨控制器迁移表述为行为适应问题：策略以部署控制器上采集的命令动作与实现运动轨迹作为上下文，并用类似Perceiver的Transformer编码器压缩成固定256个token，条件化一个π0.5 VLA策略。训练时结合解析的控制器重标记扩充数据，并用与目标轨迹不相交的交互上下文消除重标记带来的多模态动作冲突。
article.results: 在5个真实操作任务、6种控制器类型和连续增益设置上，零样本跨任务行为上下文的平均成功率为50.0%，高于SysID的27.0%和仅控制器元数据的12.0%，接近同控制器上界75.0%。未见控制器模式下成功率为50.3%，朴素联合策略为17.5%（提升32.8个百分点）；未见增益下为52.0%，朴素池化为28.5%、仅重标记为23.5%。复用工具头插入的上下文条件化USB插入达到35%成功率，保留78%的域内性能。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作为利用多实验室、多遥操作设置中动作解释不一致的数据提供了路径，有望减少为每种控制器单独采集密集演示的需求。接触丰富任务中，策略还能从交互历史推断出顺应或搜索等控制器相关策略，而不仅是重映射动作。
article.limitations: 作者指出，解析重标记假设阻抗式因果，可能不直接适用于导纳控制器；结论也仅基于一种VLA架构和单一实验室环境。跨任务上下文复用并非显式监督，而是作为涌现泛化能力评估，仍需更多验证。

page_papers.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
page_papers.abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.
