Appendix C
The algorithm of customization style transfer and color style transfer
Due to the page limitation, we summarize the process of customization style transfer in Algorithm
1
and color style transfer in Algorithm
2
.
To tackle the text-alignment issue in personalized image generation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages.

Appendix D
More details about the implementation details
As mentioned in Sec.3.1 of the mainbody, due to page limitation, we further provide more details about the implementation details as follows:
Datasets.
We evaluate
Dual-FDM
on combined datasets covering image customization, style transfer, and text-to-image (T2I) generation:
•
Image Customization
: 1)
DreamBench
Ruiz et al. (2023)
+
TI benchmark
Gal et al. (2022)
: a well-known single-object personalized image generation dataset comprising 38 subjects, covering unique objects and pets such as backpacks, stuffed animals, dogs, cats, sunglasses, and cartoons, with each subject associated with 25 prompts; 2)
DreamBench++
Peng et al. (2025)
: the latest human-aligned personalized image generation benchmark, comprising 65 object classes, 20 human classes, and 45 animal classes. For each image, 9 text prompts are generated by GPT-4o to span a range of difficulty levels.
•
Style Transfer
: 1)
IS-Plus benchmark
Wang et al. (2024b)
: a style evaluation benchmark containing 104 images across diverse styles; 2)
StyleBench
Gao et al. (2024)
: a style evaluation benchmark covering 73 distinct styles, ranging from paintings, flat illustrations, and 3D rendering to sculptures with varying materials. For each style, 5–7 distinct images with variations are collected. In total, StyleBench contains 490 images across diverse styles.
•
T2I generation
:
T2I-CompBench++
Huang et al. (2025a)
: an enhanced benchmark for compositional text-to-image generation. T2I-CompBench++ comprises 8,000 compositional text prompts categorized into four primary groups: attribute binding, object relationships, generative numeracy, and complex compositions. These are further divided into eight sub-categories.
Based on the above, we construct several combined datasets for different joint tasks: 1) for customization style transfer (small-scale), we concatenate
DreamBench
and
TI benchmark
as the customization references, and use
IS-Plus benchmark
as the style references; 2) for customization style transfer (large-scale), we take
DreamBench++
as the customization references and
StyleBench
as the style references; 3) for color style transfer, we combine
InstantStyle-Plus
and
StyleBench
as the color and style references, while text prompts are provided by
T2I-CompBench++
for stylized image generation.
Metrics.
We consider 9 evaluation metrics from three aspects to evaluate our
Dual-FDM
:
•
Text and Image Reference Alignment
: we follow previous methods and adopt two representative models,
CLIP
2
2
2
Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.
and
DINO
Caron et al. (2021)
, for evaluation. Specifically,
CLIP-T
measures the similarity between generated images and the given text prompts;
CLIP-TC
and
CLIP-TS
evaluate the similarity between generated images and customized (or style) reference images while jointly considering the text prompts; finally,
CLIP-CS
assesses the similarity between generated images and dual-reference images.
•
Image Generation Quality
: we employ Image Reward (
IR
)
Xu et al. (2023)
to model human preferences for image quality and
HPS V2
Wu et al. (2023)
that combines perceptual studies with deep learning for comprehensive visual and semantic assessment. Both metrics measure the semantics consistency of the high-quality image generation aligned with human standards;
•
Time Complexity
: We employ the inference time (
Times
) and Video Random Access Memory (
VRAM
) consumption to evaluate the computational efficiency and memory footprint of different methods during image generation.
Model Configuration.
Our main experiments are conducted on the pre-trained IP-Adapter-Plus
Ye et al. (2023)
with SDXL
Podell et al. (2023)
model as the text-to-image diffusion model, configured with 30 sampling steps and and a fixed random seed of 42, to ensure high-quality outputs. We use the recommended hyper-parameters for each method across all images to ensure fair comparison. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and conducted on a NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist
1.
Claims
Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We confirm the main claims reflect the paper’s contributions and scope.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.
•
The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A
[No]
or
[N/A]
answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.
•
The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.
•
It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.
2.
Limitations
Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: The paper have conducted a discussion of limiations in the Appendix.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper has no limitation while the answer
[No]
means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.
•
The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.
•
The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.
•
The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.
•
The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.
•
The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.
•
If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.
•
While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.
3.
Theory assumptions and proofs

[N/A]

Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include theoretical results.
•
All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.
•
All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.
•
The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.
•
Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

[Yes]

D
of the Appendix and carefully described the experimental metrics in the experimental chapter. The information we provide is sufficient and detailed for replication purposes.
Guidelines:
•
The answer

means that the paper does not include experiments.

If the paper includes experiments, a
[No]
answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example
(a)
If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

article.headline: 用频域解耦双参考图，兼顾定制与风格迁移
article.lede: 合工大团队提出 Dual-FDM：在扩散模型频域中拆分双参考图的低/中频分量，缓解文本提示被参考图压制的问题。
article.problem: 个性化图像生成要同时用参考图定制前景、迁移背景风格，但现有扩散模型常出现文本错位：定制任务里参考图前景压过文本描述的背景，风格迁移任务里背景风格泄漏到前景、导致生成图与提示词（如物体数量、空间关系）不符。作者把根源归到去噪过程中低、中、高频段的纠缠——低频管颜色、中频管全局结构、高频管局部纹理，而早期高噪声阶段以低中频为主，二者在单一参考图内互相强化，压制了文本引导。
article.method: 方法先用 DCT 把参考图的前景或背景变换到频域，用二值掩码按坐标和切出低、中、高频段；通过 SVD 分解解耦交叉注意力中的 key 投影矩阵，并将奇异值取倒数构造背景矩阵，以抑制前景、增强背景。定制风格迁移（Dual-FDM_cust）把风格参考背景的中频段替换为定制参考前景的中频段；颜色风格迁移（Dual-FDM_cost）把风格参考背景的低频段替换为颜色参考前景与背景的低频段，替换后的频段作为 key/value 重建去噪图像的 query。两个任务再用替换频段的信息熵比值自适应划分早期/晚期去噪时间步。
article.results: 在 DreamBench/TI benchmark 与 DreamBench++ 等数据集上，Dual-FDM_cust 的 CLIP-T 为 0.3194、CLIP-TC 为 0.5031、IR 为 5.3487、HPS 为 2.6007，均高于表中最强基线 MS-Diffusion（CLIP-T 0.3123）及 MS-Diffusion+CSGO 组合；颜色风格迁移在 T2I-CompBench++ 上 CLIP-TS 0.5015、CLIP-S 0.7178、DINO-S 0.4970，高于 StyleAligned 的 0.4832/0.7256/0.5171 中的 CLIP-TS 与部分子项。效率上单次推理 10.26 秒、显存 12.48 GB，优于 MS-Diffusion 的 14.68 秒、16.85 GB。附录频域统计显示去噪过程中低频指标基本不变（Mean Gray 119.5→120.9），高频指标显著上升（Avg Gradient 59.01→233.88）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「参考图压过文本」这一经验性缺陷落到频段纠缠上，并给出无需重训练的即插即用替换策略，对定制化生成与风格迁移的统一建模提供了一个可复用的频域视角。
article.limitations: 作者自述当风格参考只含极稀疏的线条式图案时，中频定制线索会削弱高频风格细节，导致风格信息不完整；此外实验只在 IP-Adapter+SDXL、30 步、固定随机种子的设置下评测，未报告误差棒或显著性检验，部分指标（如定制任务的 CLIP-TS 0.4516）并未超过基线。

HERO: Learning
H
umanoid
E
nd-Effector Cont
ro
l for Visual Whole-Body Open-Vocabulary Object Grasping
Runpei Dong
†
†
thanks:
Equal contribution.
Ziyan Li
1
1
footnotemark:
1
Arjun Gupta
Xialin He
Saurabh Gupta
Affiliation:
University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Affiliation:
hero-humanoid.github.io
Abstract
Visual loco-manipulation of arbitrary in-the-wild objects requires accurate
end-effector (EE) control and a generalizable understanding of the scene from
visual inputs (
e.g.
, RGB-D images). Existing imitation and sim2real methods
jointly learn both these aspects via monolithic end-to-end learning and are
thus hard to scale. In this work, we bring to bear the best tools for each
of these problems – large vision models for generalizable scene understanding
and simulated training for accurate EE control – leading to an overall modular
loco-manipulation system that exhibits strong generalization. Our core
technical innovation is HERO, an accurate residual-aware EE tracking policy
made possible by combining classical robotics with machine learning. It uses a)
inverse kinematics to convert residual end-effector targets into reference
trajectories, b) a learned neural forward model for accurate forward
kinematics, and c) goal adjustment and replanning. Together, these innovations
reduce the end-effector tracking error to 2.44cm, outperforming the strongest
prior method by 5.5
×
\times
. Our overall system operates in diverse
real-world environments, from offices to coffee shops, where the robot reliably
grasps various everyday objects (
e.g.
, mugs, apples, toys) on surfaces ranging
from 43cm to 92cm in height. Systematic modular and end-to-end tests
demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed design. We believe our advances
open up new ways of training humanoids to interact with daily objects.
Figure 1:

So what are the ingredients of building a highly accurate end-effector tracker?
Our accurate end-effector control algorithm is based on multiple innovations.
First, rather than directly trying to get the end-effector to the target
location, we use a motion planner to generate an upper-body reference motion
that gets the end-effector to the desired target. Second, the policy receives
as input not just the current and target joint angles (output of the motion
planner), but also the current and target end-effector position. Third, it is
important to obtain a high-quality estimate of the current end-effector
position, as we found that the default analytical forward kinematics and odometry on a
low-cost humanoid robot like Unitree G1 are not accurate. We mitigate this
issue by training neural forward models: an upper body model that provides
accurate EE pose relative to the base, and a base odometry model that provides
an accurate base pose relative to the stationary feet.
Fourth, because whole-body balancing causes the planned reference to drift relative to the target, we periodically replan from the current state and odometry-corrected goal in a closed loop.
Finally, a goal-adjustment loop iteratively nudges the commanded pose to remove the systematic sim2real gap.
Using this performant end-effector tracking policy, we develop a modular
system for picking up open-vocabulary novel objects in novel everyday
environments. This modular system leverages an open-vocabulary perception module
to detect and segment the target object using large pre-trained vision
models (Grounding DINO 1.5
[
47
]
and SAM-3
[
5
]
).
We next use the AnyGrasp model
[
11
]
to
produce parallel jaw grasps on the candidate object. We retarget them to the
Dex-3 dexterous hand on the Unitree robot. Finally, we use our tracker as a low-level
controller to achieve the grasp pose. In real-world testing for grasping
open-vocabulary object queries in novel environments, our system achieves a
success rate of 90% on 10 daily objects across standard and short table
heights, 73.3% success rate on generalization to 10 daily scenes, and 80%
success rate on cluttered scenes.

Residual Neural Leg Odometry.
Different from fixed-base object manipulation tasks, where the robot’s base is fixed and stable, humanoid robots’ base needs to be dynamically balanced during whole-body reaching.
This movement makes the original reaching target inaccurate, as the reaching target defined in the robot frame is no longer the same place where the object lies.
One might consider using the egocentric visual information for replanning or motion adjustment.
However, as shown in
Fig.
4

As a result, using the robot’s odometry to adjust the reaching goal is critical.
We assume the feet to be static on the ground and use the lower body joint angles to predict the base pose.
By assuming the robot ankle joint as the root joint and the robot base as the end-effector, we can compute the base pose using forward kinematics.

Discussions and Limitations
We present a modular humanoid system that separates open-vocabulary
action planning
from simulator-trained
action controller
, achieving 90% success on daily-object grasping without large-scale real-world imitation.
This decomposition lets large vision models handle visual generalization while a learned motion tracker executes whole-body reaching. The experiments show two lessons: task-space state must be accurate (analytical FK has 1.30cm EE error while ours reaches 0.50cm), and explicit error feedback during closed-loop execution effectively reduces real-world drifts (our tracker reaches 2.5cm error).
Remaining limitations include restricted egocentric FoV for far or high targets, motivating active neck control and visual servoing
[
57
,
90
,
81
]
; inefficient motions, motivating learned motion priors; and modular failures
[
46
,
19
]
plus dexterity limits, motivating better hands and retargeting.

A.3
Moving Object Grasping with Visual Replanning
HERO derives target grasping poses from vision and language queries, enabling the robot to capture moving objects through closed-loop replanning.
Fig.
13
(a-b) illustrates this dynamic adaptation: while the system initially generates an EE trajectory based on the first vision perception, it re-estimates the pose as the object moves.
This visual feedback triggers the update of the target grasp, allowing the robot to seamlessly adjust its trajectory and successfully secure the moving object.
Note that, in these two trials, the robot successfully sees the object after moving, but the object can only be seen at the corner due to the rather limited field of view.

stapler
) is detected.
After successfully detecting the target object, the robot stops walking and grasps the object via whole-body coordination.
The robot can only see the object within 0.6m, which makes it hard for the robot to search for the object in a random room.

article.headline: 人形机器人末端跟踪误差降至2.44厘米
article.lede: UIUC团队用大视觉模型负责「看」、仿真训练的策略负责「动」，让人形机器人抓取任意物体。
article.problem: 视觉loco-manipulation要求人形机器人在没有参考动作、也没有动捕等特权传感器的真实环境中，仅凭机载RGB-D推断物体位置，并把手准确地送到目标处。现有的端到端模仿学习受限于真实数据采集，仿真视觉强化学习（RL）受限于场景真实度和物体类别，这两类方法都难以泛化到新物体和新环境。更关键的是，现有方法控制人形机器人手部的精度不足：领先的跟踪器SONIC在真实世界中的末端跟踪误差为13.38厘米，远达不到抓取所需。
article.method: HERO把末端目标经逆运动学转成上身关节目标和基座高度，交给无碰撞运动规划器生成参考轨迹，再由仿真中PPO训练的全身策略以50Hz跟踪，并将学习的残差前向运动学与残差腿部里程计算出的末端位姿误差作为反馈输入。为消除全身平衡带来的参考漂移和sim2real系统偏差，系统每300步（6秒）用当前状态和里程计校正后的目标重规划一次，并以阻尼方式微调指令抓取位姿。感知端用Grounding DINO 1.5检测、SAM-3分割、AnyGrasp生成平行夹爪抓取，再重定向到Unitree G1上的Dex-3三指手。
article.results: 真实动捕测量下，HERO末端平移误差2.44厘米、姿态误差8.22度，相比SONIC的13.38厘米降低5.5倍（PD控制为12.09厘米、40.82度）。在10种日常物体、标准0.74米与矮桌0.56米两种高度上抓取成功率为90%（27/30），PD控制为10%，自动SONIC为16.7%；10个日常场景泛化为73.3%（22/30），杂乱场景为80%（12/15）。仿真中HERO平移误差为2.48厘米，优于SONIC的4.10厘米、AMO的8.29厘米和FALCON的13.57厘米。学习的FK把末端估计误差从解析FK的1.30厘米降到0.50厘米；去掉重规划后，真实世界误差从2.44厘米升至5.17厘米。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明，不依赖大规模真实模仿数据，把现成的大视觉模型和仿真训练的高精度末端控制器组合起来，人形机器人也能在新场景里响应开放词汇指令抓取新物体。
article.limitations: 论文承认机载第一人称视野受限：实验中机器人在1.28米处看不到目标，只有走到约0.6米内才能检测到，远处或高处目标需要主动颈部控制和视觉伺服；此外动作效率不高，模块化流程存在级联失败风险，Dex-3手灵巧度也限制了抓取。开门演示中，门被事先保持未上锁。
article.figure_caption_zh: HERO依据“冰箱把手”语言指令定位并抓取把手，随后在返回默认姿态的过程中把门拉开。

figure.caption: {Door opening with HERO}. (a) The egocentric RGB-D visual inputs. (b) Given a language query for the door handle ( , {``fridge handle''} prompted here), our modular system obtains the grasping pose, same as the pipeline for picking up objects. (c) The robot executes the reaching trajectory and closes the hand when reaching the target poses closely, and then returns to the default pose with the door opened. Note that while the door is heavy, HERO successfully manages to open the door with a smooth and stable door motion.

Abstract
In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations.
Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning.
In a randomized, double-blind crossover study (
N
=
60
N{=}60
matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts.
The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs (
p
<
0.0001
p<0.0001
), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric (

p

p<0.001
), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%,
p

p<0.001
).
Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model’s clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294,
p
<
0.0001
p<0.0001
).
To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%,
p
<
0.0001
p<0.0001
).
Substantial clinical gaps nonetheless remained, with comprehensive and appropriate treatment recommended in only 46.7% of human-evaluated encounters, at least one critical intake question omitted in 60.6% of simulated intakes, and acute safety risks under-triaged in 12.9% of adversarial presentations.
Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters. However, addressing residual diagnostic, management, and safety limitations, alongside integrating external safeguards and clinician-supervised workflows, remains necessary before prospective clinical validation with real patients.
1

Introduction
Clinical dialogue is foundational to patient-facing medicine, but in psychiatry, the clinical interview itself remains a principal diagnostic instrument
144
. In psychiatric presentations, the psychopathology itself can directly compromise how history is communicated, and patients often do not recognize the relevance of prior treatment failures or comorbid medical conditions causing their symptoms
25
;
10
;
39
. As a result, the quality of the history depends on both systematic inquiry into these complex causes and interpersonal trust, with a stronger therapeutic alliance supporting more complete diagnostic formulation and improved treatment outcomes
149
;
119
;
180
. Competent clinical dialogue couples two skill domains, diagnostic reasoning (differential diagnosis, psychopharmacology, risk stratification) and interpersonal processing (reading affect and psychological defenses, crisis de-escalation, shared decision-making, stigma-sensitive communication)
92
;
2
;
176
. In psychiatry, both dimensions are especially entangled. A clinician who probes aggressively risks rupturing rapport; one who overprioritizes validation may never arrive at a diagnosis. Here we investigate whether language models can acquire these capabilities through training in simulated clinical environments.
Figure 1:
Overview of contributions.
The proposed framework involves training a language model in a simulated environment and evaluating it with human experts.
Left (Training in Simulation),
The training process comprises three components:
a,
Scenario Generation, which synthesizes clinical, behavioral, and demographic data into verified patient scenarios using a language model;
b,
Simulation, where the model engages in multi-turn interactions with a simulated patient; and
c,
Reinforcement Learning, which uses an autorater to grade conversation transcripts against a clinical rubric and updates the policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
Top Right (Evaluating with Standardized Patients),
The trained model (trained in simulation) and its base model act as the clinician in randomized, double-blind text conversations with board-certified psychiatrists acting as standardized patients. Separate independent, board-certified psychiatrist evaluators (blinded to whether transcripts came from the trained or base model) and the role-playing clinician-patients score the encounters across multiple dimensions (e.g., perceived empathic behavior, diagnostic formulation, clinical safety, and management plan), as compared across normalized domain scores in the radar chart.
Bottom Right (Evaluating in Simulation),
Automated evaluation across expert-validated scenarios shows that the simulation-trained agent achieved a higher composite clinical reward than its base model overall and across all four difficulty tiers (overall, 0.56 vs. 0.29; easy, 0.65 vs. 0.34; edge, 0.51 vs. 0.25; all
p
<
0.0001
p<0.0001
; left chart). Under 256 adversarial stress-testing presentations (right chart), the trained agent reduced measured safety failure rates relative to its base model, including contraindications (0.8% vs. 6.2%,
p
=
0.001
p=0.001
), missed red flags (6.2% vs. 10.9%,
p
=
0.04
p=0.04
), and clinical under-triage (12.9% vs. 30.5%,
p
<
0.0001
p<0.0001
).
Large language models now perform strongly on clinical question-answering
162
;
163
, clinical reasoning
127
;
14
;
109
;
81
, and conversational diagnosis
176
;
15
;
99
, and a growing body of work applies them to mental health
31
;
166
;
134
;
47
, including psychiatric evaluation datasets
128
;
104
;
35
, clinician-facing decision support
183
, and patient-facing conversational systems. Evaluations of conversational medical AI have nonetheless largely excluded psychiatric presentations
176
;
15
;
99
;
75
. In the general medical settings those systems target, the conversation gathers a history that physical examination and laboratory testing can subsequently supplement; in psychiatry, where critical history and risk factors often emerge through skilled inquiry, the quality of the conversation itself determines the quality of the diagnostic information obtained
144
;
55
;
161
. If eventually validated for clinical use, conversational intake systems may supplement static screening questionnaires in supervised pre-visit workflows by gathering preliminary history, conducting a medical review of systems (i.e., a structured inventory of physical symptoms across organ systems to screen for somatic causes) and medication reconciliation, and organizing a provisional differential diagnosis for the evaluating clinician to review and verify
75
;
131
.
In medical education, clinical competence is developed through structured practice with standardized patients and assessed through Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs)
7
;
61
;
68
. Psychiatry uses the same instrument to rehearse de-escalation, risk stratification, and rapport building under acute ambiguity
137
;
67
. Language models can likewise acquire conversational and sequential decision-making capabilities by interacting with simulated clinical environments, with reported generalization to unseen patient profiles, out-of-distribution diagnostic categories, and multi-turn dialogue settings
100
;
32
;
41
;
88
;
176
, and generative patient simulators increasingly incorporate behavioral phenotypes, biases, and changing emotional states
152
;
151
;
86
. Whether these approaches are sufficient to improve conversational psychiatric competence remains untested.
Here, we trained a large language model with multi-turn reinforcement learning across simulated psychiatric encounters, optimizing jointly for diagnostic accuracy, patient-centered communication, and clinical safety (Fig.
1
). To isolate the effect of training, the simulation-trained agent and its base model were prompted and evaluated identically within each evaluation, sharing the same clinical system prompt and structured tools. We validated the resulting agent in three complementary evaluations:

Results
We report three findings. First, in a randomized, double-blind OSCE with psychiatrists role-playing patients, the simulation-trained agent outperformed its identically prompted base model, with gains in clinical examination skills, patient-centered communication, differential diagnosis formulation, and initial management planning (Section
2.1
). Second, under automated evaluation the same advantage held across 127 expert-validated intake scenarios, and a three-way comparison on the 60 OSCE scenarios located where simulated evaluation departs from the human study (Section
2.2
). Third, under adversarial presentations, training reduced but did not eliminate unsafe behavior, and the residual failures were mainly under-triage and missed red flags, including errors of omission that post-hoc output filters cannot intercept because no overtly harmful text is generated, such as failing to ask the probing questions needed to uncover a concealed crisis or failing to escalate care (Section
2.3
).
2.1

Discussion
We trained a language model with multi-turn reinforcement learning across simulated psychiatric encounters and validated it against its identically prompted base model in three settings. In a randomized, double-blind crossover OSCE with board-certified psychiatrists role-playing standardized patients, the trained agent received a higher independent transcript score than the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs, with gains in clinical examination skills, patient-centered communication, and differential diagnosis formulation (Section
2.1
). Across an automated evaluation of 127 clinician-validated psychiatric intake scenarios, it nearly doubled its base model’s pre-penalty clinical rubric score and substantially improved composite clinical reward, with gains across all four difficulty tiers (Section
2.2
). Under 256 adversarial presentations designed to elicit unsafe clinical behavior, training more than halved under-triage relative to the base model, although residual failures remained (Section
2.3
). Comparing the post-trained agent against its untuned base checkpoint under an identical clinical system prompt, tool interface, and reasoning-token budget isolates the combined effect of the simulation RL pipeline (spanning both adaptation to dynamic patient states and alignment to structured clinical rubrics) from prompt engineering or test-time compute. Because on-policy RL updates model weights from scalar rewards on self-generated trajectories without additional medical corpora, these results also show how far procedural gains carry across clinical tasks. In psychiatric intake, diagnostic reasoning and communication are more tightly coupled than in general medical consultations
176
;
15
, where core symptom histories are less contingent on trust; accordingly, diagnostic formulation scaled with interpersonal and history-taking gains, consistent with building rapport and sustaining structured inquiry unlocking the gated patient disclosures needed to double differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3% in the OSCE). Conversely, downstream management tasks that generally depend on static clinical knowledge rather than conversational elicitation, specifically comprehensive treatment planning (46.7% vs. 26.7% appropriateness across pharmacological and psychotherapeutic recommendations), showed more modest gains and likely remained constrained by both the base model’s parametric capacity and the greater case-level subjectivity of psychiatric treatment selection
75
.
Gains in patient-centered communication were broad, and clinician-patients rated the trained agent as displaying more empathic behavior than the base model during live interaction. These are best read as gains in procedural communication and structured empathic responding, captured in the same direction by all three communication instruments (PCCBP, GMCPQ, and the patient-facing PACES items), rather than as evidence of therapeutic alliance formation, which develops over sustained multi-session relationships
45
. Frequent not-applicable responses on the WAI-SR, an instrument designed for multi-session psychotherapy
62
, are consistent with this distinction (Appendix
A.3
). Whether simulation training also improves alliance in longitudinal settings remains an open question.
Automated multi-turn evaluation complements clinician-enacted assessment by gating diagnostically critical information behind rapport and targeted inquiry, testing interactive clinical interviewing rather than static knowledge recall; the training gain was preserved under an independent out-of-family evaluator (Section
2.2
; Appendix
C.2
). In the adversarial evaluation, simulation training substantially reduced contraindications, missed red flags, and under-triage, but did not eliminate failures when acute risk was concealed behind benign complaints. The composition of these residual failures has direct implications for safety governance. Deterministic guardrails can intercept generation-side harms such as a contraindicated prescription, because the harmful content is present in the output and can be filtered. They cannot address omissions in which the agent never asks the question that would have surfaced a concealed risk, because a post-hoc safety layer has no corresponding content on which to act. Mitigating omission failures therefore requires process-level safeguards external to free-text generation, including structured state-tracking checklists that gate encounter termination on mandatory safety and review-of-systems inquiry, real-time supervisory monitors that audit dialogue state for unprobed red flags, and clinician-in-the-loop verification at handoff. Beyond evaluating our trained model, the clinician-validated intake suite, adversarial stress-testing protocol, and Delphi taxonomies (Table
1
) provide a structured methodology for auditing both commission and omission failures across conversational systems proposed for mental health settings.
How closely automated evaluation tracks clinical judgment is quantified by the three-way comparison on the 60 OSCE scenarios (Section
2.2
). The autorater correlated moderately with the psychiatrists’ ratings on the same transcripts (

Simulated evaluation can therefore order and stress-test models, but neither estimate the size of their differences nor identify the scenarios on which one model outperforms another. As a training environment, however, the same simulator proved sufficient: the gains it produced held when psychiatrists role-played the patients and graded the transcripts.
A documented gap in access to mental health services motivates this line of work. More than 75% of individuals with mental disorders in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment
191
, and even in high-income settings, fewer than one in five individuals with major depressive disorder receive minimally adequate care
173
. Tele-psychiatry supports effective evaluation and treatment delivery for many presentations
71
, which suggests that the encounter format is not the primary barrier to competent assessment, but it does not change the supply of clinician time, since a synchronous consultation occupies a psychiatrist for its full duration whether remote or in person. Addressing this bottleneck does not, however, imply automating psychiatric evaluation or replacing psychiatrists, social workers, or intake clinicians. Given the complexity of psychiatric care and the substantial error rates observed even after simulation training, our findings do not support autonomous deployment of the present system; rather, any prospective near-term clinical role should be strictly assistive and clinician-supervised

;
131
;
53
, such as conducting a structured pre-visit intake to generate a provisional history and symptom summary that a supervising clinician reviews, verifies, and builds upon during the clinical encounter, potentially supplementing routine psychosocial intake or static questionnaires with structured medical review of systems, medication reconciliation, and preliminary differential screening for somatic mimics.
Limitations.
Several methodological and clinical limitations constrain what these results support. First, while multi-institutionally validated synthetic cases help address the scarcity of shareable psychiatric clinical data
75
and allowed training and automated evaluation to scale across the diagnostic taxonomy, simulated and clinician-enacted patients cannot reproduce the full range of rare conditions, backgrounds, motivations, or disorganized communication encountered in clinical practice; unlike trained professional standardized patients (such as those used in clinical trial rater calibration) or real patients, psychiatrists role-playing patients may present symptoms in overly structured, textbook patterns, making validation with professional standardized patients and real patient cohorts essential next steps. Second, our study uses a controlled within-model design comparing a lightweight policy model (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite) against its identically prompted base checkpoint rather than against larger frontier models or human clinicians (such as psychiatrists or psychiatric social workers); while this design keeps multi-turn GRPO rollouts computationally tractable and isolates whether simulation training improves upon static prompt instructions, smaller model capacity likely constrained the ceiling on knowledge-intensive tasks such as comprehensive treatment planning (46.7% comprehensive and appropriate treatment in the OSCE), and future studies evaluating clinical readiness must incorporate human clinical comparators alongside ablations against non-interactive rubric fine-tuning and oracle-history baselines. Third, the training reward and scenario reference rubrics were generated within the same model family (Gemini 3.1 Pro) that served as the primary automated evaluator, introducing circularity risks including verbosity bias, stylistic mimicry, and reward hacking
203
;
182
. Cross-evaluator validation with GPT-5.6-Luna confirmed that a substantial training gain persisted under an independent judge (difference between models 0.165, attenuated from 0.270 under the in-family Gemini evaluator against which the policy was trained), though agreement between language-model judges does not exclude shared stylistic preferences, underscoring why evaluation grounded in human clinical judgment remains essential.
In the three-way concordance analysis (Section
2.2
), only the in-family autorater was compared against psychiatrists on the OSCE transcripts. Furthermore, because each OSCE transcript was graded by a single psychiatrist (with different evaluators across each pair), cross-rater reproducibility could not be estimated directly (Appendix
A.6
). Although transcript formatting and turn-count metadata were standardized and independent evaluators graded unpaired transcripts, the trained agent’s substantially longer consultations (median 60 vs. 8 clinician turns) could partially cue crossover clinician-patients during live interaction; however, independent psychiatrist score gains were not significantly correlated with turn-count differences across scenarios (

The simulated and clinician-patient settings also used different interfaces (Methods, Section
4.4
), and we did not separate patient from interface effects on interview length or score. The training gain nonetheless held under an OSCE interface that differed from the one used in training.
Clinically, our findings are restricted to single-encounter text-based intake rather than ongoing care. Single-encounter intake aims at a provisional formulation and triage plan, whereas ongoing psychiatric care, including longitudinal medication management and psychotherapy, requires sustained therapeutic relationships and adaptive treatment planning across repeated contact
180
;
118
. Moreover, text restricts assessment to a text-inferable Mental Status Examination (Methods, Section
4.3
); written dialogue exposes thought process, thought content, orientation, and expressed insight, but structurally excludes physical, behavioral, and non-verbal observations on which several diagnostic discriminations depend, including separating negative symptoms of schizophrenia from depressive psychomotor retardation, identifying catatonic features, and detecting acute intoxication or withdrawal
121
;
84
. A text-based agent therefore cannot perform a comprehensive psychiatric examination or substitute for a psychiatrist, and at most could support preliminary, clinician-supervised pre-intake information gathering. In addition, all scenarios and consultations were conducted in English and the clinical norms encoded in our rubrics reflect US psychiatric practice, whereas linguistic expressions of distress, diagnostic conventions, emergency hold criteria, and duty-to-warn mandates vary across languages and jurisdictions
64
;
49
, and the agent was trained for semi-structured intake as opposed to scripted diagnostic instruments such as the SCID-5
42
. Finally, deploying AI in psychiatric care raises domain-specific ethical risks
20
. Reinforcement learning to overcome guardedness corresponds in human practice to motivational interviewing
111
, but under unconstrained optimization has a potential risk of discovering manipulative conversational shortcuts, and individuals in distress are susceptible to anthropomorphic projection and parasocial attachment
87
. Any future translation would therefore require safeguards architecturally external to the learned policy, including hard output-level vetoes on clinical disposition and prescribing, anti-sycophancy auditing, clinician oversight, and deterministic escalation protocols for acute risk
154
.
Conclusion.
A simulation-trained agent conducted standardized psychiatric intake at a level that board-certified psychiatrists rated above its identically prompted base model across clinical examination skill, patient-centered communication, and diagnostic formulation. Standardized patient OSCEs are an established milestone in medical education, but they do not substitute for prospective validation in real patient populations; the environment, agent, reward functions, rubrics, and evaluation scenarios described here are research prototypes, and none has been cleared by any regulatory authority for clinical use. Prospective study under institutional clinician oversight, with real patients and longitudinal follow-up, is the necessary next step. Such text-based systems are not a substitute for psychiatric clinicians and are not ready for autonomous psychiatric assessment; the immediate clinical question for future research is whether, as strictly assistive tools operating under direct clinician oversight, they can help expand the reach of clinician-led care
191
;
173
;
75
. Answering that question requires the psychiatric community to define the evaluation standards and governance boundaries
75
;
47
, and the evaluation framework, rubrics, and taxonomies described here are offered as one contribution toward that goal.
4

Methods
Training an agent for psychiatric care requires a corpus that captures the diagnostic breadth, clinical ambiguity, and relational complexity of outpatient practice. A training set clustered on common presentations (such as uncomplicated depression or generalized anxiety) risks producing an agent that fails to generalize to diverse clinical encounters. Building on
Liévin et al. Super
, we developed a four-stage clinician-designed generation pipeline covering the diagnostic, demographic, and behavioral spectrum of outpatient psychiatry (Fig.
5
). Of 50,000 initial generation requests, 48,243 scenarios passed quality verification and deduplication against the held-out evaluation scenarios.
4.1

OSCE study design
Standardized patient methodology is an accepted standard for assessing diagnostic formulation, communication, and clinical safety
7
;
61
;
68
. Role-play by board-certified psychiatrists provides clinical fidelity and expert calibration without exposing patients to experimental systems
176
;
100
, but does not reproduce real clinical care.
The OSCE cohort comprised 60 scenarios drawn from the 127 clinician-validated intake evaluation scenarios (Section
4.6
) by sampling across diagnostic domain, difficulty tier, patient demographics, and crisis content, covering major psychiatric categories, occult somatic mimics, and complex ethical or legal presentations. Thirty-two board-certified psychiatrists (59.4% female; median experience 12.5 years, IQR 8–18; Supplementary Table
5
) served as clinician-patients in a within-case crossover design. Psychiatrists were selected for this role rather than lay actors because executing each scenario’s conditional information-gating protocol required real-time clinical judgment of whether the agent’s inquiry warranted disclosing guarded diagnostic facts, alongside expert calibration when scoring post-encounter communication instruments, while avoiding any exposure of real patients to an experimental system. Each received a detailed role sheet specifying the patient’s history, presentation, psychological defenses, and disclosure triggers (Appendix
A.1
). The clinician-actor conducted separate, blinded, synchronous text consultations with the identically prompted base model and the simulation-trained agent. Presentation sequence was randomized and counterbalanced, with a 48-hour washout period between paired consultations. Clinician-actors and independent raters were blinded to model identity and training condition.
To prevent affective halo effects from live role-play, evaluation used a two-perspective protocol. Clinician-patients provided post-encounter perceptions immediately following the chat. Separately, an independent panel of 15 board-certified psychiatrists drawn from the 54-member expert validation cohort (disjoint from the 32 clinician-patient actors) independently evaluated full consultation transcripts and clinical outputs, formatted as standardized clinical records stripped of AI identifiers (Appendix
A.2
; Supplementary Table
4
). Independent transcript evaluators scored an 18-item clinical-skills rubric derived from the Royal College of Physicians PACES examination
40
(which, together with the four patient-facing communication items rated by clinician-patients, comprises the 22-item PACES framework; Supplementary Table
1
); a four-dimensional differential diagnosis rubric; and structured items covering investigations, treatments, management plan appropriateness, and clinical confabulation (Appendix
A.4
; Supplementary Table
2
). Clinician-patients completed a post-encounter battery comprising the 11-item General Medical Council Patient Questionnaire
17
(nine Likert and two binary items), the four patient-facing PACES items, the 11-item patient-centered communication checklist operationalizing the Kalamazoo consensus essential elements
108
, and the 12-item Working Alliance Inventory Short Revised (WAI-SR
62
; Appendix
A.3
; Supplementary Table
3
).

4.6
Simulated psychiatric intake evaluation design and expert validation
The automated psychiatric intake evaluation comprises 127 expert-validated scenarios, instantiated from clinician-authored specifications, spanning the diagnostic, demographic, and difficulty taxonomy of outpatient psychiatry; the 60 scenarios used in the human OSCE (Section
4.5
) were drawn from this validated set by stratified sampling. Whereas the training corpus uses prevalence-weighted stochastic sampling to maximize conversational breadth during reinforcement learning (Section
4.1
), the evaluation suite was constructed through a separate, stratified factorial pipeline designed to give equal weight to all presentations and to pair each case with an explicit disclosure schedule and clinician-verified scoring key. All 127 scenarios gate clinically critical facts behind specific clinician behaviors, including direct inquiry, empathic probing, or sustained trust-building. Accurate diagnosis requires active clinical elicitation rather than retrieval of overt symptoms. Existing medical AI evaluations assess clinical knowledge through static question-answer pairs

;
162
;
8
or simulated patients in general medical domains
152
;
86

100

151

75
; Appendix
E
situates our evaluation methodology against this literature in full.
Overall, the evaluation cohort spans eight diagnostic and competency domains, including six core psychiatric categories (consolidating the 15 training diagnostic domains; mood, anxiety and stress-related, psychotic spectrum, substance use, personality and complex presentations, and other presentations including ADHD, eating disorders, sleep disorders, autism spectrum disorder in adults, and gender dysphoria), medical mimics requiring workups for somatic causes (e.g., autoimmune encephalitis

Extended Methodology
A.1
Psychiatrist-as-Patient Recruitment and Protocol
Board-certified psychiatrists were recruited to role-play patients in a blinded, counterbalanced, within-scenario crossover design. During the OSCE, clinician-patients received only the Patient Role Sheet specifying the patient’s clinical background, behavioral traits, disclosure rules (what to share freely versus what to reveal only if trust is established or if asked directly), communication style, and resistance patterns, without the ground-truth diagnostic or management scoring key. Although some clinician-patients had participated months earlier in scenario validation (where each reviewer inspected a small subset of candidate scenarios; Appendix
C.1
), each scenario’s two crossover encounters were enacted by the exact same clinician-patient under strict blinding to model identity and condition order, ensuring that any prior familiarity was held constant across paired conditions.
From the 127 expert-validated psychiatric intake evaluation scenarios (Appendix
C.1
), 60 were selected for the crossover OSCE via stratified sampling across diagnostic domain, difficulty tier, patient demographics, and crisis content. Each scenario produced two text-based encounters (one with the identically prompted base model and one with the RL-trained agent) in counterbalanced order with a mandatory 48-hour washout period. Post-encounter, clinician-patients completed the WAI-SR (Appendix
A.3
), GMCPQ (11 items; comprising nine 5-point Likert communication items used to compute the GMCPQ composite and two binary global retention items), PACES patient-facing communication and empathy items (4 items), and PCCBP patient-centered communication items (11 binary items). Clinician-patients also provided qualitative feedback.

article.lede: 双盲标准化病人OSCE显示，模拟环境多轮强化学习训练的模型在76.7%配对场景优于基础模型，但治疗规划与安全遗漏仍是短板
article.problem: 精神科临床接诊访谈本身就是主要诊断工具，既要求系统追问病史，也依赖信任建立后患者才披露关键信息。现有医学对话AI评估多聚焦一般内科，精神科接诊中的诊断推理与人际沟通耦合尚未被系统检验。语言模型能否通过模拟训练获得这类多轮接诊能力，此前没有被验证。
article.method: 作者在模拟精神科接诊环境中用多轮强化学习训练模型：先生成并验证患者场景，再让模型与模拟患者多轮互动，最后用自动评分器按临床量表打分并通过GRPO更新策略。验证采用N=60配对、120次会诊的随机双盲交叉OSCE，32名精神科医生扮演标准化病人，15名独立精神科医生评分；另在127个专家验证场景和256个对抗性呈现上做自动与安全压力测试。
article.results: 在双盲OSCE中，训练后模型在76.7%的配对场景获得更高的独立转录评分（p<0.0001）；PACES临床技能为3.04对2.32（满分5），以患者为中心沟通为82.0%对65.2%，鉴别诊断适当性为68.3%对33.3%。127个专家验证场景中，临床量表分为0.706对0.379，复合奖励为0.564对0.294（p<0.0001）。256个对抗性呈现中，禁忌症为0.8%对6.2%（p=0.001），漏报危险信号为6.2%对10.9%（p=0.04），分诊不足为12.9%对30.5%（p<0.0001）。
article.why_it_matters: 结果表明模拟环境既能作为精神科对话代理的训练场，也能作为压力测试平台，且部分增益可迁移到精神科医生扮演患者的会诊中。但作者明确将近期临床角色限定为医生监督下的辅助性预问诊，而非自主评估或替代精神科医生。
article.limitations: 残余缺口仍大：人工评估中综合且适当的治疗建议仅占46.7%，60.6%的模拟接诊至少漏掉一个关键问诊问题，对抗性呈现中仍有12.9%的急性风险分诊不足。研究限于单次文本接诊，患者由精神科医生角色扮演而非真实患者，奖励与评分和主评估器同属一个模型家族带来循环性风险，且文本无法覆盖非言语精神检查。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图示框架：先在模拟环境中进行场景生成、患者模拟和GRPO强化学习，再用精神科医生双盲OSCE及自动与对抗评估验证。

figure.caption: {Overview of contributions.} The proposed framework involves training a language model in a simulated environment and evaluating it with human experts. {Left (Training in Simulation),} The training process comprises three components: {a,} Scenario Generation, which synthesizes clinical, behavioral, and demographic data into verified patient scenarios using a language model; {b,} Simulation, where the model engages in multi-turn interactions with a simulated patient; and {c,} Reinforcement Learning, which uses an autorater to grade conversation transcripts against a clinical rubric and updates the policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). {Top Right (Evaluating with Standardized Patients),} The trained model (trained in simulation) and its base model act as the clinician in randomized, double-blind text conversations with board-certified psychiatrists acting as standardized patients. Separate independent, board-certified psychiatrist evaluators (blinded to whether transcripts came from the trained or base model) and the role-playing clinician-patients score the encounters across multiple dimensions (e.g., perceived empathic behavior, diagnostic formulation, clinical safety, and management plan), as compared across normalized domain scores in the radar chart. {Bottom Right (Evaluating in Simulation),} Automated evaluation across expert-validated scenarios shows that the simulation-trained agent achieved a higher composite clinical reward than its base model overall and across all four difficulty tiers (overall, 0.56 vs.\ 0.29; easy, 0.65 vs.\ 0.34; edge, 0.51 vs.\ 0.25; all $p < 0.0001$; left chart). Under 256 adversarial stress-testing presentations (right chart), the trained agent reduced measured safety failure rates relative to its base model, including contraindications (0.8\% vs.\ 6.2\%, $p = 0.001$), missed red flags (6.2\% vs.\ 10.9\%, $p = 0.04$), and clinical under-triage (12.9\% vs.\ 30.5\%, $p < 0.0001$).

Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers

1,3
,  Weichen Fan
2
,  Haiwen Diao
2
,  Zhongang Cai
3
,  Ziwei Liu
2,

1

2
Nanyang Technological University,
3
SenseTime,
†
\dagger
Corresponding author
Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

1   Introduction
Pixel-space generative models learn directly from noise to pixels, eliminating the separately trained autoencoder and its compression bottleneck. This simplicity, however, comes with a computational cost: the full-resolution image must be represented as Transformer tokens. Most pixel-space Transformers use one token per spatial patch, so the patch grid simultaneously determines what the model reads, what each token predicts, and how many tokens participate in global attention. As a result, finer image detail directly increases attention cost: on a
256

Existing methods address this cost from different directions, but largely retain the coupling between output detail and token communication. JiT routes every patch token through the global sequence
[

[

[
36

4

31

55

. Spectral Forcing brings in frequency structure, but only to filter the noisy input; its tokens remain spatial patches
[
19
]
. Across the pixel-space generators discussed above, output detail remains tied to a spatial patch grid, even when communication is compressed or restricted.
Our key observation is that finer detail does not necessarily require proportionally more global communication: in the frequency domain, low-frequency structure carries broad image organization and benefits from long-range exchange, while fine detail is largely local. A token carrying broad structure therefore stands to gain from exchanging with the whole image, while a token carrying fine detail mostly does not. Yet in existing designs, what a token communicates is fixed by where it sits, not by what it produces. Can a token’s output role also determine how it should communicate?
SpecSlot builds on this idea by making output roles explicit and using them to control communication. It organizes computation around three operations:
Read
,
Allocate
, and
Route

K
K
indexed slots, with each slot assigned a disjoint radial group of DCT coefficients. Route then uses these spectral roles to decide communication: only the slot assigned the lowest-frequency group from each anchor enters the global stage, while all slots interact locally within the anchor. This separates fine-grained output representation from the length of the global sequence. A spatial head further reuses the same slot states to add a local correction to the spectral prediction, without introducing additional tokens. Figure
2
illustrates this design.

At ImageNet-512, W256/K4 lowers FID by 2.84 over our FLOPs-matched JiT control (JiT-CM) with 3.9% fewer GFLOPs, and trails JiT-B/16 by 0.69 FID at 38.2% lower cost. Larger output windows cover more pixels while the global sequence remains fixed; the larger improvement over JiT-CM is consistent with this within-anchor allocation. 2   Related Work
Diffusion and pixel-space generation.
Diffusion and score-based models learn to reverse a gradual noising process and provide the iterative foundation of modern image synthesis

[

This line has followed several routes: Simple Diffusion and Hourglass DiT reduce the state internally, cascaded models and PixelFlow distribute generation across resolutions, and JiT shows that a direct large-patch Transformer can remain a strong pixel-space baseline

SpecSlot complements this line with a single-backbone allocation: indexed slots carry fixed output and communication roles, so detail can be subdivided without making every output token global.
Frequency structure and transform-domain generation.
Frequency offers a complementary view of this problem. It has entered generative modeling through the state or forward process, through generation order or conditioning, and through the training objective or analysis. In the first line, inverse heat dissipation, wavelet models, sparse transform codes, and DCTdiff change the representation or process used for generation

The communication literature provides the other half of the problem by restricting how tokens exchange information. Swin uses local windows with shifted boundaries, Longformer combines local windows with a few global tokens, and Perceiver routes information through a small latent bottleneck
[

SpecSlot fixes the graph from the allocation: one lowest-frequency slot per anchor is the global carrier, and all slots interact locally, so cross-anchor communication is spent on the role that also carries the low-frequency scaffold.

SpecSlot organizes pixel-space generation around one idea: tokenization as allocation—assigning each token a fixed output role and dividing a fixed token budget between anchor density and spectral subdivision. Global attention is then spent only on the role that needs it; the rectified-flow state, target, and loss remain in pixel space.

7   Conclusion
SpecSlot recasts tokenization as allocation: a fixed token budget is split between anchor density and spectral subdivision, while global attention is assigned by role. On ImageNet-256, it reaches a comparable final FID to the FLOPs-matched JiT control and descends faster early in training; on ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over that control and approaches JiT-B/16 at 38% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, the same design surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench (62.21 vs. 61.15) at 40.6% lower forward cost. These results show that, in the evaluated pixel-space settings, output detail and global-communication cost can be decoupled through tokenization. Our diagnostics find the lowest-radial role is recovered earliest, supporting its use as the carrier. Allocation gives pixel-space models a new way to trade detail for communication.

article.headline: 频谱分槽：让细节不再推高全局注意力成本
article.lede: SpecSlot 按 DCT 频带拆 token，仅最低频槽进全局注意力；ImageNet-512 上 FID 比同算力
article.problem: 像素空间生成 Transformer 通常一个图像 patch 对应一个 token，因此更细的细节需要更多 token，全局注意力的二次成本随之上升。现有方法虽用窗口、稀疏注意力或额外细节头压缩计算，但大多仍把输出细节绑定在空间 patch 网格上，通信成本与表示精度没有真正解耦。
article.method: SpecSlot 是一种像素空间 rectified-flow Transformer：Read 用空间锚点收集输入证据，Allocate 把每个锚点扩展为 K 个 slot，每个 slot 固定拥有一组不相交的径向 DCT 系数。Route 只让每个锚点中最低频的 slot 作为 carrier 进入全局块，所有 slot 在锚点内做局部混合；另有一个零初始化的空间头在同一 slot 状态上输出局部像素校正。生成状态、目标和损失都保留在像素空间，全局序列长度为 W 而非 WK。
article.results: ImageNet-256 上，W256/K4 的 FID 为 6.59，与 FLOPs 匹配的 JiT-CM（6.68）相当且收敛更快；ImageNet-512 上 W256/K4 将 FID 从 JiT-CM 的 11.98 降至 9.14（低 2.84），GFLOPs 少 3.9%，与 JiT-B/16 的 8.45 仅差 0.69 FID，成本低 38.2%。文生图方面，SpecSlot 在 DPG-Bench 上得 62.21，超过 JiT-B/8 的 61.15，前向成本低 40.6%；GenEval 为 26.99，低于 JiT-B/8 的 29.78。
article.why_it_matters: 它把 tokenization 从单一 patch 尺寸选择变成了“锚点密度 vs 频谱细分”的显式预算分配，并让通信资格由固定的频率角色决定。对像素空间生成模型而言，这提供了一条在不扩大全局序列的前提下增加输出细节的设计路径。
article.limitations: 作者指出，ImageNet-512 上更大的增益与锚点覆盖更多像素的机制一致，但实验本身没有单独隔离原因；固定 token 预算下“更多锚点优于更多槽”的结论也仅限所测范围。另有诊断显示 K 从 2 增至 8 时熵有效槽占比从 0.803 降至 0.495，说明增加槽并不等于等量增加有效容量。

Robotic Data Inoculation
Qiyang Li   Zhiyuan Zhou   Charles Xu   Sergey Levine
UC Berkeley
data-inoculation.github.io
Abstract
Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover.
Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it.
In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves
during data collection
to collect more useful data.
We propose
Data Inoculation (DI)
, a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make.
These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human’s continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, “inoculating” the dataset against the learner’s future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.
Figure 1
:
Data inoculation (DI).
Left
: During data collection, we train a residual inoculative policy with online RL to perturb the human’s closed-loop teleoperation commands. The perturbations steer data collection towards the mistakes the policy trained on the data would make, and elicit human’s corrective feedback, “inoculating” the dataset against such mistakes.
Right
: We test DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks that require precise manipulation, and DI consistently improve success rate of policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL.
1
Introduction
Modern robot learning systems have shown promise in acquiring complex manipulation skills (
e.g.
, shirt-folding
[
7
]
, tea/juice-making
[
28
]
) from demonstration data.
While there has been extensive recent research on the design of these models, the quality of the data the models are trained on is every bit as critical. Good data should have high coverage: it should contain a wide range of states to maximize the chance that the policy generalizes to the states that it actually visits at test time. In practice, coverage is determined by the scenes where data is collected and the behaviors of the teleoperators, which must strike a balance between consistency and variety. Improving data quality and coverage through task design and operator instruction is largely heuristic and ad hoc. Can we instead directly modify how the robot behaves
during
data collection to provide for more useful data?
Existing solutions largely sit at the two extremes of how the robot is being controlled. Aside from the human-driven teleoperation which exhibits obvious drawbacks above, a learned policy may control the robot autonomously and collect data. While this allows us to run RL online which improves the policy upon its own experience overtime, real-world exploration can be sample inefficient and unsafe. DAgger-style methods partially address this by using learned policy to drive the robot until it makes a mistake, where a human intervenes and corrects it, often through teleoperation. This is reactive: each intervention requires a failure to occur naturally, and rare failure modes may take many rollouts to appear, and for many tasks (
e.g.
, that require working with delicate objects that may break) failures cannot be corrected once they occur.
In this paper, we argue that autonomous policy rollout and human control should
not
be mutually exclusive, and a shared-control framework in which a learned agent and the human drive the robot together allows for better data collection. Our framework is simple: the human retains closed-loop teleoperation of the robot that supplies the demonstration signal as usual in the form of control commands, but these commands are perturbed by a residual policy, which is trained online on the growing dataset, in a way that mimics the mistakes a policy trained on the current data might make. We call this residual policy an
inoculative policy
because it exposes data collection to controlled, human-corrected “doses” of the learner’s expected mistakes, so that the policy learned from the collected data is already robust to them. The human can therefore correct policy-like deviations continuously throughout every data collection episode rather than only after a visible failure while ensuring safety because they are always in control of the robot. The resulting data collection strategy, which we call
Data Inoculation (DI)
(
Figure
1
), produce data that are favourable for downstream policy extraction—it contains near-failure states paired with actions that allow recovery from these states, which is exactly the good coverage data that would help behavior cloning (BC) to learn the recovery behavior directly but also help offline RL to learn better value functions.
Our main contribution is the new data collection strategy (DI). We evaluate DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks and show that DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of the policies extracted from both behavior cloning (BC) and offline RL. These results demonstrate the benefits of proactively
inoculating
data collection so that the policies become more robust at deployment time.
2
Related Work
Human-in-the-loop learning
methods address a common failure mode of imitation learning on passive data, where the learned policy may visit states different from the training distribution and suffers from compounding errors. They typically work by alternating between executing the current policy and collecting human correction data in the form of action re-labeling
[
21
]
or intervention trajectories
[
9
]
. Interventions can be triggered automatically by the model
[
30
,
2
,
18
]
or initiated by human
[
9
,
16
,
15
,
13
,
4
,
6
]
. In real-world robotics, intervention-based approaches are often more convenient and natural to human because the corrective trajectories are collected under human’s continuous, closed-loop control of the robot. However, this also comes with a limitation: once the control is switched to human, the trajectory may quickly go out of the learned policy’s state distribution. As a result, only the first few transitions right after the switching point provide direct supervision to the mistakes made by the policy.
In contrast, rather than using a binary switching from the learned policy’s distribution to the expert’s distribution after intervention, our method constructs a controlled distribution by combining human demonstrator actions with residual actions from an
inoculation policy
, allowing the human to provide corrections of the policy’s mistakes throughout a data collection trajectory.
Prior work trains assistive residual policies in simulation, using a model trained on a fixed set of demonstrations to approximate human control, then deploys them with human operators
[
23
,
22
]
.
In contrast, our method doesn’t depend on simulation and directly train the residual inoculation policy online as data accumulates. This also yields a broader range of corrective demonstrations as updates to the residual policy expose humans to different errors during its training.
Data perturbation
approaches broaden the distribution of observations
[
26
,
11
,
29
,
31
]
, actions
[
31
,
8
,
3
,
17
]
, or even environment and its dynamics
[
5
,
27
,
20
,
25
]
during training so that the model is robust. These approaches typically directly perturb either a simulator (
e.g.
, domain randomization) or previously collected data (
e.g.
, data augmentation), but do not directly interact with how a human demonstrator collects trajectories, which our method does. The closest line of work injects zero-mean Gaussian noises during data collection, exposing human demonstrator to random mistakes and thereby eliciting recovery behaviors
[
10
,
19
,
24
]
. In contrast, our method injects directed residual actions produced by a state-dependent
inoculation policy
trained online to approximate the mistakes that a policy learned from the growing dataset would likely make. This allows the collected trajectories to target policy-specific failure modes like DAgger-style approaches, rather than relying on symmetric random perturbations. Furthermore, while prior approaches mostly focus on improving imitation learning performance, we additionally demonstrate that our technique allows for improved offline RL performance and the quality of learned value functions.

First of all, when the inoculative policy is optimized using the same reward-maximizing objective as a downstream offline RL algorithm later uses for policy extraction, its deviations are expected to closely mirror those a downstream learned policy would produce. Furthermore, early in collection, the critic is barely trained and inaccurate which causes the residual policy to exploit the critic’s errors, steering the robot into suboptimal states that require explicit recovery behaviors. Robot setup and tasks.
We evaluate our method on three real-robot tasks that require precise manipulation. We focus on these tasks because successful executions require precise control of the robot, making it a challenging testbed for data collection and policy learning.
We use a Franka robot arm with a Robotiq gripper and two wrist cameras attached near the end effector. We use a spacemouse to control the robot’s end effector position and rotation during data collection at a frequency of
10
10
Hz.
Illustrations of the three tasks are shown in
Figure
1
, and we describe them in detail below:
1.
t-cube
requires the robot to pick up two colored cubes and carefully balance them on top of another yellow cube, resulting in a T-shape
[
1
]
. While this seems like a simple pick and place task, this in fact requires very precise manipulation skills and is arguably the most demanding task of the three: the robot needs to stack the two top cubes diagonally on top of the yellow cube with the centers of the three cubes roughly aligned, and any misalignment would cause one or two of the top cubes to fall off.
2.
cable
is a precision insertion task where the robot needs to pick up a USB-C cable and insert it into a port hole on a desktop machine that is barely bigger than the cable itself. Without changing the difficulty of the task, we only use the side plate of the desktop machine for ease of task setup.
3.
keycap
tasks the robot to use a keycap puller to remove the Q keycap from a keyboard. The robot must pick up the tool, locate the Q key, position the puller over the keycap, and lock its two hooks onto both sides of the keycap. Successful removal requires precise, directionally controlled force rather than a large brute force pull, which could cause the keycap to fly off. The robot must therefore learn a sequence of small lateral wiggling motions to loosen the keycap before pulling it out and placing it on the table.
Data collection procedure.
Since data collection through tele-operation is unavoidably a subjective process and can vary across different operators and collection trials, we conduct experiments on all tasks and data collection strategies with multiple operators and trials, which we refer to as “seeds”. Before data collection, each operator spent time to practice on the task to achieve a sufficient level of expertise before collecting any data.

Figure 4
:
Amount of human corrective demonstrations over different phases
. DI elicits the most corrections at the most critical phase of the
t-cube

7
Discussion
In this paper we introduce Data Inoculation, a data collection strategy that trains a residual RL policy online to aid human teleoperated data collection in a shared-control framework. The residual inoculative policy perturbs the human’s control of the robot to a wider range of states and can elicit recovery demonstrations in critical phases of the task, and eventually lead to higher data collection success rate as the residual policy is trained. Data collected with DI also improves the success rate of downstream policy learning.
Our work serves as a step towards a new paradigm of robot learning where data collection is shared between humans and autonomous policies, each helping the other.
Several challenges remain and is promising for future work. First, our approach trains the residual policy from scratch using online RL, which offers near-random perturbations at the beginning of training. A natural next step is to develop mechanisms for directed exploration that can more quickly provide useful perturbations, such as boostrapping training from an existing offline dataset.
Second, our approach assume the human operator to be fully in-the-loop during data collection, which is expensive in human time. One interesting direction is to explore whether we can automate parts of data collection to be autonomous gradually during training and leave only important correction for human operators.

Task
t-cube
. The scene contains three acrylic cubes (red, pink, and yellow). The robot must grasp the two cubes (red and pink) together and carefully balance it on top of an equal-sized yellow cube. This task is inspired by the T-Block task from
Ghugare et al. [1]
. Balancing the two cubes on top of the yellow cube requires a lot of precision. A misalignment of a few millimeters would fail the balance. Nearly all failures of this task occur at placement, making this the most precision-demanding task. An episode succeeds when both cubes rest on top of the yellow cube without falling off.
Task
cable
. The scene contains a side panel of a machine case and a USB-C cable. The robot must pick up the cable lying on the table and then insert it through a port hole on the side panel that is barely bigger than the cable head. The insertion is a contact-rich process where the robot must search locally and find the right motion that allows the USB-C to go through the port hole. An episode succeeds when the USB-C passes through the port hole and rests there without falling (with the arm away).
Task
keycap
. The scene contains a mechanical keyboard and a keycap-puller tool. The robot must pickup the keycap tool and remove a transparent “Q” keycap from the keyboard. This requires the arm to seat the tool’s two hooks on the opposite sides of the keycap, loosen the keycap, and then pull it off the switch. An episode succeeds when the keycap is detached and placed on the table.
