article.headline: 共享控制下用残差策略接种演示数据
article.lede: UC Berkeley 提出 Data Inoculation：在人类遥操作上叠加在线 RL 残差扰动，让纠正数据覆盖策
article.problem: 机器人模仿学习依赖高覆盖演示数据，但纯遥操作数据状态分布窄、缺少恢复行为。在线强化学习探索虽能扩展状态，却存在安全与样本效率问题。DAgger 式干预还要求策略先自然失败，稀有失败模式难以触发。
article.method: DI 让人类保持闭环遥操作，同时用在线 RL 训练残差策略，在人类控制命令上叠加有界扰动。残差策略在持续增长的数据集上异步训练，并与下游策略共享奖励最大化目标。人类对扰动的连续纠正被记录为恢复演示，使数据提前覆盖学习器可能犯的错误。
article.results: 在三个真实机器人任务上，cable 的 BC 成功率从 clean 的 0.37±0.06 提升到 DI 的 0.66±0.04，离线 RL 从 0.35±0.07 提升到 0.67±0.06；t-cube 的 BC 从 0.38±0.04 提升到 0.50±0.03，RL 从 0.42±0.06 提升到 0.59±0.02；keycap 的 BC 从 0.63±0.09 提升到 0.72±0.05，RL 从 0.81±0.06 提升到 0.84±0.06。结果按 t-cube 9 个 seed、cable/keycap 各 5 个 seed，每个 seed 20 次评估平均。
article.why_it_matters: 它把数据收集从启发式操作指令变成人机共享控制，用策略自身易错状态定向 eliciting 人类纠正，有望同时改善行为克隆和离线 RL 的演示数据覆盖。
article.limitations: 仅验证三个真实任务，种子数为 9/5/5，keycap 下游提升有限，且收集阶段 DI 成功率 94.0% 低于 clean 的 95.8%。残差策略初始近随机会拉低收集成功率，人类全程在环也带来较高成本。
article.figure_caption_zh: DI 在数据收集时用在线 RL 残差策略扰动人类遥操作命令，使人类持续给出纠正；右图对比三个真实机器人任务上的下游策略成功率。

figure.caption: {dmc}{ {Data inoculation (DI). }} {Left}: During data collection, we train a residual inoculative policy with online RL to perturb the human's closed-loop teleoperation commands. The perturbations steer data collection towards the mistakes the policy trained on the data would make, and elicit human's corrective feedback, ``inoculating'' the dataset against such mistakes. {Right}: We test DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks that require precise manipulation, and DI consistently improve success rate of policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL.

page_papers.content:
Abstract
One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement.
Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution.
Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network.
We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision.
A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly.

Introduction
Diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality images, but their repeated network evaluations impose substantial inference cost
(
Ho et al., 2020
;
Song et al., 2020
;
Lipman et al., 2022
;
Liu et al., 2023
)
. One and few-step generation reduces this cost by learning a much shorter sampling process. The challenge is to accurately render the details specified in the prompt using only one or a few sampling steps. Long-text rendering makes this challenge concrete: many characters must remain legible and correct within a coherent image
(
Geng et al., 2025b
;
Wu et al., 2025a
)
. It therefore provides a demanding test of whether fast generation retains detailed conditional information.
Distribution matching distillation (DMD) trains a fast generator to match a reference distribution
(
Yin et al., 2024b
;
Yin et al., 2024a
)
. A score describes the local direction of increasing log density. A pretrained teacher supplies the reference score, while an auxiliary fake-score network estimates the score of the current generated distribution. Their difference guides updates to generated samples. These updates are applied sample by sample, but their direction depends on both distributions. Distribution matching can complement trajectory-based training: rCM combines score regularization with continuous-time consistency training
(
Zheng et al., 2025
)
.

article.headline: 一步生成加显式矩约束，强化提示细节还原
article.lede: 研究者在一阶蒸馏的反向KL分解中加入生成器EMA特征空间的矩匹配损失，用1至2步采样检验文生图细节保真度。
article.problem: 扩散与流匹配模型生成质量高，但需要反复评估网络，推理开销大；一步或少步生成虽然缩短了采样过程，却只剩极少的机会修正细节。长文本渲染是其中的极端情形：一张图里许多字符都要清晰正确，正好用来检验快速生成是否真的保留了提示中的条件信息。
article.method: 方法沿用分布匹配蒸馏（DMD）的框架，用内部速度分支估计参考分布与生成分布之间的得分差，省去单独的假得分网络。作者把反向KL场分解为高斯矩成分与非高斯残差，据此指出哪些统计量可以被显式约束。于是除内部DMD损失外，在生成器的EMA特征空间再加一项特征矩损失，形成完整的训练目标。
article.results: 系统级对比在单张A100（BF16）上进行，吞吐以batch=10的samples/s计、延迟以batch=1的秒数计，但论文未给出具体数字。基座模型Z-Image约需100 NFE，蒸馏模型Z-Image-Turbo为8-NFE；受控消融在1 NFE与2 NFE下评测，比较“v+x”对照（不含矩损失）与完整方法。GenEval按六个类别计分并取平均，FID/CLIP一并报告，但文中未给出各项的具体分数。
article.why_it_matters: 如果矩约束确实能补上DMD得分监督缺失的分布信息，那么一步生成在文字、构图等细节上的短板就可以用训练目标而非更多采样步数来弥补。这也给“回归式蒸馏会压低方差”这一常见担忧提供了一个可检验的分解视角。
article.limitations: 提供的材料中没有给出FID、CLIP、GenEval或长文本渲染的任何具体数值，方法相对基线的实际增益尚无法判断；外部参考模型APEX训练于更小的数据集合，与消融配置不完全可比。附录的协方差收缩命题只在预测器真正实现平方误差意义下的条件均值时成立，作者也明确它不构成“一步生成器普遍低估方差”的结论。
article.figure_caption_zh: 多步采样迭代精炼样本，一步生成则直接学习从噪声到数据的映射；本方法在生成器EMA特征空间中同时施加内部DMD损失与特征矩损失，右图为单次评估推理下的理想对齐示意。

Mix Forcing: Causal Pre-Training via Mixture Attention for Interactive World Models
Zelin Gao
,
Hao Ouyang
,
Jiapeng Zhu
,
Qiuyu Wang
Jingye Chen
,
Zichen Liu
,
Xing Zhu
,
Yujun Shen
,
Yinghao Xu
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Robbyant
*
Project Lead
†
Corresponding Author
Abstract
While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality.
In this paper, we introduce
Mix Forcing
, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (
MoBA
) attention.
Mix Forcing
jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training.
In self-attention,
Mix Forcing
leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors.
To support online text interaction,
Mix Forcing
further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk.
Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator.
Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control.
Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts.
Project Page:
https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing
Figure 1:
Long-horizon interactive video rollout with camera control and memory.
Top: a single one-hour autoregressive rollout generated by our model trained with
Mix Forcing
, following successive prompt updates under keyboard camera control.
Bottom: a memory case, where the camera looks away and later returns, and previously observed regions (A: waterfall; B: red foliage) remain consistent when revisited.
1
Introduction
Interactive video world models
[
19
,
34
,
10
,
49
,
53
,
33
,
14
,
47
]
, which predict future states conditioned on historical context and user inputs, have shown great potential for world simulation, video gaming, and embodied intelligence.
Since users act based on past observations, each video chunk must be generated without access to future frames or future instructions, which calls for causal autoregressive generation.
Recent works
[
34
,
53
,
14
]
build upon pretrained video diffusion models to leverage their strong visual priors.
However, these priors are learned for bidirectional generation, where all frames are jointly denoised with access to both past and future frames.
Some methods
[
16
,
43
]
directly distill bidirectional models into few-step causal generators via ordinary differential equation (ODE) initialization and distribution matching distillation (DMD), but the trajectories of the bidirectional teacher depend on future information, preventing the causal student from converging to the target flow map.
To address this, other methods
[
54
,
50
]
first adapt pretrained models into many-step causal models with teacher forcing before few-step distillation, making this causal pre-training stage the foundation of the final generator.
However, teacher forcing departs from the pretraining setting of bidirectional video diffusion models in two aspects.
In attention, each chunk attends only to its history rather than the full video; in noise level, each noisy chunk is predicted from clean historical context rather than jointly denoised with other chunks at a shared noise level, which encourages velocity prediction to over-rely on clean context.
Both deviations disrupt pretrained visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality.
Moreover, causal pre-training methods typically condition the whole video on a single global prompt, which exposes future events to the current chunk.
Streaming methods
[
40
]
support prompt updates by recaching the history under each new prompt, which rewrites the context of past frames.
In this paper, we introduce
Mix Forcing
, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the
Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (
MoBA
)
attention block.
The key idea of
Mix Forcing
is to mix teacher forcing and bidirectional training: teacher forcing learns causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while bidirectional training retains the pretraining setting in both attention and noise level, preserving pretrained visual priors during causal adaptation.
In addition,
Mix Forcing
conditions each teacher forcing chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, enabling online text interaction without exposing future instructions to the current chunk or recomputing the KV cache of past chunks.
Based on
Mix Forcing
, we build an interactive video world model with camera control and online text interaction (
Fig.
1
).
Starting from a 14B image-to-video model, we perform causal pre-training with
Mix Forcing
, and then apply consistency distillation (CD)
[
31
]
and DMD to obtain a four-step generator for KV-cached autoregressive rollout (
Fig.
2
).
Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control, and sustains high-fidelity generation over one-hour rollouts.
Ablation studies further show that
Mix Forcing
provides a stronger initialization for few-step post-training than teacher forcing alone.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We propose the
MoBA
attention block, which mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors during causal adaptation, with chunk-wise prompt conditioning for online text interaction.
•
We build an interactive video world model through causal pre-training with
Mix Forcing
and few-step post-training with CD and DMD, supporting camera control, online text interaction, and four-step KV-cached autoregressive rollout.
•
Experiments on internal and public benchmarks show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control.

Autoregressive video models generate frames or chunks sequentially

In

Methodology
In this section, we present
Mix Forcing

We first review flow matching and teacher forcing for interactive video modeling (

3.1

We then introduce the

attention block that implements

However, teacher forcing departs from the pretraining setting of bidirectional video diffusion models.
In attention, each noisy chunk attends only to itself and its history instead of the full video; in noise level, it is predicted from clean historical latents instead of being jointly denoised with other chunks at a shared timestep.
Both deviations can disrupt pretrained visual priors and degrade generation quality.

Experimental Setup
Benchmarks.
We construct an internal benchmark (InBench) to evaluate event-following ability and camera-control precision.
We use GPT-Image 2.5
[
27
]

(i) an interactive subset covering environmental changes and character interactions (32 cases); and
(ii) a roaming subset covering human characters and virtual objects (64 cases).
Each case is evaluated with a video of 8 to 35 seconds, and each interactive case contains 3 to 5 prompt updates.
We also evaluate on WBench

]
and SANA-WM-Bench
[

]

On both the simple and hard 60-second splits, our model achieves the highest average

These results demonstrate that our model maintains visual fidelity throughout minute-long autoregressive generation; one-hour qualitative results and average quality scores measured every five minutes are further provided in Figure. S12 in the Appendix.
Although competitive, our camera errors are not the lowest on SANA-WM-Bench.

Conclusion
We present
Mix Forcing
, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models.
Implemented with the
MoBA
attention block, it mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors, and uses chunk-wise prompts for online text interaction.
Combined with CD and DMD, our four-step model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with camera control over one-hour rollouts.
Limitations.
Our implementation targets video DiT architectures with separate self-attention and cross-attention modules, and its extension to unified attention
[
21
]
remains to be verified.
Moreover, our model is designed for chunk-wise local prompts, and its camera control is less precise when only a single global prompt is available, as observed on public benchmarks.
We leave these directions for future work.

A.1
Training Data
Data Acquisition.
We collect 100k video clips totaling 974 hours.
We collect egocentric recordings, videos from games and Unreal Engine environments, and web videos.
These sources cover first-person interactions, controlled synthetic scenes, and diverse real-world content.
Data Filtering.
We split videos at shot boundaries and remove clips with decoding errors or unsuitable duration and resolution.
We further filter clips using visual quality, exposure, text occupancy, and motion statistics.
A vision-language model assesses the remaining clips for editing artifacts, viewpoint, and interaction content.
Prompt Annotation.
For each clip, we generate a shared environment prompt describing the scene and a global prompt summarizing the entire video.
We separately annotate subject visibility, motion, interactions, and environmental changes, then combine the active annotations into local prompts.
We refine these prompts for consistent wording and temporal alignment, removing descriptions of future events or actions unsupported by visual evidence.
Each local prompt is shared by four consecutive latent frames, consistent with the cross-attention setting in the main paper.
Camera Annotation.
We estimate camera poses using COLMAP for 70% of the video clips.
The remaining 30% are used without camera annotations, with all-zero Plücker embeddings as the conditioning input.

User Study
We conduct a pairwise user study on InBench to evaluate visual quality, interactive following, and motion clarity.
Pairwise Comparison.
Each trial compares our model with one of five baselines: HY-WorldPlay, JoyAI-Echo-WM, LingBot-World-Fast, Matrix-Game 3.0, and SANA-WM-Streaming.
The two videos use the same initial image and source control sequence and are displayed side by side at the same size using the 480p evaluation outputs.
They are labeled only as
Video A
and
Video B
, with the left/right position of our model randomized independently for each trial.
Model identities and numerical evaluation scores are hidden from participants.
Case Allocation.
The study uses the full InBench case pool, comprising 96 cases: 64 roaming cases and 32 interactive cases.
Each session contains 20 pairs of videos (40 videos in total), corresponding to 10 interactive cases and 10 roaming cases, with no case repeated within a session.
Each baseline appears in four trials per session.
We shuffle the baseline assignments and select cases within each subset, prioritizing case–baseline pairs with fewer previous assignments.
The two subsets are presented in separate blocks, and no case is repeated within a session.
Evaluation Questions.
For each applicable question, participants select
Video A is better
,
They are the same
, or
Video B is better
.
The three evaluation dimensions are:
•
Visual quality (both subsets).
Participants compare overall appearance, temporal stability, natural motion, and visible artifacts.
•
Interactive following (interactive subset).
Participants compare how well the videos perform the requested events as the corresponding local prompts become active.
•
Motion clarity (roaming subset).
Participants compare scene detail during camera movement, focusing on blur, smearing, and ghosting. They judge frames during movement and select a tie when clarity is similar or no viewpoint change is visible.
Each trial therefore collects a visual-quality judgment and one judgment specific to its subset.

reports the complete results on the Navi-158 subset of WBench

, covering generation quality, setting adherence, and navigation performance.

article.headline: 混合强制：交互视频世界模型的因果预训练
article.lede: 论文提出 Mix Forcing 因果预训练，用 MoBA 注意力混合教师强制与双向训练，保留视频扩散先验并支持在线文本
article.problem: 交互视频世界模型必须按块自回归生成，不能看到未来帧或未来指令。直接用教师强制把双向视频扩散模型改造成因果模型，会在注意力和噪声水平上偏离预训练，破坏视觉先验；全局提示还会把未来事件泄露给当前块，流式重缓存则改写过去上下文。
article.method: 作者提出 MoBA 注意力块：训练时混合教师强制（TF）与双向（BID）分支，TF 块只关注自身和干净历史，BID 潜变量相互双向注意，用稀疏掩码隔离并在一次前向中联合优化。交叉注意力让每个 TF 块条件于共享环境提示和自身局部提示，BID 块用全局提示，从而在线更新提示时不重算过去 KV 缓存。基于 14B 图像到视频模型做因果预训练，再用一致性蒸馏和分布匹配蒸馏得到四步 KV 缓存自回归生成器。
article.results: 在 InBench 上，模型平均质量 75.1，EA 94.4，OT1.5s 96.8，Rot/Trans/CMC 为 0.296/0.316/0.539。SANA-WM-Bench 的 60 秒简单/困难轨迹平均 Quality 为 74.8/74.7，SIQ 为 66.7/66.4；一小时生成每 5 分钟质量均值在 67.3–71.6，末段 69.3、首段 71.0。四步 CD→DMD 模型质量 70.9、EA 55.1、OT1.5s 64.3。
article.why_it_matters: 它为交互视频世界模型提供了一条在因果化时保留双向视频扩散视觉先验、同时支持在线文本交互和长时自回归生成的预训练路径。
article.limitations: 作者指出方法只验证了分离自注意力和交叉注意力的视频 DiT，扩展到统一注意力尚待验证；且模型依赖分块局部提示，只有单一全局提示时相机控制精度下降，在 SANA-WM-Bench 上相机误差并非最低。
article.figure_caption_zh: 给定初始图像和环境提示，四步因果视频模型根据 KV 缓存历史、用户相机位姿和局部提示，逐块自回归生成潜变量并由 VAE 解码为视频。

figure.caption: {Pipeline of our interactive video world model.} Given an initial image and an environment prompt $ {p}_{e}$, an interactive world is simulated by our four-step causal video model. Based on the KV-cached history context and user inputs, including the camera pose $ {e}_{i}$ and the local prompt $ {p}_{i}$, each latent chunk is generated autoregressively and decoded into a video clip by the VAE decoder.

When Requirements Interact:
Scaling Long-Horizon Coding via Interdependent Specifications
Yishuo Cai
Minzheng Wang
Liang Zhao
Linghao Zhang
Lei Li
Shicheng Li
Xu Sun
Fuli Luo
Abstract
To succeed in real-world long-horizon software development, coding agents must satisfy multi-dimensional task specifications, such as interface compatibility and error handling, and do so without breaking existing dependencies. However, current works lack specification in both quantity and diversity, often emphasizing primary goals while ignoring complex constraints. Synthesizing tasks to bridge this gap presents two challenges: naively adding specifications risks reducing tasks to trivial checklists rather than compelling joint reasoning, and verifying these subtle interactions risks overlooking hidden flaws or rejecting valid alternatives. To address these challenges, we introduce
CodeSpecWeave
, a framework for synthesizing tasks with rich, interdependent specifications. Grounded in real developer seeds, a synthesis agent iteratively develops both coupled task requirements and executable tests, while a review agent audits solution trajectories from multiple models to guarantee test reliability. Using this pipeline, we construct 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. Applying Reinforcement learning on these tasks significantly improves performance over the base model on DeepSWE-v1.1, largely outperforming existing baselines. Furthermore, we curate
CodeSpecWeave
-
Bench
, a rigorous benchmark comprising 100 tasks and 1,044 specifications, which clearly separates frontier models and reveals significant headroom in handling interdependent engineering constraints.

*

†
Corresponding authors.
‡
Work done during an internship at Xiaomi.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled coding agents to explore repositories, modify code, execute tests, and iteratively refine their solutions
(
Yang et al., 2024
;
Jimenez et al., 2024
;
Deng et al., 2026
;
Tan et al., 2026b
)
. As these agents navigate the increasing complexity of real-world software architectures, they must implement changes without breaking behavior that other components already depend on
(
Jimenez et al., 2024
;
Deng et al., 2026
)
. In practice, these expectations span multiple requirements, such as interface compatibility, state consistency, and error handling
(
Han et al., 2024
;
Ruan et al., 2025
)
. Together, they form concrete task specifications that an agent must satisfy throughout exploration, coding, and testing.
Figure 1:
Comparison of task specifications across datasets.
Top:
Mean extracted specifications and distinct behavioral categories per task across existing SWE training datasets and
CodeSpecWeave
, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Category counts follow the taxonomy in Table
5
.
Bottom:
Example task structures. Prior datasets typically contain few independent rules (left), whereas
CodeSpecWeave
tasks feature multiple interdependent specifications tied together by shared execution contexts and lifecycle constraints (right).
Developing this capability requires a large number of executable tasks that encompass these diverse engineering requirements. Existing works typically construct executable tasks by mining issues and pull requests
(
Pan et al., 2025
)
, with limited attention to the role and properties of task specifications. Our empirical analysis reveals that existing data fall significantly short in both specification density and structural diversity (Figure
1
, top), often emphasizing the primary development goal while leaving compatibility, state consistency, and error handling unaddressed. Consequently, agents trained on such partial specifications often fail in practice, as they struggle to satisfy the intricate constraints inherent in real-world repositories. This deficiency underscores the need for a scalable pipeline to synthesize tasks grounded in realistic and diverse specifications.
However, synthesizing such tasks presents two connected challenges. First, purely adding specifications may inadvertently reveal solution paths
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
or reduce the task to a checklist of independent edits. Specification design should therefore organize requirements into interdependent specifications where individual implementation choices constrain one another, compelling agents to coordinate across requirements through joint reasoning to achieve globally coherent implementations (Figure
1
, bottom). Second, verifying such interdependent specifications is uniquely challenging: the subtle interactions among requirements make it easy for tests either to miss hidden flaws
(
Sun et al., 2026
;
Tan et al., 2026a
)
or to reject valid solutions
(
Chowdhury et al., 2024
)
. Reliable verification requires strict alignment with both individual requirements and their interactions, while accommodating different implementations that satisfy them.
To this end, we introduce
CodeSpecWeave
, a framework for synthesizing coding tasks with rich, interdependent specifications. Grounded in specification seeds derived from real developers, a synthesis agent explores the repository context and develops the task requirements and executable test suites together in an iterative loop, intentionally designing coupled constraints that require simultaneous satisfaction while refining the tests to strictly align with them. To ensure test reliability, a review agent further examines the solution trajectories and patches from multiple models, filtering out tests that accept incomplete implementations or reject valid alternatives. Using this pipeline, we construct 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. Applying Reinforcement learning on these tasks significantly improves performance over the base model on DeepSWE-v1.1. In addition, we curate
CodeSpecWeave
-
Bench
through careful manual review, compiling 100 tasks with 1,044 specifications to evaluate coding agents under interdependent specifications. Benchmarking leading models clearly separates their capabilities, revealing shared failure modes and significant room for improvement.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce
CodeSpecWeave
, a synthesis framework that builds on real developer specification seeds to generate coding tasks with interdependent specifications and reliable verifiers.
•
We construct a scalable training set of 4,670 tasks across 2,865 repositories and demonstrate its effectiveness through reinforcement learning, yielding substantial performance gains on DeepSWE-v1.1 over strong training baselines.
•
We present
CodeSpecWeave
-
Bench
, a benchmark comprising 100 tasks with 1,044 specifications. Evaluations across leading coding agents reveal notable performance gaps and substantial headroom under interdependent requirements.
2
CodeSpecWeave
CodeSpecWeave
transforms requirements observed in real software development into coding tasks, addressing two connected challenges: compelling agents toward holistic exploration and joint reasoning under rich specifications, and scaling reliable test verification aligned with stated requirements.
We first introduce the task formulation (Section
2.1
) and design principle (Section
2.2
).
The framework consists of two core stages (Figure
2
):
task synthesis
constructs interdependent requirements and linked tests guided by specification seeds (Section
2.3
);
validation and repair
reviews trajectories generated by multiple model trials to identify and repair misalignments between queries and tests (Section
2.4
).
Figure 2:
Overview of

The synthesis agent repeatedly consults specification seeds, explores the repository, and runs generated tests to refine a task and its verifier. Schematic links between specifications and test cases illustrate many-to-many coverage. Solver trials and trajectory review then assess difficulty and query–test alignment. Accepted task–verifier pairs are retained; selected candidates with false positives or false negatives are repaired and revalidated.

Design Principle: Interdependent Specifications
Integrating rich specifications into coding tasks requires organizing how requirements relate to one another, rather than merely accumulating them.
In our initial synthesis attempts, we observed that when relying solely on specification count, the synthesized tasks remained trivial: language models achieved high success simply by satisfying each requirement in isolation.
This observation motivates distinguishing
additive specifications
, whose requirements admit largely separate decisions, from
interdependent specifications
, where a choice made to satisfy one requirement constrains the feasible options for another.

2.3
Task Synthesis
To reflect real-world developer requirements, we extract specification seeds from open-source repositories by mining commit histories, issue discussions, and pull requests.
After filtering out conversational chatter and raw code fragments, normalized deduplication yields 104,182 candidate specification units across six natural languages.
These seeds inform a compact specification reference containing examples, definitions, and boundary guidance for task synthesis.
Given a repository
ℛ
\mathcal{R}

It combines complementary requirements, anchoring them to the same state transitions or core components so that satisfying one requirement constrains the implementation of others.
For instance, a task may couple input validation, transactional rollback, and backward compatibility for existing readers, ensuring that satisfying any single requirement in isolation still violates the broader contract.
The agent iteratively drafts the task request

These tests map flexibly to specifications, allowing multiple checks to validate a single requirement or an integration test to cover several obligations simultaneously.
Throughout this process, the agent executes generated tests directly in the repository and refines them based on runtime feedback.

We qualitatively review unsuccessful attempts to examine implementation errors in satisfying task specifications. We identify two main error patterns: (1) patches contain code or tests targeting a specification, yet their behavior still violates it. 4
Related Work
Coding Data Synthesis.
Prior work constructs coding tasks from source code, repository changes, and agent feedback.
Magicoder
(
Wei et al., 2024
)
generates coding problems and solutions from open-source code snippets, while KodCode
(
Xu et al., 2025
)
draws on programming exercises, algorithm implementations, and library documentation.
At the repository level, R2E-Gym
(
Jain et al., 2025
)
derives tasks from commits through test generation and back-translation, SWE-smith
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
modifies working code to create repair tasks, and SWE-Flow
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
uses unit tests and runtime dependencies to construct incremental development tasks.
Other methods expand how task content is generated: SWE-Mirror
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
transfers issue semantics across repositories, ADR
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
recombines semantic elements extracted from seed problems, and TaskPilot
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
uses solver feedback to refine jointly generated tasks, reference patches, and tests.
CodeSpecWeave
makes the coverage and interaction of engineering requirements explicit objectives of task synthesis.
Guided by developer specification seeds and repository context, it constructs tasks that require joint reasoning about interdependent specifications.
Software Specifications.
Software specifications make the behaviors and constraints of a development task explicit.
ArchCode
(
Han et al., 2024
)
organizes functional and non-functional requirements from problem descriptions, while SpecRover
(
Ruan et al., 2025
)
infers intended behavior from issue descriptions and repository context.
REAgent
(
Kuang et al., 2026
)
produces structured requirements that include root-cause analysis and proposed edits, while CodeSpec
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
constructs cross-component functional chains to guide feature development.
Specifications also structure evaluation and learning: DevAI
(
Zhuge et al., 2025
)
organizes development requirements as dependency graphs, SWE-AGI
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
evaluates system construction from standards and RFCs, and SpecCoder
(
Li et al., 2026
)
trains models to produce specification analyses and code through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
CodeSpec uses executable specifications to maintain consistency between a functional-chain design and its implementation.
CodeSpecWeave
instead uses interdependent specifications to construct the task: requirements are coupled so that the choices made to satisfy one constrain the valid choices for others.
The agent must explore the repository and develop an implementation that satisfies these requirements together.
5
Conclusion
We introduced
CodeSpecWeave
, a framework for synthesizing executable coding tasks with interdependent specifications in real repositories.
Starting from specification seeds drawn from developer interactions, a synthesis agent jointly refines task requirements and tests, while a review agent examines solutions from multiple models to identify verification errors.
The resulting training set contains 4,670 tasks across 2,865 repositories.
Reinforcement learning on these tasks substantially raises the base model’s success rate on DeepSWE-v1.1, with gains over the base model on all four evaluated benchmarks.
We also introduced
CodeSpecWeave
-
Bench
, comprising 100 manually reviewed tasks and 1,044 specifications.
Evaluations reveal substantial performance differences across agents and remaining challenges in satisfying interacting requirements.
Limitations
Our approach has three practical limitations.
First, using the synthesized tasks to improve model performance through RL requires substantial computational resources for training experiments.
Second, each task has an associated container image and runs in a Kubernetes pod.
Training and evaluation therefore require infrastructure to manage many containers concurrently.
Third, producing high-quality tasks relies on strong models and multiple rounds of filtering, which discard a large fraction of generated candidates.

Appendix A
Data Construction
A.1
Agents
The synthesis and review agents use MiMo-V2.5-Pro.

A.2
Manual review
The authors manually reviewed the 100 tasks included in
CodeSpecWeave
-
Bench
, examining task descriptions, executable verifiers, code patches generated by models, and execution trajectories.
The review focused on whether tasks reflected realistic development scenarios in their repositories, whether requirements were clear and mutually consistent, and whether tests covered the explicitly stated requirements.
They also checked whether verifiers omitted required behavior or imposed constraints absent from the task descriptions, including implementation details that could lead to valid solutions being rejected.
The authors further examined successful and failed trajectories to assess the verification results.
For solutions that passed the tests, they checked whether the implementations actually satisfied the task requirements; for those that failed, they distinguished implementation defects from verifier restrictions and environment issues.
Solutions that were close to correct but failed verification helped identify hidden constraints and problems in handling boundary cases.
The review also considered missing dependencies, environment errors, and flaky tests to reduce their influence on the evaluation of model capabilities.

Appendix D
Task Example
This task illustrates how a new feature is constrained by compatibility and boundary requirements.
It asks to change how Skycoin’s transaction builder allocates coin hours across payments while preserving its existing behavior for a single recipient.
Task
The CLI already supports building a raw transaction from a wallet through
createRawTransaction
/
send -m
, but its multi-recipient hour policy is not useful to callers: it divides recipient hours equally, can give a larger payment no more hours than a tiny payment, and can strand a recipient with zero hours when the available remainder is small. Make the raw-transaction builder allocate coin hours from the selected inputs according to the requested payments while preserving its existing transaction and wallet semantics.
For a non-empty multi-recipient request, after the normal required fee is reserved, allocate the recipient share in proportion to each recipient’s coin amount using deterministic integer rounding: the recipient hours must sum exactly to the assignable recipient share, and any rounding remainder must be assigned deterministically without depending on map iteration or randomness; when fractional remainders tie, earlier entries in the request order receive the extra hours first. If there are enough recipient hours for every output to receive one, no recipient may receive zero. When a change output is present, split the post-fee hours between recipients and change using the existing 50/50 policy (the extra odd hour goes to change), then apply the proportional allocation only within the recipient share; all unassigned hours remain on the change output. When there is no change, do not burn or discard hours merely because the change output is absent. Keep output order stable: the
to
entries remain in request order and a non-zero-coin change output, if any, is last.
Do not regress the established single-recipient behavior: its existing coin-hour cap and output values must remain unchanged. Continue to reject requests that cannot produce a fee-valid transaction, and do not create zero-coin outputs.
The requirements jointly constrain allocation, rounding, and output construction (Table
7
).
The new proportional rule applies to multiple recipients, while the legacy cap must remain limited to a single recipient.
Applying both rules to every request would violate the new allocation policy.

We identify editing and testing actions from tool names and shell commands in the main-agent trajectories.
An edit–test loop consists of one or more edits followed by a test invocation in a later turn.
Edits include source code, tests, and auxiliary files.
Within the first 40 turns, the proportion of trajectories with at least two edit–test loops changes from 44.0% to 54.7% for MiMo-V2.5 and from 47.7% to 45.7% for Flash-SFT.

Appendix F
Failure Analysis
We use a frontier agent to inspect the prompt received by the solver, its final patch, and verification output, consulting test implementations and tool records where needed.
We first establish whether the prompt explicitly requires the failed behavior, then inspect the corresponding implementation and the execution evidence for its violation.
Figures
9
and

illustrate error patterns (1) and (2) from Section
3.1.1
, respectively.
Failure pattern (1): incomplete enforcement.
The SimpleX patch in Figure
9
includes link recognition and punctuation handling, and the agent’s probe recognizes a parenthesized URL.
However, a URL following
See(
remains plain text in the final evaluation.
The targeted boundary requirement therefore holds only in some input settings.
Failure pattern (2): interacting requirements.
The Iroha patch in Figure
10
addresses both signature union and state isolation.
Transactions are cloned on insertion, but a whole-state copy retains shared transaction objects.
Adding the required signature through the copy also changes the original.
The same update therefore fulfills the merge requirement while violating isolation.

The patch includes link recognition and punctuation handling, and the agent’s probe recognizes a parenthesized URL. Yet a URL following the text prefix remains plain text in the final evaluation. The patch addresses both signature union and state isolation. After a whole-state copy, however, both states share a transaction. The update adds the required signature to the destination transaction while also changing the original, violating isolation. Thus the same update fails to satisfy both requirements together. The original-state count is measured by the verifier.

article.headline: 以相互牵制规范合成编码任务与基准
article.lede: CodeSpecWeave 把需求设计成彼此牵制的规范，合成 4,670 个训练任务与含 1,044 条规范的基准。
article.problem: 现有 SWE 训练数据在规范数量和多样性上都不足，多强调主目标而忽略接口兼容、状态一致与错误处理等约束，智能体训练后仍难以应对真实仓库中的复杂约束。单纯堆叠规范又会让任务退化为可逐条完成的清单，无法促使智能体进行联合推理；而验证相互牵制的规范本身又容易漏检隐藏缺陷或误拒合法实现。
article.method: CodeSpecWeave 从真实仓库的提交、issue 与 PR 中抽取规范种子（去重后 104,182 个候选单元、覆盖 6 种自然语言），由合成智能体在探索仓库的同时迭代生成彼此耦合的任务需求与可执行测试，并刻意把规范锚定到同一状态迁移或核心组件上。多条规范与测试之间是多对多覆盖，测试在仓库中实际运行后按反馈修正。随后用多个模型的求解轨迹做审查，定位假阳性或假阴性并修复、重验；最终在合成任务上做强化学习。
article.results: 在 3,067 个候选任务中，自动审查发现 2,267 个（73.9%）存在对齐缺陷；一个 14,905 任务的生成批次经难度过滤后保留 3,275 个，再经审查只通过 766 个，最终训练集为 4,670 个任务、2,865 个仓库。CodeSpecWeave-Bench（100 个任务、1,044 条规范，平均每任务 10.44 条）上各前沿智能体通过率介于 44.0% 与 74.0% 之间，最强的 GPT-6 Astra 为 74.0%，平均输出 17.2k token。强化学习后，MiMo-V2.6-Flash-SFT 的 DeepSWE-v1.1 从 54.42% 升至 62.98%、四基准平均从 60.54% 升至 67.60%；MiMo-V2.5 的 DeepSWE-v1.1 从 12.39% 升至 25.30%、平均从 44.69% 升至 50.15%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把规范密度与相互依赖度变成任务合成的显式目标，而不只是继续从 issue/PR 中挖掘任务，这提示训练数据的约束结构可能与数量同样重要。基准上不同模型之间的明显差距也说明长时程编码仍有大量提升空间。
article.limitations: 论文自陈三条局限：RL 训练需要大量算力，每个任务都要独立容器镜像并在 Kubernetes pod 中运行、需并发管理大量容器，高质量任务依赖强模型与多轮过滤且丢弃大量候选；此外基准仅 100 个任务、由作者人工审查，规模和对齐质量仍有限。
article.figure_caption_zh: CodeSpecWeave 总览：合成智能体反复查阅规范种子、探索仓库并运行生成的测试，规范与测试之间为多对多覆盖；随后用求解试验和轨迹审查评估难度与查询-测试对齐，假阳性或假阴性候选经修复后重新验证。

{surveycover}
Video Generation Meets Agent Harness
Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
Liaoyuan Fan
∗
Yuhao Zheng
∗
Dongxing Mao
∗
Hangyu Ran
∗
Siyuan Hu
∗
Weijia Mao  Rui Zhao
Weijia Wu  Guian Fang  Yanzhe Chen  Zeyu Zhu  Yuxin Jiang  Yiren Song  Yuchao Gu  Junchao Yi  Qi Hu
Dan Kong  Alex Jinpeng Wang  Kevin Qinghong Lin
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Mike Zheng Shou
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Wei Liu
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Video Rebirth National University of Singapore Nanyang Technological University Hong Kong University of Science and Technology University of Science and Technology of China Central South University University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Abstract
Abstract:
Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, in which planning, tool use, and feedback produce coherent multi-shot videos with greater control. Meanwhile, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures and can serve as interactive environments for agents. We study this intersection through the
agent harness
: the executable runtime that constructs an agent’s context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces budgets around models such as video generators. The report is organized around three directions.
First, we study agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate script and shot planning, asset management, shot production, and editing, and we discuss what the evaluation of such systems must separate. Second, we examine agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state, including designs in which a game engine or a program written by a coding agent holds the world state while the video model renders it, and where agents and world models test and improve one another. Third, we examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) for video model development: we separate revisions of a current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the procedure that produces later updates, and we identify the channels through which an improvement could re-enter development.
Across these directions, we analyze the agent capabilities that video imposes, from audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, and memory to interaction through code and computer use, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent organization.
We conclude with open challenges, including autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance and cost accounting, and evaluation that links video quality and task performance to sustained improvement of models and harnesses.
Keywords
: Video Generation, Agent, Harness Engineering, World Models, Recursive Self-Improvement
Webpage
:
https://agentic-videogen.github.io/
GitHub
:
https://github.com/agentic-videogen/awesome-agentic-videogen
Figure 1:
Video generation meets agent harness.
This report explores how agent harnesses revolutionize video generation across key areas: agentic video generation, agentic world modeling, and recursive self-improvement.
Contents
1
Introduction
1.1
Motivation
1.2
Contributions and Positioning
1
Introduction
1.1
Motivation
Video generators produce increasingly realistic, controllable, and temporally
coherent clips
[
kong2024hunyuanvideo
]
. A generator alone, however, does
not organize the decisions needed to complete a video task. A creative brief
must become coherent shots;
references must persist across scenes; takes must be inspected; edits must
preserve what is correct
[
huang2026vimax
,
vista2025
]
. Interactive
video must also support continuing actions grounded in observations, not
just a finished clip
[
gao2026lingbotworld2
]
.
These requirements motivate a transition from video generation
to agentic video generation: a goal-directed process in which generated results
inform subsequent decisions. An agent can revise a plan, retrieve a reference,
select a tool, or localize a failure in response to actual outcomes
[
li2026videogenagent
]
.
Agentic video generation denotes a system-level perspective, not a new generator
architecture: the video model provides synthesis or predicted transitions,
while the agent makes consequential choices around those capabilities.
Video couples these choices over time. References affect later shots
[
chen2026cinecrew
]
,
actions change subsequent observations, and local repairs can disrupt
temporal consistency elsewhere. Plausible footage may still violate a
narrative requirement or fail to realize an intended action, so a quality
score alone rarely specifies what to do next
[
liu2024videogenerationevaluation
,
ding2026playworld
]
. Effective control
requires connecting observations to localized decisions while maintaining
project or interaction state and accounting for generation cost.
The development from large language models (LLMs) to agents offers a
foundation for this control. Rather than only generating a response, an
LLM can operate within a cycle of reasoning, tool use, and observation,
as demonstrated by ReAct
[
yao2023react
]
. Planning and memory extend
this cycle to tasks requiring multiple decisions
[
weng2023agents
]
.
Making these capabilities operational requires an agent harness:
the executable runtime around the model that constructs its context,
exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions
and budgets
[
weng2026harness
,
ning2026code
]
(Section
).
For video generation, the harness is where a creative brief or an
interactive goal becomes executable operations on generators, editors,
and world models. The central question shifts from generating a good
clip to reliably completing a video
task through feedback. Agentic video generation and video world-model interaction are two
concrete settings. A further question is whether experience from these tasks
can improve the system that will perform future tasks.
Figure 2:
Agent involvement across three directions of video generation.
Representative works branch from a shared video generation foundation into
agentic world modeling, agentic video generation, and development toward
recursive self-improvement (RSI). These directions connect video models to
sustained world interaction, coordinated production, and the improvement of
models and the agent harness. Vertical position reflects increasing agent
involvement, from No Agent through Agent Assistance and Agent Guided
Improvement to Self Improvement.
Feedback changes different objects at different timescales. Prompt revision
or take replacement targets the current artifact
[
vista2025
]
;
retaining a skill targets subsequent tasks
[
wei2026videoweaver
]
;
updating a dataset, critic, or generator targets later model
versions
[
liu2025videoalign
]
. These outcomes
should not be conflated: effective repair of a current video does not by
itself establish improvement in future capability.
Beyond repairing individual outputs, context engineering considers
how instructions, retrieved evidence, memory, and execution records are
selected and organized for subsequent decisions
[
weng2026harness
]
.
Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), for example, accumulates and revises a
structured context from execution feedback rather than updating model
weights
[
zhang2025ace
]
. Such work shifts attention from a current
response toward reusable knowledge, while leaving open whether the
mechanisms that construct and update that knowledge can themselves improve.
Recent work on automated research extends these ideas to model
development. The AI Scientist links idea generation, coding, experiments,
and reporting
[
lu2024aiscientist
]
;
autoresearch
runs a bounded
loop of training code modification, experimentation, and validation-based
acceptance
[
karpathy2026autoresearch
]
. These workflows connect proposals
to empirical feedback, but automating a fixed experiment loop is not the
same as improving the loop itself. Research on self-improving agents,
exemplified by the Darwin Gödel Machine and Regularized Recursive
Self-Improvement (RRSI), explores changes to the
agent’s own code or harness
[
zhang2025dgm
,
xia2026rrsi
]
.
Such work motivates examining the processes that generate and validate
subsequent improvements.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) asks whether a system can improve
the procedures that produce further improvements
[
chen2026surveyr04
,
duan2026surveyn21
]
.
Video-specific targets include failure diagnosis, data collection,
supervision construction, update
selection, and candidate validation. Repeating a fixed collection-and-training
pipeline is iterative improvement. The recursive direction additionally
allows evidence to revise that pipeline, changing how a later round discovers
and addresses weaknesses.
An agent harness provides an executable surface for this direction.
Its context construction, tool orchestration, memory, testing
workflow, and update-selection rules can be inspected and, where authorized,
revised
[
weng2026harness
]
. This does not make every harness
self-improving: a revision must be retained and independently evaluated on
later tasks or improvement rounds under stated resource constraints
[
xia2026rrsi
]
.
Existing video research supplies parts of this connection: feedback can
revise reusable production skills
[
wei2026videoweaver
]
, uncertainty can
guide data acquisition for adaptation
[
savov2025autoexplore
]
, and
validation can govern critic renewal for later training
[
yang2026dualipo
]
. These are
building blocks rather than evidence that one system has completed the full
RSI loop. Our survey therefore connects three questions: how harnesses
organize agentic video generation, how they support video world-model interaction,
and how they may drive video-generation development toward RSI. The first
two establish task execution and sources of experience; the third examines
persistent capability and the procedures used to improve it.
Figure
2
maps representative work from a shared video
generation foundation into the three directions corresponding to the questions
below.
1.2
Contributions and Positioning
The survey addresses three questions about the influence of the agent harness
on video generation (Figure
1
), each corresponding to
one core chapter.
How does the agent harness enable agentic video generation?
Agentic Video Generation (Section
) studies
how harnesses coordinate planning, execution, tool use, memory, editing, and
watermarking around shared project state, and what the evaluation of such
systems must separate. We examine how feedback changes
generation and editing decisions and how those changes affect video quality, consistency,
and efficiency.
How can the agent harness be integrated into video
world models?
Agentic World Modeling
(Section
) locates where a harness can intervene in
observation, control, execution, event organization, and state management,
and examines designs in which an engine holds the world state
while the video model renders it.
We examine how these interventions support sustained interaction, control
fidelity, state continuity, and agent-driven evaluation. The focus of this
question is how a harness enables reliable interaction with a video world
model.
How can video generation systems move toward recursive self-improvement?
Toward RSI in Video Generation
(Section
) examines how advances in video
generators and the agent harness can feed back into the process that produces
subsequent model improvements. We review foundation model improvement,
agent harness improvement, and evaluation, and identify the channels through
which gains in these components can strengthen failure diagnosis, data
curation, training, and validation in later development rounds. The goal is to identify mechanisms
and evidence needed for recursively improving development processes that
can support next-generation video generation models.
These questions connect through feedback: agentic video generation and world interaction
can expose failures, while development can turn selected evidence into
changes deployed in later tasks. Section
compares the shared
agent capabilities that support all three settings.
Differentiating Our Work from Existing Surveys
Existing surveys provide complementary accounts of video generation.
Work on spatiotemporal consistency examines generation models,
representations, training strategies, and evaluation, emphasizing the
mechanisms that maintain coherent video sequences
[
yin2025spatiotemporal
]
.
Post-training and alignment surveys organize methods for adapting video
generators to human intent, including supervised fine-tuning, distillation,
preference optimization, and inference-time adaptation
[
li2026videoposttraining
]
.
Evaluation surveys examine perceptual quality, semantic fidelity, and
alignment with user instructions
[
liu2024videogenerationevaluation
]
.
Together, these accounts explain how video models are built, improved,
and assessed.
More directly related to our system perspective, agentic visual generation
surveys organize the conditioning, execution, and adaptation decisions
available to a controller across visual modalities
[
huang2026agenticvisual
]
,
or study autonomous multimodal content creation and the construction of
stateful artifacts
[
xu2026ags
,
wang2026artifactcreation
]
. Wu et al. place agentic generation and world-modeling generation on a single
capability ladder of visual generation
[
wu2026visualnewera
]
.
World model surveys characterize predictive and simulation capabilities
across domains, focus on action conditioning, memory, and responsiveness
in sustained interaction
[
chu2026agenticworldmodel
,
liu2026interactiveworldmodel
]
,
or treat world models as interactive proxies that supply feedback to
continually improving agents
[
yang2026quovadis
]
.
Harness surveys analyze the execution layer around text and coding
agents
[
ning2026code
,
guo2026harnessdesign
]
.
Surveys of self-evolving agents and RSI examine evolutionary targets,
adaptation stages, and feedback loops across general AI
systems
[
gao2025surveyr02
,
chen2026surveyr04
,
wu2026rsisurvey
]
.
These perspectives share concepts such as feedback, memory, and agent
control, but none of them takes the harness around a video generator as the
unit of analysis across production, interaction, and model development.
Table
1.2
compares related surveys and
adjacent studies by scope, thematic coverage (including RSI), and agent design.
Our survey complements these perspectives with a framework centered on
video generation that covers three settings in which a harness meets a video
model: as a synthesizer in production, as an interactive environment, and as
the object of development. The settings are linked through the harness:
agents organize generation and refinement, while video models provide
interactive experience that can inform agent decisions and further model
development. Where capability ladders treat agentic
generation and world modeling as successive stages of the
generator
[
wu2026visualnewera
]
, we take the agent harness around the
generator as the unit of analysis, so that one framework covers production,
interaction, and development.
Our contributions are threefold.
•
A harness-centered framework. We define a common agent–harness
execution loop (Section
) and apply it to
production, organized by workflow function
(Section
), and to world-model interaction,
organized by the interfaces through which a harness intervenes,
including designs in which an engine or a program holds the world
state (Section
).
•
An account of improvement. We separate revisions of the current
output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and
evaluators, and from changes to the development procedure. We identify four channels
through which an improvement could re-enter video development.
No surveyed system yet revises the procedure that trains and
validates the generator (Section
).
•
Evaluation requirements and open problems. We state how the agent harness
supports active testing and reciprocal evaluation of agents and
world models (Section
), what the
evaluation of agentic production must separate
(Section
),
which capabilities video imposes on agents
(Section
), and which challenges remain
(Section
).

through a unified agent-harness framework.

article.headline: 综述：智能体执行框架如何重塑视频生成
article.lede: 综述以「智能体执行框架」为分析单元，串联智能体视频生成、视频世界模型交互与递归自我改进三条路线。
article.problem: 单个视频生成器能产出越来越真实、可控、时序连贯的片段，却不负责组织完成一个视频任务所需的决策：创意简报要变成连贯镜头，参考要在场景间保持，素材要检查，编辑要保住已正确的部分。交互式视频还要求动作能基于观测持续进行，而不只是给出一段成片。核心问题因此从「生成一段好片段」转向「通过反馈可靠完成视频任务」，而单靠质量分很难指出下一步该做什么。
article.method: 作者提出以 agent harness（围绕模型的运行时：构造上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈、约束预算）为中心的统一框架，先定义通用的 agent–harness 执行循环，再分别按工作流功能组织生产侧（智能体视频生成），按 harness 介入的接口组织交互侧（智能体世界建模，包括由游戏引擎或编码智能体写的程序持有世界状态、视频模型负责渲染的设计）。在改进层面，论文把「修补当前产物」与「更新 harness 状态、生成器参数、评估器」以及「改变产生后续更新的流程」区分开来。作者据此归纳出改进结果可以重新进入视频研发流程的四条渠道。
article.results: 论文将工作组织为三条主线、三个核心问题，并提出改进可回流研发流程的四个渠道；作者明确指出，在被调研的系统中尚无一个会去修改「训练与验证生成器的流程」本身，即完整递归自我改进回路尚未被演示。作为综述，本文未给出具体数字的实验结果与基准对比，论文未给出具体数字；图 1 中的场景缩略图仅为视觉示意，作者注明不是实验结果。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「视频生成」从单模型能力问题重新表述为系统与运行时问题，为生产流水线、交互式世界模型和模型自我改进提供了同一套分析坐标。对做视频生成与智能体系统的研究者来说，这组区分（修补产物、更新状态、更新参数、更新流程）可作为评估「到底改进了什么」的判据。
article.limitations: 这是一篇立场与框架型综述，不含受控实验，框架中的组件被明确说明「特定系统不必全部实现」，因此其分类的覆盖力与可操作性尚未被实证检验。作者也承认尚无系统完成完整 RSI 回路，且缺少把视频质量与任务表现关联到模型和 harness 持续改进的评估方法。

figure.caption: {From video generation to harness-mediated world interaction.} Conditional visual generation remains the shared core. In a video world model, one-shot conditioning becomes sustained control, temporal context must support continuing state, and output frames become observations for the next decision. Around this core, the harness observes, decides, translates controls, schedules generation, and incorporates returned feedback and relevant history. The central interfaces translate controls, coordinate execution, and interpret returned observations. External memory and tracking are distinct from model-side state or context. The diagram summarizes shared, adapted, and added components; a particular system need not implement every component. Abstract
How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales?
Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly.
We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world.
In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders.
Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior.
BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models.
Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects.
Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found
here
.

Vision-Language-Action Model, Robot Data Generation

1
Introduction
Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation into policies for robotic control
[
40
,
14
,
4
,
3
]
.
As VLA models increasingly benefit from larger and more diverse datasets, an important question is whether current architectures are ready to effectively exploit large-scale language-conditioned robot trajectories.
Investigating this question requires robot datasets with controllable scale and diversity, together with evaluations that distinguish different aspects of model behavior
[
21
,
39
,
35
]
.
However, collecting diverse demonstrations on physical robots remains costly
[
12
,
23
]
, which motivates a more scalable setting for such studies.
Robotic drawing provides a complementary data regime with several practical advantages for such studies.
Starting from the same blank canvas, the agent cannot infer the requested drawing from the initial observation alone, eliminating a potential visual shortcut
[
37
]
.
Language prompts can be systematically increased in semantic complexity by composing objects, attributes, and spatial relations.
The same instruction can admit many valid trajectories that differ in stroke order, starting point, and drawing direction, this intrinsic multimodality forces model to understand the concept, rather than memorizing the action sequence.
The resulting canvases and execution trajectories make semantic, spatial, and action-execution failures directly inspectable, supporting fine-grained diagnosis of model behavior.
Drawing therefore provides a scalable setting for testing whether VLA architectures can learn complex language-conditioned and multimodal robot trajectories before scaling up costly real-world data collection.
Motivated by these properties, we introduce BURGER, a scalable benchmark and data-generation pipeline for language-conditioned robotic drawing, shown in Fig.
1
.
Our pipeline generates target sketches from natural-language prompts and converts them into robot end-effector trajectories executable in simulation and on a real robot.
Using this pipeline, we construct 132 single-object tasks and 150 compositional tasks, with 100 demonstrations per task.
The dataset spans diverse objects, spatial compositions, and trajectory realizations.
As illustrated in Fig.
2
, drawing trajectories in BURGER exhibit substantially greater diversity in the plane for a given instruction than manipulation trajectories in LIBERO
[
18
]
.
We introduce a DINOv3-based metric for scalable evaluation of generated drawings and validate its agreement with human judgments in a single-object user study.
We use BURGER to examine how representative VLA models learn from larger datasets, capture trajectory diversity, and generalize to new compositions.
The flow-matching models generally improve as either the number of demonstrations per task or the number of training tasks increases, suggesting that some existing approaches can benefit from scaling robotic drawing data.
The
π
\pi
-family models
[
4
,
3
]
can autonomously produce recognizable drawings after fine-tuning.
Beyond visual recognizability,
π
0
\pi_{0}
retains multiple modes of the drawing trajectory distribution, as shown in Fig.
2
.
We further observe that evaluated policies can generate unseen spatial compositions of familiar objects, but struggle to draw object categories absent from training.
Inspecting the resulting drawings and trajectories reveals semantic, spatial, and geometric failure patterns that are difficult to distinguish through task-success metrics alone.
We further demonstrate successful real-robot drawing after fine-tuning on 100 real-robot demonstrations alone, as well as sim-to-real transfer of a policy co-trained on 13,200 simulated BURGER demonstrations.
Although robotic drawing simplifies the contact-rich interaction and object dynamics involved in manipulation, it retains important demands on language grounding and action generation.
Following a drawing instruction requires translating object descriptions and spatial relations into long-horizon continuous actions, while the range of valid drawings and stroke sequences provides a setting for evaluating multimodal behavior modeling.
These capabilities are also central to language-conditioned manipulation, making BURGER a distinctive lens for examining the readiness and limitations of current VLA architectures in learning from larger and more diverse training datasets.

2
Related Work
Vision-language-action (VLA) models
map visual observations and language
instructions to robot actions. Recent VLAs broadly follow autoregressive or continuous
generative paradigms. Autoregressive models, such as OpenVLA
[
14
]
,
predict actions sequentially, with recent variants improving action representations,
chunking, and parallel decoding
[
13
,
24
,
29
,
32
,
20
]
. Continuous generative models produce action chunks
using flow matching or diffusion
[
17
]
:
π
0
\pi_{0}
and
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
use flow matching
[
4
,
3
]
, while RDT-1B and GR00T N1 adopt diffusion-based generation
[
19
,
2
]
. Hybrid methods such as
DiffusionVLA
[
36
]
combine autoregressive reasoning with
diffusion-based action generation. BURGER evaluates these paradigms under
multimodal, long-horizon, and semantically rich drawing data.
Benchmarking of VLA systems
has moved beyond measuring binary task success rates toward more diagnostic evaluation. Recent benchmarks evaluate VLA abilities in long-horizon reasoning, spatial and semantic grounding, robustness to scene or language perturbations, structured behavioral metrics, and memory-dependent manipulation
[
39
,
35
,
33
,
7
,
6
]
. These efforts show that similar success rates can hide different failure modes in grounding, planning, robustness, or temporal consistency. BURGER  follows this capability-oriented evaluation direction, but uses language-conditioned drawing as the diagnostic domain. Unlike goal-oriented manipulation, drawing admits many valid stroke orders, geometries, and trajectories for the same prompt. This makes the more dedicated abilities directly observable from the generated canvas and rollout trajectory.
Data scaling in VLA learning
has been studied in robot imitation learning and generalist policy training. Prior work analyzes how data quantity and data composition affect manipulation-policy generalization, including object and environment diversity, camera viewpoints, spatial arrangements, and dataset fragmentation
[
16
,
26
,
37
]
. BURGER  considers a related scaling question in a controlled language-conditioned drawing domain.
Robotic drawing and painting
have been studied primarily as a control and planning problem.
For example, Lee et al.
[
15
]
formulate robotic sketching as a deep decoupled hierarchical reinforcement learning problem, where separate policies learn stroke-based rendering and motor control from scratch.
FRIDA
[
27
]
develops a collaborative robot painting system with a differentiable real2sim2real planning environment, enabling a robot to generate paintings from high-level human inputs such as language descriptions or reference images.
More recently, IMPASTO
[
34
]
studies robotic oil-painting reproduction by integrating learned pixel dynamics models with model-based planning.
These works advance robotic drawing by improving stroke planning, motor control, and real-world execution.
In contrast, our work studies sketching as a language-conditioned VLA benchmark.

The policy is not given a target sketch at inference. Canvas observations change as strokes accumulate, while pen-lifting transitions separate disconnected strokes. The benchmark therefore involves both drawing geometry and decisions about when to move without marking the canvas.

3.3
The BURGER Dataset
To collect representative and diverse drawing trajectories, we adopt the setting
from the Google Quick, Draw!
[
10

dataset, which contains 345
object classes and millions of human-drawn sketches. We select 132 classes that
are commonly found in the real world and can be easily drawn by a robot arm. We further define 150 compositional classes by pairing two of the 100 base classes
with spatial relations. Among them, 100 classes use left-right relations, while the
remaining 50 use vertical relations such as “over” and “under”. For each class,
we generate 100 trajectories using the pipeline described above, resulting in 15,000
compositional trajectories and 28,200 trajectories in total.

The dataset is, to our

and we hope it can serve as a valuable resource for future research on VLA model

3.4
Quantifying Robot Trajectory Quality
Valid drawings can differ in geometry and stroke order, making drawing quality difficult to evaluate with image-text similarity alone. Contrastive metrics such as CLIPScore
[
11
]
measure global image–text alignment, but prior work
[
ahmadi2023robustness
]
shows that such metrics can fail to detect fine-grained errors.
To obtain a more human-aligned and fine-grained evaluation metric, we design a contrastive
feature-based evaluator trained directly on the BURGER drawing distribution. Our evaluator builds a sketch-specific metric space on top of a frozen DINOv3 backbone
[
28
]
, which allows us to score each drawing by its similarity to the target-class prototype. For compositional tasks, we separate the two objects at the minimum-connectivity boundary and evaluate their identities and spatial relation. Appendix
B.2
provides the metric architecture, training objectives, and scoring procedure. In a user study covering 10 classes, our metric agrees more closely with human judgments than CLIPScore across Spearman correlation, Kendall’s
τ
b
\tau_{b}
, and pairwise agreement. Details are also provided in Appendix
B.2
.
4
Experimental Results
Our experiments evaluate the capabilities and limitations of
VLA models on language-conditioned robotic drawing tasks in BURGER. Concretely,
we investigate three questions: (1) whether BURGER can serve as a diagnostic benchmark
for comparing VLA models across several dimensions, including data scaling, language
grounding, spatial-relation understanding, and multimodal behavior modeling; (2) whether
the benchmark can expose characteristic failure behaviors and help diagnose differences
among VLA formulations; and (3) whether policies
trained with BURGER data can transfer to real-world drawing and support closed-loop
interaction under human modifications.

Language-conditioned Generalization

We diagnose language grounding and semantic generalization across the
π
\pi
-family models along two dimensions. First, we evaluate language-conditioned
instruction following by varying the object names in the prompts. Starting from
the same blank canvas, different language instructions lead the policies to
generate different objects corresponding to the requested categories. Across
the in-distribution tasks, we observe no evident confusion between objects. In contrast, when the instruction specifies an out-of-distribution object category, the models fail to generate the
corresponding object. This suggests that the learned language
grounding is effective for the trained semantic categories but does not directly
generalize to unseen object concepts.
Second, we evaluate spatial understanding using compositional drawing tasks with
prompts of the form “draw A on the left of B”, “draw A under B”, and
“draw A over B”. Our goal is to study whether VLA models can generalize simple
spatial relations beyond memorized object compositions. For this evaluation,
policies are trained on these compositional tasks. As shown in the right-most
column in Figure
5
, VLA models can generate valid left-right and
over-under object compositions even for object pairs that are not observed during
training. For example, a policy can draw a cup to the left of an apple despite
never being trained on this specific composition. We also observe that the
policies correctly distinguish different spatial instructions. These results
suggest that the policies can generalize beyond memorized object compositions and
apply learned spatial relations to unseen object pairs.

Real Robot Results
Figure 10:
Real-robot drawing results. The first row shows robustness to camera-angle changes; the second shows visual feedback through object completion and human intervention; the third shows multimodal real-robot behaviors.
Using the real-robot demonstrations introduced in Sec.
3.3
, we fine-tune
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
directly on data collected with the Franka Panda platform. As shown
in Figure
10
, the resulting policy can reliably execute
real-world drawing tasks, demonstrating that the BURGER data-collection pipeline
can directly support real-world policy learning. The first row further shows that
the policy remains effective under changes in camera viewpoint, indicating moderate
robustness to visual observation variations.
We further examine closed-loop visual feedback through completion and interaction
tasks. Given a partially completed cup, the policy can add the missing handle. In
the bicycle example, after a human draws the rear wheel, the robot observes the
updated canvas, skips the completed component, and continues with the remaining
structure. The third row additionally shows that the policy can produce different
valid trajectories for the same drawing task, preserving multimodal behavior on
the real robot. Together, these results demonstrate visual closed-loop interaction
and multimodal real-world execution.
5
Conclusion and Limitations
We present BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark that supports scalable generation of diverse robot trajectories and fine-grained evaluation of semantic grounding, spatial reasoning, multimodal behavior modeling, and action generation.
Our experiments reveal how representative VLA models respond to increasing data scale and task diversity, while exposing distinct failure patterns beyond binary task success.
Real-robot experiments further demonstrate drawing with visual feedback, including responses to human-added strokes.
Although BURGER provides a scalable and diagnostic testbed for evaluating language-conditioned robotic drawing, several limitations remain in our benchmark.
First, our setup abstracts away many physical complexities of painting.
Unlike robotic painting systems that model brush dynamics
[
34
,
27
]
, BURGER focuses on sketch-level stroke generation with a drawing tool.
This simplification makes the benchmark scalable, but limits its coverage of contact-rich artistic media such as brush painting.
Second, the dataset may inherit biases from the automatic generation pipeline.
Our stroke-order heuristics may introduce drawing styles that differ from human demonstrations.
As a result, the dataset may not fully represent natural human drawing behaviors.

A.1
Prompting and Sketch Generation
PNG Generation.
We use GPT-Image 2
[
22
]
to generate
sketch images from language prompts. To improve generation efficiency, each query
produces a
4
×
4
4\times 4
grid of subfigures, which is later split into individual
PNG sketches. The image-generation prompt is shown in Figure
11
.
We substitute the object name into a fixed template, while optionally varying the
diversity instruction to obtain multiple minimal line-art candidates. The
generated grid image is subsequently split into individual PNG sketches.
Prompt sent to the image generator:
Create one image containing exactly 16 ultra-simple black
line-art
<object>
icons arranged in a clean
4
4
by
4
4
grid.
Each cell contains one centered icon with generous white space. All icons
must be recognizable as the same object category, and their basic outer
shape should remain mostly consistent. Every icon should still look slightly
different through small pose, size, angle, or detail changes.
Important view constraint: regardless of pose or angle, the object’s
front/main recognizable face must be mostly visible. Avoid rear views,
back views, extreme side views, hidden fronts, heavy occlusion, or
cropped-off main faces.
Make diversity come from combining several simple differences, without adding
line complexity. Use clear size variation across the grid, but keep every
icon isolated and easy to cut out. For animals, combine pose, slight
front-facing angle, head direction, tail/ear shape, and body proportion changes.
For objects and still lifes, combine front-facing orientation,
silhouette, placement, proportion, and one tiny detail change.
Use these variation types: small silhouette differences, slightly different
sizes, small pose or action changes for animals, small orientation or placement
changes for objects and still lifes, slight viewing angle changes, and one
tiny contour/detail change.
Avoid repeating the same design twice. Do not create very different
object types, complex shapes, dense internal lines, realistic texture,
horizontal compositions, extreme tall shapes, extreme wide shapes, and extra
props.
Hard line-count constraint: each icon should be composed of only 5 or 6
total simple strokes/lines whenever possible. Use only the outer contour
plus at most 1 or 2 tiny internal detail lines. Avoid many details, many
small marks, texture, shading, filling, decorations, dense internal
lines, or line-heavy patterns. Each icon should be a clean minimal
outline, easy to cut out, with a compact simple shape. Black lines only,
white background, no color, no shading, no filled areas except tiny solid
black dots used only for animal eyes as specified below, no text, no watermark,
no extra objects. Each icon should fit comfortably inside an imaginary square
cell with similar margins on all sides.
Category-specific rules: For animals, always draw the full whole body in
each cell—never head-only, face crop, or partial-body views; every
animal must have clearly visible eyes (never omit eyes). For food, never
show bites or eaten/missing chunks; do not draw plates, bowls, or other dishware;
if the food has cream, frosting, or similar topping, keep the same topping
type and overall shape across every icon (only its scale or amount may
vary slightly). For furniture, clothing, or animals, every icon must stay
the same specific type within that category (one furniture piece kind, one
garment kind, or one animal kind—do not mix different types). For
animals whose eyes would normally be a large solid black patch or filled
black area, render each eye as a single small black dot instead. For
simple symbolic or single-form subjects with only one natural type (for example
diamond, envelope, eye, star, or heart), keep that exact same shape and meaning
in every cell—do not invent alternate variants— and create variety only through
slight rotation, tilt, mirroring, or small in-plane skew.
Output:
one PNG image containing a
4
×
4
4\times 4
grid of
minimal sketch icons.
